title: Players to watch | QB Demond Williams Jr., WR Dezmen Roebuck lead 1-dimensional Washington offense
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
Penn State will make the cross-country trip to Washington against a team that’s very similar to the Nittany Lions.

The Huskies will get their quarterback Demond Williams Jr. back on Saturday, but safety Alex McLaughlin remains questionable ahead of the game. Washington brings a much stronger defense than Penn State saw against Purdue, with the rushing defense having a little bit more success.

Here’s some players to watch for the Huskies.

Demond Williams Jr., quarterback

Williams is one of the most dangerous rushing quarterbacks in the country, and while he may not be 100% healthy, he’ll still be the centerpiece of Washington’s offense.

The quarterback has been in and out of the lineup over the last three games, playing in just two of them. He’s had to split time with backup quarterback Elijah Brown, who transferred in from Stanford after the 2025 season.

When he’s on the field and healthy, Williams has proven to be a reliable dual-threat passer, with Matt Campbell calling him “the most mobile quarterback in our conference” on Wednesday. He only has 211 rushing yards, which gets offset with being sacked 21 times, the most in the Big Ten.

His ability to break contain and get into open space is what the concern is for opposing defenses. Williams has run the ball 68 times, averaging just under 10 rushes per game. Penn State’s defense will have to be on full alert for the dual-threat quarterback, who’s essentially become Washington’s run game when he’s healthy.

Dezmen Roebuck, wide receiver

One of Williams’ top targets is Dezmen Roebuck, who leads Washington in receptions on the season.

Roebuck has 53 catches for 509 yards and three touchdowns. He’s already caught more passes in 2026 than he did in his freshman season, when had 42 receptions. While Penn State’s cornerbacks have been some of the best in the conference, it struggled against USC’s receiving core.

The Husky has had very similar success to those Trojan receivers, with his agility and route running standing out as his strength. Despite averaging just 63 yards per game, he’s part of a one-two punch with wide receiver Chris Lawson, who leads Washington with 638 receiving yards.

With those two receivers, they open up threats to keep focus on both of them, rather than one singular top target, something that has allowed them to both be successful this season.

Jacob Manu, linebacker

Linebacker Jacob Manu is Washington’s leading tackler in the front seven. Manu, however, is an undersized linebacker, and could face some matchup issues against Penn State’s big tight ends if he’s caught in coverage.

Manu has 28 solo tackles on the season, with his consistency coming together in Big Ten play. After a season-high 11 tackles against Washington State in the Huskies’ first game, Manu has notched at least five tackles in each of the last four games.

The linebacker is well on his way to having the most tackles he’s had since 2023, when he totaled 105 with Arizona before following Jedd Fisch to Washington in 2024.

He’s expected to play a big role in the game on Saturday as Washington’s middle linebacker on a defense that’s tasked with stopping a Penn State rushing offense that woke up in Week 9.

Alex McLaughlin, safety

On the back end of the defense, McLaughlin will be the player to watch if he plays on Saturday. He’s currently listed as questionable on the availability report, but played throughout Washington’s win over Nebraska.

McLaughlin’s numbers, compared to his teammates, match those of Penn State’s Tony Rojas. He leads the team in tackles with 56, has 2.5 sacks, which is tied for the most on the team, and is tied for the lead in interceptions with three.

The most important of those three picks was at the conclusion of the Huskies’ game against Nebraska. He picked off Anthony Colandrea to seal the game, as Washington scored two touchdowns within 15 seconds of game time.

McLaughlin is a player that Rocco Becht is going to have to keep an eye on in the secondary. If Becht pushes the ball down the field, there’s a strong likelihood McLaughlin is going to be one of the players in the area.

title: State College Police respond to alleged swatting incident at Mount Nittany Elementary School
author: Marek Horgas | For the Collegian
description:
The State College Police Department responded to a hoax “swatting” incident at Mount Nittany Elementary School this morning, according to a press release from the department.

The school allegedly received a “threatening phone call,” prompting a shelter-in-place protocol at Mount Nittany Elementary, Mount Nittany Middle School and Panora Village buildings, State College Area School District (SCASD) Superintendent Curtis Johnson said in an email to SCASD families and employees.

The call was immediately reported to the State College Police, who determined there was no credible threat. The call is believed to be related to hoax swatting incidents across the state, State College Police said in the release.

According to the department, the individual responsible for the call has not been identified. Out of “an abundance of caution” the police department will provide increased law enforcement presence at schools district-wide today.

The three buildings that went into shelter-in-place will remain throughout the day, according to Johnson’s email. This means that people can move freely inside the buildings, but no activities will occur outside the schools.

“To be clear, we have no cause for concern at any of our buildings,” Johnson said in his email.

This comes after school districts in Butler County, Pennsylvania went into lockdown for a “swatting incident” on September 30. In April 2025, State College Police intercepted plans for an attack on State College Area high school, which led to a new wave of concerns over school safety.

On October 22, Governor Josh Shapiro signed into law Act 75, which imposes steeper penalties upon those who make swatting calls, including having to pay back the money spent in response to the non-credible threat.

The State College Police ask anyone with information to reach out to them at (814) 234-7150, their email or through an anonymous tip on their website.

title: Lions and line dancing | Happy Valley Live’s Country Night welcomes all
author: Sophie Fried | For the Collegian
description:
State College got its own taste of southern charm at Happy Valley Live Thursday at 6 p.m.

Happy Valley Live, a Penn State-themed restaurant and music venue, hosts its very own Country Night, where customers can enjoy country music, line dancing and a mechanical bull

Inside the venue, the bottom floor is nearly entirely dedicated to dancing, allowing for attendees to get their country groove on with room to spare. In another room, the mechanical bull sits, awaiting its next participant.

Lauren Wellar has been line dancing for over a year, and she feels a strong connection to Happy Valley Live's Country Night because of the overwhelming sense of Penn State culture it embodies.

“We have a lot of Penn State proud people, alumni and students,” Wellar, a Penn State graduate student, said. “I feel like being in this room really makes us feel like we're a part of the Penn State voice and community still.”

People are welcome to arrive in whatever attire they’re comfortable in, but the line dancing regulars who attended went all out in cowboy boots and hats, with some wearing flannels too.

Kathryn Brodeur, the front-of-house lead for Happy Valley Live, has watched the establishment grow since its beginning, initially working as a hostess. She praised the work of Fawn Hosterman, the line dancing instructor, because of her ability to gradually increase the level of difficulty for dances as the night goes on.

“She's a fantastic, fantastic leader in teaching everyone line dances down there," Brodeur said. "They're very beginner friendly."

Fawn Hosterman, of Bellefonte, has taught at a handful of venues in the State College area. She said this event stands out due to how open-dance focused the night is, in comparison to other settings.

“Some of the other venues I teach at might be a lot more lessons and breaking down the dances," Hosterman said. "This one we take more requests. We only teach a couple songs throughout the night versus some of the other venues.”

Hosterman also mentioned that the Country Night draws in a wide variety of attendees and the audience shifts depending on the time of year.

“We have some regulars," Hosterman said. "But then we also have folks that are here because of the games, or they're here because they’re parents of students moving in. We have students that come and visit us. Then we have people from the hotel who stop over, so it's constantly changing.”

Hosterman encouraged people to come try out line dancing, even if it's something they may be new to or nervous about. She reminded those new to the experience that it’s ok to make mistakes or take a wrong step, and dancers should give themselves grace when learning new things.

Savannah Sollie, 21, of Murrieta, California, works at Happy Valley Live and loves to take on the dance floor during Country Night. Sollie initially started line dancing back in California, but she became a frequent line dancer when a friend of hers began teaching it.

“It’s nice because there's no cover, so it’s always open,” Sollie, a fourth-year studying kinesiology, said. “It's every week, so it's good to be consistent.”

Sollie appreciated the inviting atmosphere of the event and wants others to feel the same. She said it's definitely worth attending and those who decide not to come are likely to regret it.

“We're very welcoming," Sollie said. "We want to teach a lot of people, and our goal is to just get people to have a fun time and get people out on the floor and have them come back.”

title: Is Cam Wallace’s breakout here to stay? | The 107k Podcast
author: The Daily Collegian Football Staff
description:
On this week’s episode of “The 107k Podcast,” co-hosts Lexie Linderman, Andrew Deal and Andrew Mercer discuss Penn State’s rushing performance in its first Big Ten win over Purdue and whether that success is sustainable moving forward. They specifically touch on Cam Wallace, who ran for 135 yards and a touchdown in the victory, debating if he can be the No. 1 running back moving forward. The crew then touches on wide receiver Chase Sowell’s status for Saturday’s matchup against Washington and how his availability will prove critical in this matchup. Finally, our writers briefly preview the contest and give their score predictions.

title: Shanghai Ballet’s ‘Giselle’ captivates with movement, passion
author: Ava Troup | For the Collegian
description:
Shanghai Ballet’s rendition of “Giselle” captivated Penn State audiences on Thursday night, diving deep into the meaning of love through music and motion at the Eisenhower Auditorium.

For the first time in five years, Shanghai Ballet, one of China’s leading ballet companies led by Artistic Director Xin Lili, graced North America.

“Giselle,” first performed in 1841, is the tragic story of a young girl who loves dance and unknowingly falls in love with a nobleman, Count Albrecht. The girl, Giselle, originally believes he is a villager like herself. Their love story continues to develop until Albrecht’s true identity as a nobleman is revealed, and the shock weakens Giselle’s already delicate heart, resulting in her death.

The ballet wordlessly and effortlessly navigates themes of passion, betrayal and how far people will go for those they love.

Prior to the start of the event, the audience filled the auditorium with energy and excitement for the show to come.

As a State College resident and previous dancer, Cora Martz was thrilled to see the ballet, as it reminded her of her past passion for the craft. In attendance with Martz was Penn State alumna, Jennie Hampton, who said she read about the company and heard great reviews.

“For me, it was a cultural event that was very close to my house, so I’d be crazy not to take advantage of it,” Hampton said. “I do love stories where the lover falls in love with the peasant girl, and he's trying to hide himself. It’s like storybook stuff.”

Penn State student Maddy Washburn said she was drawn to the show by her love for the performing arts.

“My roommate said it was going to be really sad, so I wanted to see all the emotion behind it and see how it affects me personally,” Washburn, a second-year studying chemistry and secondary education, said. “I just want to sit here and be entertained, and have a good time.”

Leah Shope, 26, of Altoona, Pennsylvania, used the performance as a way to return to her roots.

“I used to be a ballet dancer, so getting to see it again holds a special place in my heart,” Shope, a jeweler, said. “I’m very impressed with the company and very impressed with the show so far and the music.”

Dwaina Thomas, a graduate student, felt strongly impacted by the performance and said that students should try to attend a ballet when they have a chance.

“I thought it was absolutely amazing,” Thomas said. “It was my first ballet, so it was nice to see the different interactions of the scenery, the costumes, the music and then the overall storyline.”

Even without the use of spoken language, “Giselle” captivated the audience’s emotion and attention, according to Thomas.

“It says a lot about the interpretation of the story,” Thomas said. “Being able to tell a whole story with just pure body language and facial expression is absolutely amazing.”

At the conclusion of the ballet, the audience showed their overwhelming support with a standing ovation honoring the company.

Shei Ramos and Amina Abdikul appreciated the engaging and impactful storyline that left audiences with a unique experience.

“I think it was very romantic and inspiring, the way the people were moving and representing the script,” Ramos, a graduate student, said. “Since it's live and they are not allowed to speak, it’s very difficult to achieve, and they were able to do it very nicely and clearly.”

Abdikul decided to read Act 1 before seeing the performance, and she was impressed by how the dancers brought the words to life.

“Performances are always better than something that I could see on TV, for example, or on screen,” Abdikul, a graduate student, said. “It’s just more emotions, and you can see all of the details in real life, and it’s brilliant.”

title: Military Appreciation Week starts Nov. 6. Here’s Penn State’s events, activities and more
author: Jackson Malenke | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State will host a series of events honoring military service members, veterans and their families from Nov. 7 to Nov. 14.

The university’s 15th annual Military Appreciation Week will include volunteer opportunities, ceremonies, activities and athletic events.

Nov. 7

Veteran Gravesite Cleanup

Volunteers will gather at Pine Hall Cemetery in State College to clean the gravesites of veterans as a community service event.

Volunteers can register for a morning shift 9 a.m. to noon, an afternoon shift from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m., or both shifts. Lunch will be provided for those participating. Registration is required.

Nov. 10

Marine Corps Birthday Celebration

The Penn State Student Veterans Organization will host a celebration honoring the birthday of the U.S. Marine Corps.

This event is open to everyone and will be held at 12:30 p.m. at the Student Veteran Center in Room 100 of the Ritenour building. The event is open to the public.

Paint with Pugs

The Student Veteran Center will host this activity from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m. Participants will follow Instructor Jackie Gianaco, of Painting with Jackie, to create a painting they can take home. The center’s staff members will bring their pugs along, too.

No previous painting experience is required; registration is required.

Nov. 11

Veterans Day Ceremony

The Penn State Students Veterans organization will host its annual ceremony at Old Main at 11:11 a.m.

In case of inclement weather, the event will be moved to Heritage Hall in the HUB. A livestream of the ceremony will be available here.

Zumba Drop-in Fitness Class

This fitness class will be held at the Intramural Building in Room 123 at 5:30 p.m. No dance experience is necessary, and an instructor will be there to guide participants.

Registration is required, and participants will need to bring their Penn State IDs.

Nov. 12

Military Appreciation Luncheon

The Military Appreciation Committee will host its annual luncheon for Penn State students, employees or community members who are veterans or are currently serving in the military.

The luncheon will begin at noon at the Hintz Alumni Center in 110 Robb Hall. Registration is required.

Trivia Night

At Antifragile Brewing in State College, there will be an evening of trivia for the appreciation week for those who are 18 and older.

Trivia night will begin at 6 p.m. No registration is required.

Men’s Basketball Game vs. Mercyhurst

Penn State Men’s Basketball will host Mercyhurst for its annual Military Appreciation game at the Bryce Jordan Center.

The game is scheduled to begin at 6:30 p.m. Additional ticket information will be available soon, according to Penn State’s site.

Nov. 13

Pickleball Tournament

A pickleball tournament will take place at the East Hall courts on campus. It’ll take place from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. at the East Courts near East Halls on University Park campus.

In case of inclement weather, the event will be moved to room 124 of the Intramural Building. Register is required, and can be completed here.

Nov. 14

Military Appreciation Tailgate

The annual Military Appreciation Tailgate will begin three hours before kickoff of Penn State’s game against Minnesota. The event is open to military service members, veterans and their families, and will include food, family friendly activities and special guests.

Tickets to the game are not required for entry to the tailgate, but participants must show proof of military service.

Military Appreciation Football Game

Penn State will host Minnesota at Beaver Stadium for its annual Military Appreciation game. It will recognize service members and veterans through in-game tributes and acknowledgements.

Service members and veterans also have the opportunity to participate in an on-field American flag unfurling ceremony, which requires a separate registration and ticket to the game.

It’ll take place at 7 or 7:30 p.m; the exact time will be announced closer to the game.

title: Dressed in green among Navy blue, Penn State Marines say the corps ‘creates brothers for life’
author: Taylor Gottfredson | For the Collegian
description:
At around 5 a.m. Monday, most students hadn’t yet stirred for their morning classes, so campus was relatively barren — save for the some 150 Naval Reserve Officer Training Corps (NROTC) students already having begun their day.

Most of them are dressed in dark blue, with the word "Navy" written across their backs. But a handful are adorned in green as they run six miles, then take some more laps and do core exercises before the sun peeks behind Central Pennsylvania’s mountains. They’re looking to serve in the United States Marine Corps.

Just last year, the Marines Corps celebrated 250 years since its creation. Established on Nov. 10, 1775, Gunnery Sgt. Nicholas Nicholas Sangastiano, 32, of Newark, New Jersey, said it's a big mark, given its among the smaller forces of the six branches comprising the U.S. Military.

Sangastiano has been serving in the U.S. Marine Corps for 14 years. He enrolled in Penn State's NROTC program to pursue a business management degree and is on track to graduate in spring 2028.

"We do the most with the least. We are the first in, we're there the longest and we leave after everyone's gone,” Sangastiano said. “It's because of all of the Marines who have come before and have left that, you know, high physical, moral standard.”

There are usually two fleet weeks: one on the West Coast and one on the East Coast. Last year, however, the Marines returned to land multiple times over several months for the special commemoration, according to Sangastiano, which consisted of various events and the Marine Corps Birthday Ball.

Sgt. William Skiles, who has served in the corps for seven years, said it’s remained a steady standing force throughout the years — making the anniversary a significant milestone.

"A lot of Marines take a lot of pride in how long that we've been around and how long we've been serving our country," Skiles, 25, of Mission Viejo, California, said.

Although the Marine Corps doesn't have the same resources other branches have, he said, it has the capacity to make do with what they do have. Skiles said it can provide its own air support, its own ground forces, its own artillery and it's “capable of sustaining our own force.”

He said it’s a very independent force, but added that there’s still a strong sense of camaraderie for those serving in it.

"I think that's actually one of the reasons why I'm still a Marine," Skiles said. "It creates brothers for life. I've made best friends. Like, I definitely have my whole groomsman lined up already."

Similarly, Gunnery Sgt. Washington Erazo, who has served in the corps for 16 years, said it doesn’t have the “manpower” other branches have. But it does “more with less," he added.

And Erazo, a fourth-year studying organizational leadership, also said there’s a strong sense of brotherhood behind the corps.

"If I were to talk to you and you were one of my Marines, I wouldn't care where you came from,” Erazo, 33, of Orlando, Florida, said. “It doesn't matter — like, the walk of life you had before that. Now we're here, you and I are here and we have this one task to accomplish… I'm going to have your back and you're going to have mine.”

title: Rehearsal to performance, Bounce Dance Organization sets stage for students to bond, grow as group
author: Isabella Gearhart | For the Collegian
description:
Last semester, Doni Anderson was in search of a creative space on campus, so she joined Bounce Dance Organization, hopeful it’d fulfill her artistic streak. It lived up to her expectations: Her time with the group has helped her discover abilities she hadn’t recognized before, she said, and she’s now the group’s showcase manager.

Through a mix of dance performances and cultural expression, Bounce Dance Organization offers members a space to develop their skills and find a likeminded community. It was founded in 2015 as Penn State’s first Asian-based dance group, but through the years, it evolved to draw dancers from every background to practice hip-hop, jazz, funk and K-pop together.

Anderson, 24, of Detroit, Michigan, serves as Bounce’s showcase manager. She helps coordinate preparations for its showcase, including selecting music, organizing forms and managing technical details. Over time, she’s become more confident in her skills, she said.

“It's really nice to be able to see how I've grown in different avenues,” Anderson said.

Daniela Collins, 20, of Dallas, Texas, said her interest in dance sparked during her freshman year. As a self-taught dancer, she wanted to expand her experience. She was interested in taking more classes and learning different styles upon coming to Penn State, which is how she wound up auditioning for Bounce.

“I’ve done their workshops, and I’ve been a guest performer in their showcase since my freshman year, but this is officially my first year that I joined,” Collins, a fourth-year studying anthropological science and Spanish, said.

Autumn Mink, 21, of Pittsburgh, had heard many positive things about the group. This, compounded with her love for dance, led her to join.

Mink said one of her favorite parts of being involved has been the friendships she’s developed with other members. She added that she’s become a more well-rounded individual.

“Having the experience of being around different girls has made me treat my life differently, like my major or how I approach new relationships with people,” Mink, a third-year studying cybersecurity analytics and operations, said. “I feel inspired by them to work hard at everything I do, just like how hard they work in this club.”

Mink encourages students who are considering joining to take the chance and not let nerves hold them back.

“Give it your all, it’s a very non-judgmental area because we all know that we’re there for fun," Mink said. "Everyone is super friendly."

Anderson said the variety of the organization’s dance styles and forms allows members to explore different forms of movement while celebrating the cultures and communities tied to them.

The organization also has a connection to Asian cultural dance groups at Penn State. Anderson said Bounce was established as the first Asian-based group in 2015. The organization has since helped shape the space Bounce occupies within the university’s dance community.

The diversity of dance backgrounds within the organization also creates opportunities for members to learn from one another. Collins said some dancers have classical training and ballet experience, while others, including herself, developed an interest in street dance style independently.

Collins said the collective creative environment is one of the most rewarding parts of being involved in Bounce.

“I made a good handful of friends when I joined,” Collins said. “Bounce makes a deeper connection because rehearsals always take time. Sometimes they’re long hours, sometimes they’re frustrating hours. There’s always this fulfilling sense of accomplishment of being able to put on a show together and create something together.”

“It's really nice to be able to see how I've grown in different avenues,” Anderson said. “Whether through making friends or just gaining more confidence overall.”

Adela Zhang, 20, of Hong Kong, serves as the organization’s vice president as well as the secretary. After several senior members graduated, Zhang decided to take on additional responsibilities to help maintain the organization.

She said it’s been very satisfying being able to get the organization to receive funds from Penn State that go toward their showcases.

“I really love this work, so I want to be able to keep helping everyone,” Zhang, a third-year studying communication sciences and disorders, said.

title: How No. 7 Penn State women's hockey currently fares
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s season has been interesting thus far, to say the least.

Coach Jeff Kampersal's squad is currently 9-3 with two early-season losses to No. 1 Ohio State and a 5-4 overtime upset loss to Syracuse. After a 2-3 start to the season, the Nittany Lions have caught fire with three straight series sweeps against Lindenwood, St. Lawrence and RIT, resulting in a seven-game winning streak.

With a week off of play, here’s where the blue and white stand going forward.

What changed?

The glaring thing that stands out during the Nittany Lions' recent stretch of games has been the defensive consistency.

After allowing 13 goals through its first five games, the Nittany Lions blueline has only surrendered six goals throughout their seven-game win streak, recording four shutouts during that stretch. This shows as a significant improvement in the defense’s ability to keep opposing offensive units off the scoreboard, even as the blue and white get deeper into its AHA slate.

Competing goalkeepers Maddy Campbell and Morgan Stickney have seemed to push the improvement of the defense as well, with the two combining for a .927 save percentage through the team's first 12 games. Kampersal not only has talent in between the pipes, but options going forward.

The blueliners have also contributed massively offensively for Penn State during this stretch, being led by Sophie Morrow, who has 13 points through 12 games as the Nittany Lions’ third leading scorer.

Morrow's game has really taken a step up after a freshman year where she had 16 points in 39 games. So far, the sophomore has collected two AHA Defender of the Week honors paired with a Defender of the Month nod. The Darien, Connecticut, native has begun to anchor a new-look Penn State defensive unit which was

Another standout on the backline has been sophomore Danica Maynard, who has had three goals and five assists for eight points through the Nittany Lions' first 12 games. The defender also currently has a +10 plus/minus, which is tied for the team lead with first-year Kylie Amelkovich.

What's working offensively

While Penn State has found defenensive consistency, its offensive production has been just as integral to its recent success. The Nittany Lions have averaged 3.25 goals per game during their winning streak, with breakout true freshman Sofia Ismael leading the way.

Ismael is currently the team's points leader with 16 through her first 12 games, recording six goals and 10 assists thus far. The St. George, Ontario native has taken the AHA by storm after an impressive junior hockey career with the Etobicoke Jr. Dolphins, recording 171 points in 125 games.

Ismael has proven that she has the potential to become one of the program's next great players. While Ismael has emerged as the Nittany Lions' leading scorer, Penn State's offensive success hasn't been defined by one player. The blue and white has received several contributions from players in its lineup. Mikah Keller and Abby Stonehouse both also have double-digit points this season as well, showing that Penn State isn't reliant on Ismael.

Co-captains Grace Outwater and Stonehouse have been uber important to the attack thus far, combining for 23 points. Outwater has tallied eight goals and one assist for nine points, while Stonehouse has tallied 14 points with seven goals and seven assists. Outwater's ability to find the back of the net, paired with Stonehouse's playmaking, has given the Nittany Lions another level of reliable scoring, helping create more opportunities.

What's the ceiling?

With Penn State recently clicking offensively and defensively, the main question now is how far the team can go this season. From current USCHO rankings, Penn State will play four more ranked teams this season, including matchups against No. 2 Minnesota and No. 15 Boston College in the D1 in DC tournament, along with two games each against No. 5 Princeton and No. 14 Cornell.

This upcoming stretch will provide another test for a Nittany Lions team that played No.1 Ohio State well earlier this season, allowing them to compete against some of the nation's best, potentially being able to move up the rankings before the AHA tournament, with the ultimate goal being to make the Frozen Four yet again.

Penn State will need to carry its recent defensive success against some of the nation's best. The Nittany Lions have shown they can score in bunches, but maintaining that production against stronger defensive units will be another challenge.

Continued contributions from players like Ismael, Outwater, Morrow and Stonehouse will be important, while the goaltending duo of Campbell and Stickney will need to remain consistent.

If the blue and white can maintain defensive discipline while also continuing to receive production throughout its lineup, it has the formula to make a run in the postseason.

title: Penn State women’s basketball to take on Cincinnati, Dayton
author: Sienna Pearce | For the Collegian
description:
In a few days, the Lady Lions will pack their bags and travel to Buckeye State to face their next opponents.

This Saturday, the blue and white will face the Cincinnati Bearcats at 2 p.m. in the Fifth Third Arena. On Monday, the Lady Lions will then head to the UD Arena to face the Dayton Flyers at 7 p.m.

Penn State

Penn State entered a rebuilding season after hiring a new head coach, program alum Tanisha Wright, a former WNBA player and coach. New transfers such as Devyn Quigley and Petra Božan also joined in an attempt to rectify the Lady Lions’ 11-18 overall record last season.

In its season opener on Monday, the blue and white allowed the Cleveland State Vikings to scrape by with a 62-61 win in Happy Valley.

However, the Lady Lions still remained competitive. Sophomore guard and Vanderbilt transfer Ava Black was a standout, earning 17 points and 10 rebounds for Penn State. The Lady Lions nipped at the Vikings’ heels at the half, down only two points at 27-25.

Stakes ramped up after sophomore guard Skylar Durley managed an impressive quick turnover and gave Penn State the ball back with seven seconds remaining.

The Nevada transfer and reigning Mountain West Freshman of the Year finished her Lady Lions debut with eight points and five steals.

“I think she’s definitely shown that throughout the time she's been here that she has a competitive edge and that competitive spirit,” Wright said.

But tables turned when Cleveland State guard Macie Taylor missed both of her free throws with four seconds left on the clock. Despite having the ball, the blue and white failed to take advantage of the opportunity to score and fell short of a victory.

Wright still has faith in her players’ abilities moving forward in the season.

“I look to all of them to be leaders on the court because they all bring something different to the table,” Wright said. “They all have different skill sets that we need as a team.”

Cincinnati

The Bearcats ended their season last year with an 11-20 overall record under head coach Katrina Merriweather.

Things are looking up as Cincinnati started its season off on a high note, clutching a 66-58 win against the East Texas A&M Lions on Wednesday in the Fifth Third Arena.

The Bearcats came out with a bang after sophomore Caliyah DeVillasee managed a fast-break layup in the first quarter, giving Cincinnati the advantage. They carried this momentum through the quarter, earning a 15-9 lead.

The Lions pushed back by scoring seven straight points in the third quarter to take a 45-43 lead. However, the Bearcats didn't let this faze them. They earned six consecutive points in the fourth quarter, sealing their victory.

DeVillasee finished with 15 points while Amber Bullard led the game with eight rebounds. The Bearcats finished 0-for-7 from three in their victory.

Dayton

Last season, the Flyers finished 17-14 overall under head coach Tamika Williams-Jeter. Similar to Penn State, Dayton is entering an experimental season by adding five new players to its program.

Senior transfers Cori Allen and Sophie Swanson bring Power 4 experience to the Flyers. Other Dayton newcomers include freshmen London Johnson, Brooke McLeod and Milee Smith.

Dayton will begin its season with a matchup against the Illinois State Rebirds on their home turf at UD Arena on Thursday at 7 p.m.

title: Penn State vs. Washington preview | Seattle forecast, scouting reports ahead of Saturday’s clash
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
Penn State’s annual trip to the West Coast is here, as the Nittany Lions are headed to Seattle to take on Washington at 3:30 p.m. ET, 12:30 p.m. PT.

The Huskies visited Penn State in 2024 for the White Out, marking their first-ever visit to Beaver Stadium. The Nittany Lions will now return the favor with their first trip to Washington since 1921.

It’s been a one-sided series, despite the limited number of matchups, with Penn State holding a 4-0 advantage, two of which are bowl wins.

This year, both teams have struggled on the offensive side of the ball at times, but the Huskies have snuck out one more win compared to the Nittany Lions, sitting at 5-3 after a comeback win over Nebraska.

Here’s what to expect on Saturday, from weather conditions to a scouting report.

Forecast

There is a good chance for some light Seattle rain during the matchup, with a 55% chance of precipitation in the afternoon, per AccuWeather.

The high for Saturday is 62 degrees, with a low of 51 degrees. It’ll feel like 61 during the game, and heavy cloud cover is expected.

Betting, how to watch

Penn State is the underdog on the road against the Huskies, but not by much. FanDuel has Washington as a 2.5 point favorite, while the over/under is set at 44.5 points.

The matchup is being broadcast on Fox Sports 1, while tickets are available on Ticketmaster for as low as $46.74.

About Washington

Washington’s starting quarterback, Demond Williams Jr., has been dealing with injury the last few weeks. Coach Jedd Fisch confirmed Monday, however, that Williams will play against Penn State as long as he’s healthy.

Williams is a player the Nittany Lions have seen before, as he first caught the nation’s eye against Penn State in 2024, putting Abdul Carter on skates on a rush in Washington’s 35-6 loss.

He hasn’t necessarily met expectations since he broke onto the scene as a true freshman that year, but is the best dual-threat quarterback the Nittany Lions will face this year. Williams has 1,495 passing yards, nine touchdowns and three interceptions in seven games, six of which he was the starter.

“Those types of people, you don't just stop them,” defensive tackle Keanu Williams said Tuesday. “You got to contain them, so we got to limit his running. We got to sit here and keep him in the pocket, make him play quarterback. That's the biggest thing, and that's going to be our challenge for this week because a guy like him, he's slippery.”

Washington has dealt with major injuries to its running back room, and it shows in its stats. The Huskies have just 760 rushing yards this year, and its leading rusher, Brian Bonner Jr., has 310 yards this season. Williams is second on the team with 211.

It’s the Huskies’ wide receivers, however, that create production for them. Chris Lawson and Dezmen Roebuck comfortably lead Washington in receiving yards with 638 and 509, respectively.

On the defensive side of the ball, safety Alex McLaughlin enters Saturday’s matchup as the reigning Big Ten Defensive Player of the Week after a game-sealing pick six against Nebraska.

McLaughlin has been a force in the defensive backfield with four forced fumbles, three interceptions and one forced fumble.

About Penn State

How Penn State’s offense looks Saturday depends heavily on the status of wide receivers Chase Sowell and Koby Howard. Campbell said this week Sowell is probable, while Howard is questionable.

Howard has been pretty limited at practice, according to Campbell, but also eager to get back on the field and help Penn State.

Whether the Nittany Lions have them back or not, they’ll likely try to build off the incredible rushing performance they had against Purdue last week. However, the Boilermakers have one of the worst rushing defenses in the Big Ten, so it’s unclear whether the run game actually took a step forward.

But the tight ends did, as Benjamin Brahmer led the team with 58 yards against Purdue, while Andrew Rappleyea barely trailed him with 45 of his own. Both are crucial to the success of Penn State’s passing game, especially if Howard remains out another week.

Cornerbacks Audavion Collins and Daryus Dixson are going to be critical pieces of the Nittany Lions’ defense this weekend considering Washington’s passing attack. Collins has been one of the best defensive backs in the country this year, while Dixson has taken a massive jump from Year 1 to Year 2.

The defensive line also needs to get pressure on Saturday similar to what it did last week when facing Purdue. Penn State had six quarterback hurries and one sack, and it’ll need to post a similar performance to stop Williams’ dual-threat capabilities.

title: How former Penn State men’s basketball player Dan Earl almost beat his alma mater
author: Will Horstman | The Daily Collegian
description:
Chattanooga head coach Dan Earl said he had “choice words” for his players during halftime of the Mocs’ game against Penn State on Thursday night. Earl wanted to challenge his players as they looked to overcome a 23-point halftime deficit at the Bryce Jordan Center.

Earl, a former Nittany Lion who was honored before the game, came close to achieving that. Chattanooga made it much more interesting in the second half by scoring 62 points and cutting Penn State’s lead to as little as three points, but the Nittany Lions held on for a 97-93 win.

Earl didn’t mention any technical adjustments Chattanooga made that led to the near comeback. Instead, he said he got his team to play more free after he believed they were nervous in the first half.

“You still have to be aggressive, and I think the guys just kind of let go a little bit,” Earl said. “They were like, ‘Okay, coach told us to screw it, go play hard and go attack.’ I think we were much more north-south and attacking in the second half.”

Penn State led 54-31 at halftime and held Chattanooga to just four field goals in the final nine minutes of the first half. The Nittany Lions looked to be set to cruise to victory in the second half, but that wasn’t the case.

The Mocs found many more open looks against Penn State’s defense. They shot 61.1 percent from the field, and guard Kobe McDowell-White exploded for 28 points on 10-of-11 shooting, including 7-of-8 from 3-point range.

“I think they made some adjustments to go on us quicker, attack certain matchups, put us in space, and I didn't think we guarded the ball well today,” Rhoades said. “We got to guard the ball at a high level, and we got to help.”

The Nittany Lions lacked responses to what Earl and Chattanooga were doing offensively. Even as the second half went on, shooters kept getting open, and the Mocs were also able to control the paint, where they scored 42 points.

Earl is known to lead well-coached teams. His squad played No. 11 Louisville on Monday well by only losing 84-70 after outscoring the Cardinals in the second half. So Rhoades knew a challenge was coming.

“It's an honor to have Dan Earl and his team here,” Rhoades said. “He’s a Penn Stater through and through, and he's a terrific coach. He's got a good team, and we knew we would have our hands full.”

Still, it was a concerning half of basketball for Penn State. The Nittany Lions have a much bigger roster than Earl’s Chattanooga squad, so they should’ve responded better to the adjustments.

Earl’s coaching almost led to an upset over the Nittany Lions, whom he played for from 1993-99. He was a two-time All-Big Ten selection, and he’s No. 3 on the all-time career assist list with 574. Earl also served as an assistant coach at Penn State from 2006-11.

Earl received a pregame tribute on the video boards highlighting his achievements at Penn State. Even though the result didn’t go his way, Earl was grateful for the opportunity to be a part of a game in Happy Valley again.

“This place means the world to me, and for lack of a cliché, I bleed blue and white in so many different ways,” Earl said. “Took our guys to the creamery, all that good stuff. A huge thank you to everybody at Penn State for bringing us back. Really cool for me personally.”

title: ‘The guys were pissed’ | Second-half slump nearly costs Penn State men’s basketball a win
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
When the dust settled at the Bryce Jordan Center on Thursday night, “a tale of two halves” was a phrase consistently repeated throughout postgame media. Penn State improved to 2-0 with a 97-93 win over Chattanooga, but the team’s demeanor told an entirely different story.

“When I walked in the locker room, the guys were pissed,” Mike Rhoades said. “They were quiet like they lost. And that says something about the group of guys we have and their standard for each other. I like that. We’ve just got work to do.”

After 20 minutes, Penn State held a 54-31 advantage and looked to be well on the way to another comfortable victory after beating Canisius by 30 points on Monday.

Somehow, the contest came down to the wire. The Nittany Lions allowed the Mocs to score 62 second-half points, making it a two-possession game in the final two minutes.

“That was not our brand of basketball in the second half,” Thomas Allard said. “We showed what our brand was in the first half, getting off to that lead, and we know what to work on. We're gonna come in tomorrow and Saturday and prepare.”

Much of the near-collapse can be attributed to Penn State’s poor shooting in the second frame, a trend that can be dated back to the exhibition over Drexel. Before the season, Rhoades was full of praise for his group’s three-point prowess, but they haven’t shown it so far.

In the second half against Chattanooga, the Nittany Lions shot 1-for-8 from beyond the arc after going 5-for-15 in the first 20 minutes. Against Canisius and Drexel, they shot a combined 19.4%.

“We’ve got to shoot it better,” Rhoades said. “We (haven’t shot) it well yet, but the right guys are taking the right shots. Now we’ve got to knock them down.”

A majority of Penn State’s points came from the charity stripe. The Nittany Lions shot 49 free throws and converted 43, the latter setting a new program record.

Fifth-year forward Josh Reed made 15 as part of a career-high 25-point night.

“He's our anchor,” Dasonte Bowen said. “He's the vet here. He's been here before, and it's kind of expected from him. It was a great game from him, but I think we all expect that from him.”

Penn State’s second win certainly wasn’t pretty, but with struggle comes lessons.

Rhoades noted that adversity like the Nittany Lions saw tonight is a valuable opportunity to prepare for what’s to come later this winter.

“They're high-character guys, so they're going to want more, and they're going to want to move forward and get better,” Rhoades said. “They know for us to be successful moving forward against the schedule that we have, that we can't beat ourselves, and we continue to make that a huge emphasis and work on it.”

On Sunday, Penn State will play its first Power Four opponent of the year when it takes on Pitt at the Palestra. Last season, the Panthers routed the Nittany Lions at the Giant Center, another neutral site, taking a massive 80-46 victory in Hershey.

Even with just three returners from the game, the battle between in-state rivals will carry extra significance.

“We understand what happened in the Pitt game last year,” Allard said. “We’re gonna be focused on Sunday night, and it's (all) fixable stuff, so we'll be prepared.”

title: No. 21 Penn State women's soccer falls in overtime to Purdue in Big Ten Tournament
author: Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian
description:
Facing off in St. Louis, Missouri, at Energizer Park, sixth-seeded Penn State and third-seeded Purdue competed in the final first-round match of the Big Ten tournament.

Purdue took a 2-1 victory over the Nittany Lions, sending themselves into the semifinal round and knocking the blue and white out of the tournament.

The last time the two programs met was Oct. 3 at Jeffrey Field, with the match resulting in a tough, fought 2-2 draw.

Purdue opened up play in a 4-3-3 formation, putting early pressure on the Penn State back line.

Emma Johnson gave the Boilermakers an early foul in the 3rd minute. Rosa Maalouf delivered the free kick for Purdue, but the Nittany Lion defense was able to clear the ball.

With the clearance, the blue and white found Aubrey Kulpa in transition. The junior forward gained control of a through ball and took advantage of the gold and black’s miscommunication on who was dropping defensively. Kulpa couldn’t produce, placing the ball on the outside of the net.

This scary goal-scoring opportunity for Penn State sparked a fire under Purdue’s boots. The Boilermakers were consistently creating attacking sequences in the Nittany Lion’s final third, but nothing stuck.

The gold and black almost converted in the 21st minute when Jaiden Anderson found Megan Santa Cruz at the top of the eighteen. Santa Cruz set up a shot just inside the box, but the senior midfielder’s shot was blocked by Kayleigh Herr.

Maalouf received the first yellow card of the match in the 25th minute. The junior forward pressured up too aggressively on Paige Kalal, resulting in the call for unsporting.

With Purdue consistently feeding Anderson, the junior forward located the ball again in the 33rd minute and found herself in a goal-scoring position. Anderson took the shot, but the ball couldn’t get past the Penn State back line as it was once again blocked by Herr.

Herr’s leadership kept the blue and white’s final four solid through the first 38 minutes, trying to keep the Boilermakers’ fast offense at bay.

In the 41st minute, the gold and black created their third corner kick opportunity of the night. It was ultimately deflected to Bianca Hanisch, who placed a shot in the bottom left of the net that Penn State’s Mackenzie Gress saved.

Quickly after Hanisch’s shot, Anderson once again found the ball at her feet from a long service by Zoe Miles on the right wing. The Huntington Beach, California, native struck the ball towards the bottom left of the net, her fifth shot of the match, but Gress blocked it.

With the Nittany Lions holding off Purdue’s offensive overloads, neither program could convert in the first half, sending them into the final 45 at 0-0.

The Boilermakers opened up the second half with a quick goal-scoring sequence in the 47th minute.

Santa Cruz won possession at midfield and found Anderson on the right flank. Anderson made her way through four blue and white defenders, brought the ball to her right foot, and drove a low, hard shot to the back post, right past Gress’s gloves. The gold and black lead 1-0.

The physicality level of an already intense matchup grew in the second half.

In the 54th minute, Ellie Kocher flew down the left wing, looking to make a cross into the box but was knocked down by Maalouf. Kocher went down in pain but was able to continue playing on.

During a Penn State offensive sequence in the 63rd minute, Emma Johnson drove her way into the eighteen and got a shot off. The ball rebounded off the post and found Paige Kalal’s feet. Kalal placed a put-back in the bottom right of the net, passing Grace Miller to even the playing field at 1-1.

In an attempt to clear the ball from the Nittany Lion final third, Miles pressured Bella Ayscue, knocking the junior defender down hard and receiving the second yellow card of the match for unsporting behavior in the 69th minute.

In the 76th minute, Anderson made her way inside the blue and white’s six-yard box. Despite being in a dangerous scoring position, Herr made a huge defensive play, blocking Anderson’s shot and knocking away her second-chance rebound.

Ten minutes later, Kulpa found herself in an altercation with Hanisch at the top of Penn State’s final third. Kulpa received a yellow card for unsporting behavior, the third of the match and of her season.

Despite laying it all on the line in the second half, neither team could tally the winning goal, sending both programs into overtime at 1-1.

Immediately into overtime, Anderson connected with Irene Campo in Penn State’s eighteen. Campo placed a shot on goal, but it deflected off the defense. The quick change in trajectory meant Gress couldn’t react in time, giving the Boilermakers the golden goal.

Purdue defeated the Nittany Lions 2-1 and secured the semifinal spot against Wisconsin in the Big Ten Tournament.

title: Penn State men’s basketball improves to 2-0, earns gritty win over Chattanooga
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
It doesn’t always have to be pretty, but a win is a win.

Penn State improved to 2-0 with a physical and narrow win over Chattanooga, defeating the Mocs 97-93 at the Bryce Jordan Center. Former Nittany Lions assistant coach, Penn State alum and visiting coach Dan Earl was honored pregame in his return to Happy Valley.

The Nittany Lions deployed the same starters as they did in their season-opening drubbing of Canisius. Yet that group, which got out big only a few days prior, couldn’t fight off the Mocs early.

Guard Thomas Allard got the blue and white on board early with a pair of threes and a pull-up mid-range score, which boosted it to a 6-2 advantage. Chattanooga guard Kobe McDowell-White added three downtown makes over the next few minutes, however, to tie it at 11-11.

After a whistle-heavy stretch, both squads slowed scoring until wing François Wibaut entered to catalyze the Penn State offense. The 6-foot-7 junior took it at the rack for an and-one before hitting a three in his next touch to take the lead.

A few minutes later, fifth-year senior Josh Reed got a tough putback bucket to give the Nittany Lions a 21-13 advantage, but the Mocs slowly attempted to chip away. Penn State kept trying to build a run but couldn’t gain more than a five-point lead at the midpoint of the half.

That soon changed when the blue and white’s defense prevailed in what was already a very physical game. Wibaut hit a pull-up jumper, Reed got a steal and earned points at the line, and 7-footer Ivan Jurić lunged for a ball at midcourt to force a turnover, allowing Dasone Bowen to go to the charity stripe.

When it seemed like it was all piling on for Chattanooga, Jurić swished a long-range make to push the score to 33-22.

The calls continued, as Chattanooga logged its 10th foul with still over five minutes to play until the break. Over the next five minutes, the blue and white embarked on a 16-2 scoring run, aided by trips to the line and dominant rebounding.

At halftime, the Nittany Lions led 54-31, outrebounded the Mocs by 11 and took 16 more trips to the foul line, making 95.5% of their total free throw attempts.

Penn State seemed to cool after the break, as the first two minutes of play saw only two scores, both by Chattanooga. The Mocs pounded the offensive glass to go on an eventual eight-point run before Wibaut added a fading bucket to end that skid.

Momentum, however, remained with the visitors, as McDowell-White continued to lead an offense which cut the score to 65-54 in what was another foul-heavy stretch, this time for the blue and white.

Penn State’s offense then found some life with Bowen orchestrating the attack, but it was rather fleeting as the Mocs made it a nine-point game with under 10 minutes to play. Both Wibaut and Roko Prkačin came up with big blocks, but both were called for goaltending.

With both Prkačin and Allard on four fouls, the Nittany Lions attempted to try to finish without any foul outs, as the pair was just half of the group of Nittany Lions who had three or more calls.

That fate didn’t occur down the wire until Allard got his fifth with a minute and a half to play, but luckily for the blue and white, most of the threat had been subdued by then with two-way play from Reed. Chattanooga continued to score, but the blue and white defense held and didn’t break to secure the result.

The Mocs’ McDowell-White led scoring with 28 points behind seven 3-pointers. Reed led the blue and white with 25 points, and the Atlanta native also logged five steals and five rebounds. Jurić, who had his second double-double of the season, Bowen, Allard, Prkačin and Wibaut also scored in double figures for the Nittany Lions.

The 43 free throws made by Penn State were a new program record, surpassing the total of 36 against Northwestern last season. Blue and white forward Brant Byers finished 1-of-10 from the field, with seven misses and no makes from downtown.

Up next

Penn State continues with its first game away from Happy Valley this season, taking on Keystone Clash rival Pittsburgh at the Palestra in Philadelphia. Tipoff is set for 8 p.m., and the game will stream on ESPN2.

title: U.S. Department of Justice sues Penn State over in-state tuition policy for undocumented students
author: Grace Levy | News Editor
description:
Editor’s Note: This story was updated Thursday evening to include a statement from a Penn State spokesperson.

The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) filed a lawsuit against Penn State on Thursday, alleging the university's tuition policy, which allows some undocumented students to qualify for in-state tuition, violates federal law.

The complaint, filed in U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania, names the university and the Board of Trustees as defendants.

Penn State’s policy says undocumented students, with or without DACA, can be eligible for in-state tuition if they meet the university’s residency requirements. Those requirements include attending an accredited Pennsylvania high school for at least four years and graduating or earning a Pennsylvania GED, according to the complaint.

DOJ is suing to declare the policy invalid under the Supremacy Clause and permanently bar Penn State from enforcing it, or any similar policy in the future.

Courts in Kansas, Illinois and Nebraska have ruled against in-state tuition laws for undocumented students, according to the complaint.

Penn State is aware of and reviewing the complaint, a Penn State spokesperson, Wyatt DuBois, told The Daily Collegian.

title: University Health Services urges precautions amid recent cases of adenovirus, viral illness
author: Taylor Gottfredson | For the Collegian
description:
University Health Services (UHS) is urging students and community members to take precautions amid recent cases of adenovirus, respiratory viruses and bacteria on campus, according to a Nov. 4 press release.

Cases of adenovirus, along with influenza A, rhinovirus, coronavirus and Mycoplasma pneumoniae, have been identified on Penn State's campus going into the winter season. UHS is working with the Pennsylvania Department of Health to monitor the spread, according to the release.

Although many students are healthy enough to recover on their own, those with underlying medical conditions—weakened immune systems and chronic lung or heart conditions—may be at higher risk of severe illness.

UHS encourages students to wash their hands, avoid sharing water/food, wear a mask and stay home if you start to experience respiratory virus symptoms. People may have an increased risk of contracting or spreading illnesses through travel, and UHS advises people who are sick to limit contact with others, especially immunocompromised people.

These symptoms for adenovirus can include sore throat, fever, cough, pink eye, bronchitis, pneumonia, nausea, vomiting or diarrhea. The symptoms appear similar to other viral illnesses, such as influenza.

If showing symptoms, UHS advises the best thing to do is rest, drink plenty of water, and ease with over-the-counter medication. If symptoms worsen, don't hesitate to contact a health care provider, or seek emergency care.

title: Penn State baseball unveils full spring schedule
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
As a Major League Baseball lockout looms, there are no such worries for coach Mike Gambino’s squad. Penn State announced its spring schedule on Thursday in the form of a video with the Nittany Lion.

The blue and white will begin the 2027 campaign with a previously announced three-game series against Auburn in the Bahamas. They’ll take on the Tigers, who are fresh off a trip to the NCAA Super Regionals, on Feb. 19, 20 and 21.

Penn State will then travel slightly north to the Sunshine State to face Florida Atlantic, then play a three-game set against Florida International.

Over the first weekend of March, the Nittany Lions play three previously announced games at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas. The blue and white have their work cut out for them with SEC power Ole Miss, Wake Forest and Dallas Baptist on three straight days.

After wrapping up that Amegy Bank College Baseball Series, Penn State gets just one day off before embarking on a week in Washington. The team takes on Seattle on March 9 and 10, then opens the Big Ten slate against Washington on March 12, 13 and 14.

Fifteen games after opening day, Penn State returns to Medlar Field at Lubrano Park for the first time. The Nittany Lions face Bucknell on March 17 before three games against St. John’s over the weekend. Last year, Penn State split with Bucknell, including a 9-0 home loss.

Gambino’s gang remains home for four games, a midweek game against St. Bonaventure, and then a weekend series with Michigan State.

On March 30, Penn State closes the month on the road against West Virginia. The Mountaineers bested Penn State last year on their way to their first College World Series appearance in program history.

The Nittany Lions play their next four at home, including a weekend series against Maryland and an April 7 matchup with Mercyhurst.

A visit from West Virginia is sandwiched between road conference clashes with Iowa and Indiana, then Penn State rematches Bucknell in Happy Valley on April 20.

The Nittany Lions flip the calendar to May with eight more home games. Oregon comes to town for its conference series, then it's a midweek game against Fairleigh Dickinson before another conference set against Northwestern, and they’ll wrap up the homestand with a Keystone State clash against Pitt on May 4.

Penn State heads to Piscataway to meet Rutgers on May 7, 8 and 9. The Scarlet Knights had an unremarkable 2026, but played one of the most entertaining series of the year at Medlar Field. They beat the Nittany Lions by scores of 13-11 and 4-1, and Penn State picked up a 14-13 victory.

Nonconference matchups against Rider and Marist sandwich Penn State’s final home series against Michigan on the weekend of May 15.

Penn State’s regular season comes to a close in Champaign with games against Illinois on May 20, 21 and 22.

From there, the Nittany Lions need to finish in the top 12 of the Big Ten to return to the conference tournament for the first time since 2025, when they made the semifinals.

title: ‘Be a gamer’ | Freshman WR Amarion Jackson made most of 1st collegiate start
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
As wide receiver Amarion Jackson was warming up in Beaver Stadium ahead of Saturday’s game against Purdue, he heard his name announced as one of Penn State’s two starting wide receivers alongside Brett Eskildsen.

Receivers Koby Howard and Chase Sowell were doubtful and questionable, respectively, leading up to the game and were ultimately out against the Boilermakers. So it was next man up, and the freshman earned his first career start.

“Obviously, I thought (Jackson) did a great job in terms of his opportunities,” Matt Campbell said Tuesday. “He made the most of them. I think that's a little bit of the theme of last Saturday is guys got their opportunity and they made the most of it.”

Jackson had a pair of catches for 31 yards against Purdue, the most receptions and yards of the three Penn State receivers who had a catch.

But Jackson’s impact in his first start wasn’t a shock to other players or the coaching staff. According to Rocco Becht, he “just did his job in the pass game.”

In the weeks leading up to the season, Jackson’s skillset was on display during fall camp. As Campbell said in late September, Eskildsen was banged up to start the season, which ultimately gave Jackson a chance to see more practice time.

“He was able to go in there and make some plays as a young guy, not really knowing what's going on,” Becht said. “He was able to just go out there and be a gamer, and I think that's what he's been able to do throughout this whole season.”

Jackson only contributed in two games before starting Saturday, recording a 10-yard reception in the season-opener against Marshall and a 12-yard rush against Buffalo in Week 3. While he was waiting for his moment to see the field again, he continued to grow off the field and showcase a strong work ethic.

“He's in here at 5:30 every morning catching jugs with Koby,” safety Jamison Patton said Wednesday. “Those guys work very hard together. He's talented for how young he is. He knows the game pretty well, and I think he has good size for how young he is, and he can move pretty well too.”

As those moments came and went during the nonconference schedule and practice, Jackson remained ready for his moment.

When that finally came against Purdue, Eskildsen said, “I think his poise was really impressive, and there was never a point where I was worried about him.” He said Jackson wasn’t nervous because his hard work ethic helped prepare him for the moment to step up when the team needed him Saturday.

“He always knows, and he always is doing something for the betterment of himself, which is for the betterment of the team,” Eskildsen said. “Just seeing that and how he's been able to develop and grow at such a young age has been really cool to see.”

title: Penn State Athletics announces rewards system can double a student's chances at football tickets
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
Editor's note: This story was updated Thursday afternoon to include more information regarding how many points are needed to earn an extra lottery submission.

The new Penn State Rewards system announced by Penn State Athletics in August now has a little twist.

Students can gain an extra submission into the annual season-ticket lottery for football by attending games for other teams across the athletic department.

This new system incentivizes students to see different sports and pack the stands, as many of Penn State's 31 varsity sports don't see much fan support from the student body.

Students must sign up in the Nittany Lions Mobile App.

To earn an extra entry into the lottery, students much reach 30,000 reward points by May 31, and it's only available to 10,000 students. Per the Nittany Lions Mobile App, three of those spots have already been claimed.

It costs about $130 in the app to buy that number of points.

When Penn State Rewards was announced in August, the release stated it was for both fans and students, although it wasn't clear at the time how students could benefit.

"For students, the program will provide an additional avenue to earn rewards that can enhance their Penn State experience, including opportunities related to student ticket access and the student ticket lottery," the August release said.

The rewards system was created in partnership with Playfly Sports and Uptop.

title: Good vibrations | Penn State Reproductive Justice Program hosts ‘Sex Toy Bingo’
author: Hadley Louisa-mae Milhomme | For the Collegian
description:
The Penn State Reproductive Justice Project hosted a “Sex Toy Bingo” event Wednesday night in Freeman Auditorium. Members and attendees gathered together to support sexual wellness education and encourage body positivity, all while providing safe sex resources, like grabbing a condom as they collected bingo tokens.

The event aimed to destigmatize conversation around self-pleasure and consent but also acted as a donation drive for Centre Safe, a resource center in State College that provides free, confidential services to survivors of domestic or dating violence, sexual assault and stalking.

Attendees who brought donations from the centre's list of needs, like winter clothes, menstruation products, diapers and canned foods, were given an extra bingo card. Students poured into the auditorium energized and ready to participate.

Hermione Lehosky, 18, of Pittsburgh, heard about the event through a friend last year and wanted to check it out.

“Sex is a universal thing, it’s normal,” Lehosky, a first-year in the Division of Undergraduate Studies, said. “You have to promote stuff like that.”

Between bingo games, while the winners collected their prizes, the president and other members of the club showed an educational slideshow explaining consent, contraceptive resources and more important sexual health information.

Carmelita Whitfield, associate director of community health, gave demonstrations on how to utilize different contraceptives for good, safe and consensual sex.

“We try to educate people in between the rounds, which is kind of the goal of this, to give people resources.” Nevaeh Sickles, 21, of New Jersey, said.

The Reproductive Justice Project began three years ago at Penn State, and Sickles, president, joined the organization at the very beginning.

“I was one of the very first members my sophomore year,” Sickles, a fourth-year studying premedicine, said. “It was really awesome.”

Sickles said she was excited by the turn out of this year’s bingo event and looked forward to spreading awareness of the club’s core values and mission.

The Reproductive Justice Program is a tight-knit group, welcoming any gender, major or sexuality, according to Sickles.

“It doesn’t matter who you are, where you’re from, what major you are, how old you are, it doesn’t matter,” Sickles said.

Vice President, Eloise Emel, 20, of Raleigh, North Carolina, was recruited to the organization by a previous member and was interested in joining because of the connection to her major.

“I was looking for a space that was more concentrated in reproductive justice,” Emel, a third-year studying women’s, gender and sexuality studies and psychology, said. “I think so often that people just talk about reproductive rights, which is the right to abortion and right to contraception, and those are awesome things, obviously, but I think the larger social justice framework gets lost a lot.”

Emel said events, like sex toy bingo, are important for a number of reasons.

“The more comfortable you are talking about it, the more comfortable you are going to be in your own relationship and communication with your partner,” Emel said.

Throughout the event, over a hundred attendants were loud and expressive, showing their excitement and disappointment when other winners would yell, “bingo!”

“It really, really means a lot,” Emel said. “We’re a very new club. It’s only been about three years for us. To see this club grow so much this year, and to see a big turnout for events like this, it really warms my heart that people are excited about it.”

Sickles ended the event by providing free sexual resources, including sexually transmitted infection testing and free emergency contraception at Penn State’s University Health Services.

There is also human immunodeficiency virus and sexually transmitted disease testing, birth control access and maternity services with Mount Nittany Health.

The Reproductive Justice Project already has plans to bring back the popular bingo event in the spring semester.

title: No. 11 Penn State women’s volleyball travel north for 2 ranked matchups
author: Jimmy Blair | The Daily Collegian
description:
Looking ahead to November — and beyond — the Nittany Lions have gotten their season back on track and have looked like one of the premier squads in the nation.

The blue and white currently sit at a 17-5 record and have won eight of their last nine matches, including a five-game winning streak.

Throughout this run over October, the squad took down ranked conference opponents such as Oregon, Indiana and Purdue. Kennedy Martin has continued to be one of the best players in the country, as Penn State has handled ranked opponents and put them away in three to four sets consistently.

The squad will have to continue this stretch of form, as it has two road ranked matchups this coming weekend. They’ll travel up to Minneapolis to take on the No. 19 Golden Gophers on Friday at 7 p.m. Two days later, the blue and white has a date in Madison against the No. 7 Wisconsin Badgers on Sunday at 4 p.m.

Minnesota

The Golden Gophers have had a strong season, to the tune of a 14-6 record and an 8-4 standing in conference play. Minnesota has been white-hot over the past month, putting up eight wins in nine games like the Nittany Lions, including a three-game win streak.

In their last match, the Golden Gophers swept USC away from home. Like Penn State, it's a strong team that is playing the best volleyball of its season. One thing to consider is that the Golden Gophers have fallen to ranked opponents such as Oregon and Purdue, while the Nittany Lions have consistently put squads of that caliber away.

Minnesota will have to take advantage of playing on its home floor, but will have to suppress the offensive attack of the Nittany Lions, consisting of Martin, Alexis Stucky and more. So far this season, not many squads have been able to keep up with the blue and white’s depth, let alone the high-end talent. The Golden Gophers will need to get off to a strong start and keep the momentum through the match, as the Nittany Lions have a lot to throw at them.

Wisconsin

The Badgers have been off to a very strong start this year, and are looking to keep the momentum going into the conference tournament. Despite starting 1-2, the Badgers responded with a victory over No. 3 Louisville. They have maintained strong play and currently sit at 16-6.

All six of the losses handed to Wisconsin so far this season have all been to ranked opponents. Including many of the top squads in the country such as Nebraska, Pitt, Kentucky and Texas. However, they have a total of eight ranked wins this year, which also includes wins against other top programs like the Cardinals and Florida.

This consistent play against top schools will make the Badgers even more formidable moving forward. The Nittany Lions have a chance to take a win against one of the nation's top schools in the nation on the road.

Standout freshmen Decelise Champion and Audrey Flanagan have given a boost to a rejuvenated Wisconsin team and have made them one of the most dangerous squads in the conference. Flanagan has come in as a freshman and leads the team in kills, while Champion trails in second as the only pair of teammates to have over 200 kills this season.

The matchup on Sunday is essentially a top-10 matchup against two sides who could see each other again in the Big Ten tournament. In a sense, Sunday could be a tournament preview and a big chance for the Nittany Lions to put up another high-ranked win.

title: National champion returner, Mirasola twins to headline Penn State’s top weight classes
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
There’s a week to go until Penn State takes the mat for its 2026-27 debut, and while Cael Sanderson will have a returning national champion at 197 pounds this season, there’s a big-boy battle brewing at heavyweight.

Here’s how the Nittany Lions’ upper-weight classes will shake out this season.

197

There’s no question who Sanderson will start at 197 against Bloomsburg on Nov. 12. Josh Barr will enter his junior season in the blue and white on the heels of a national title last season while compiling a 24-0 record, and will look for his second during the upcoming campaign.

Ranked as the No. 1 wrestler at 197 by InterMat, Barr was dominant at the 2026 NCAA Championships. He earned technical falls over Kent State’s Blake Schaffer and Stanford’s Angelo Posada before securing a 14-3 major decision over Wyoming’s Joey Novak and a 6-3 decision win over Oklahoma State’s Cody Merrill in the title match.

The defeat of Merrill wasn’t his first experience wrestling for an NCAA championship, though. Barr was a national runner-up in the 2024-25 season after falling to Iowa’s Stephen Buchanan in the final.

He’ll be one of three returning national champions for Sanderson this season, alongside Mitchell Mesenbrink and Luke Lilledahl.

Backing Barr up will be Mason Ellis, a sophomore out of Gurley, Alabama. He went 2-3 wrestling in tournaments as a freshman last season.

In high school, Ellis was a two-time Alabama state champion as a sophomore and junior, and he didn’t compete as a senior. He posted an 111-3 record in three seasons before joining Penn State.

285

It’s one thing to battle for a spot in the starting lineup, but it’s another to do it against your twin. That’s the situation facing Connor and Cole Mirasola this preseason.

“They’ve got to be pushing each other,” Sanderson said at local media day. "They're brothers and they care more about one another than their own success. They're both big boys and getting better and helping each other by pushing each other.”

Cole was Sanderson’s starter at heavyweight last season, where he posted a 19-8 record. He’s been ranked as the No. 6 285-pounder by InterMat going into the campaign despite not placing at last season’s NCAA Championships.

Still, there’s a chance that Connor could make a case for the starting spot. After wrestling at 197 pounds last season, he’s made the jump to heavyweight and will wrestle at the NWCA All-Star Classic on Nov. 24 against No. 7-ranked Wisconsin wrestler Braxton Amos.

Connor recently claimed a gold medal at the U23 Pan-American Championships in Lima, Peru. There, he competed at the freestyle heavyweight limit of 125 kilograms, which is about 10 pounds lighter than folkstyle’s 285-pound cap.

“He doesn't see himself as a depth guy,” Sanderson said. “He wants to be a national champion and he's right there.”

Dawson Bundy and Elijah Brown will provide depth behind the twins.

Bundy is a junior who went 8-1 last season. He battled to the third-place match at the 2026 Bloomsburg Open, but medically forfeited before taking the mat. Bundy saw no action as a freshman.

Brown, a true freshman, went 173-20 and won back-to-back state championships as a junior and senior in his four seasons at Belle Vernon High School. He was the No. 66 recruit in the class of 2026.
