title: Column | Like Dorian Gray, Penn State has a vanity problem
author: Kippi Hall | The Daily Collegian
description:
Content warning: This article contains mention of sexual assault. Resources and support are available through Penn State’s Counseling and Psychological Services.

From ranking sororities and fraternities on “hotness” to hosting Clavicular downtown, Penn State has a bit of a vain streak.

Penn State is, of course, a hub of oxymoronic youth. Still untouched by the trials of life beyond the graduation stage, we walk Pollock Road as spry and curious as children, but with the know-how of wrongdoing and independence like adults. Without a distinct check on reality, placing an emphasis on superficial status and beauty is incredibly easy.

It’s also human: We attribute personally desirable traits to those we find more attractive in a phenomenon called the “attractiveness halo,” according to a study conducted by the University of St. Andrews. How much we instinctively prefer attractive people and how far we’ll go to be beautiful ourselves is the real trap, similar to Dorian Gray.

“The Picture of Dorian Gray” was published as a novel in 1891 by Oscar Wilde, an Irish poet, as his only long-form work. The story depicts a young, impressionable man named Dorian Gray, who’s renowned for his beauty. He descends into corruption after an artist, Basil Hallward, paints his elegant portrait.

At the beginning of the novel, Dorian Gray is as innocent as one can be. More an archetype than a man, he’s described as a golden-haired, angelic creature who doesn’t fully understand the impact of his beauty.

This beauty is captured by the overwhelmed Basil, who worries his infatuation with Dorian’s looks is being treated as a thought he has “given away (his) whole soul to some one who treats it as if it were a flower to put in his coat.” The praise and adoration from Basil is only an adornment to Dorian’s continued elegance and picturesque qualities.

Outside approval is a major part of the way we perceive the good qualities of another person. Pushing aside the less-than-positive attributes in favor of tolerance due to physical attractiveness is where the trap lies, especially at Penn State.

Entire movements start on the assumption that physical prowess and status markers are king when seeking approval from others. The flock of young men and women around Clavicular, a self-proclaimed “looksmaxxer” now accused of raping a minor, only underscores the dark predisposition we have to an easy heuristic of beauty that triumphs all virtues. Without proper exposure to other perspectives, we become susceptible to this killer addiction to perfection, youth and hedonism, like the blissful Dorian Gray under the wing of Lord Henry Wotton.

Wotton consistently pushes a depraved, uncaring worldview onto Dorian, becoming the original source of his obsession with his own beauty and the depressing notion that the painting will remain gorgeous while Gray ages.

After that idea was planted in Dorian’s mind, he ends up cursing the painting’s subject to wither away while he remains young forever — the start of a Faustian bargain that damns him to moral corruption throughout the book.

Dorian’s descent into hedonistic cruelty begins when he becomes infatuated with working class actress Sibyl Vane because of her role as someone who can remain perfect as a young, tragic heroine onstage without revealing the depth and flaws of her real character. Sibyl falls in love with Dorian, calling him “Prince Charming,” which further feeds his ego and self-image as a godlike beauty.

Sibyl, feeling the full effects of real love, quits acting when she realizes how “hollow” it is in the face of true romance. Reflecting the tragic heroines Sibyl plays, Dorian breaks her heart after she makes this decision. She realizes he only liked the thrill of dating someone who changed every time she performed.

Loving or obsessing over someone for the way they boost our egos, while all too common among the emotionally immature batch of college students at Penn State, is a cruel side effect of vanity and a need to feel adored. Having someone who makes you feel like the most attractive person, who gives the thrill of novelty, is a status symbol in and of itself.

And social media gamifies it. The legions of romantic rosters on Snapchat and keeping streaks to solely increase a SnapScore adds a number to the amount of adoration we can amass online.

The only problem is the stain hurting someone for a self-esteem boost leaves on your soul: Dorian Gray’s portrait changes to a sneering painting after he hurts Sibyl. After a brief bout of remorse, Dorian pushes the matter under a label of artistic triumph and moves on, absolving him of any potential guilt.

Throughout the story, Dorian continues seeking wild pleasure without regard for the emotional destruction left in his wake, building up a reputation for being sleazy but never being rejected by society because of his unignorable, now-remaining beauty.

Disregarding the personal beliefs of a person because of the beauty or status they may exhibit is all too common today. “Pretty privilege” puts our psyches in the position to continue singing the praises of those who do or say things we’d condemn if they weren’t attractive or cool enough. This gives us weaker convictions and denies us a chance to be connected to others for genuine reasons.

“The Picture of Dorian Gray” shows us a world where it’s possible for someone to never grow old, to act out of selfishness and hedonistic aims rather than kindness and authenticity, and to disown it as a cautionary tale to avoid. In the end, Dorian has no one to reflect his shine, damned to live with the consequences of his conceit.

To upset Dorian, Lord Wotton says: “Some things are more precious because they don't last long.” I think we should celebrate the fact that the youth we have isn’t something to constantly chase.

What would happen if we looked at the growing crow’s feet at the corners of our eyes, at last year’s fashions adorning our bodies, and wound up appreciating the fleeting nature of life without trying to impress people so much? If we knew the true versions of ourselves and others instead of the most polished ones, our portraits would show someone with beauty worth capturing.

title: Keisha Lance Bottoms, Chris Pappas | Meet the candidates who made history in the 2026 midterm elections
author: Marek Horgas & Anna Nagle | For The Collegian
description:
On Tuesday, people across the United States sat with Election Day news cast on their screens as the 2026 midterm results filed in — culminating in a nationwide blue wave, with Democrats flipping both the U.S. House and Senate.

Subsequently, new kinds of representation swept in, too. The country’s first-ever Black woman governor was elected in Georgia; the country’s first-ever gay man senator took the seat in New Hampshire; and Texas, a longtime, staunchly red state shifted hues.

Here’s a look at those behind some of the country’s historic firsts.

Keisha Lance Bottoms

Bottoms won Georgia’s governor race, becoming the first Black woman governor in U.S. history and the state’s first Democrat governor elected since 1998. She bested Republican candidate Rick Jackson, securing 54.3% of votes, according to The Associated Press.

Formerly the mayor of Atlanta, her campaign focused on addressing the affordability crisis, increasing public safety, strengthening the mental health system and providing more funding for education. With her win in the historic swing state, she joins Senators Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock as Democratic leaders of the state.

Bottoms’ win was also historic as she is the great-great-granddaughter of Sheppard Peek, an enslaved man from Crawfordville, Georgia. Peek was listed among the possessions of a white man named William Peek with a value of $1,400, according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution.

“Georgia, this win is for all of us,” Bottoms said in her victory speech. “I am honored to be your 84th governor.”

Deb Haaland

Haaland, the Democratic nominee in the New Mexico gubernatorial race, was elected the first-ever Native American woman governor in the U.S., besting Republican Gregory D. Hull 57.2% to 42.8%, according to the AP.

Haaland previously served in the U.S. House of Representatives for New Mexico before serving as the Secretary of the Interior under President Joe Biden. Born in Arizona, Haaland is a member of the Laguna Pueblo tribe and a 35th generation New Mexican.

She ran on a campaign of protecting communities from ICE, improving education, decreasing crime, and lowering costs, Haaland tried to embody the struggles of New Mexico residents, a single mom herself.

“Tonight isn’t only about history. It's about our future,” Haaland said in her victory speech.

Gina Hinojosa

Hinojosa was elected the first Latina governor in Texas, one of the most prevalent red states. Hinojosa, who was elected to the House in 2017, will be the first Latina woman to serve as Texas governor, and the first Democrat to hold the Texas office since 1990.

She ran against Republican Gregg Abbott, who served as Texas’ governor for three terms. She won the vote 52.8% to 45.7%, according to the New York Times.

“I want to say something to the powerful people who have gotten very comfortable running this state,” Hinojosa said. “The voters have delivered a mandate for change, and it is change they will get.”

Abdul El-Sayed

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, was victorious over Republican Mike Rodgers in a battle for a seat representing Michigan in the Senate 52.5% to 45.5% as of 1:50 on Nov. 4, according to the AP.

El-Sayed is the first-ever Muslim senator. He ran with the slogan: “Money out of politics, money in your pocket, and Medicare for all.” He’s been a steady advocate for universal health care and a wealth tax on billionaires.

His campaign had to combat attacks on the basis of El-Sayed’s Muslim faith. He referred to the race as “one of the ugliest campaigns we have seen in our lifetimes.”

Byron Donalds

Florida’s win for governor was a close race between Republican Byron Donalds, a former congressman elected in 2020, and David Jolly, a former Republican turned Democrat. Donalds won 50% of the votes to Jolly’s 48.7%, according to the New York Times.

He will be Florida’s first Black governor and is a recent endorser of current President Trump.

“Tonight, I want to send a very special thank you to the people of Florida. Even if you didn’t vote for me, I will be your governor too,” Donalds said in his victory speech. “Tonight, we celebrate, and tomorrow we go to work. And over the next four years, we take Florida to a whole new level.”

Amy Acton

Democrat Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a former presidential candidate, in Ohio’s gubernatorial race. Acton will be Ohio’s first Democratic governor since 2011, and she won 52.3% to 44.4% with 98% of the votes counted, according to NBC.

Acton, who appealed to lower and middle-class voters, said in her victory speech that “the healing starts today.” It was a race marked by big spending: Elon Musk, for one, invested approximately $5 million into the Ramaswamy campaign, which, much like El-Sayed’s campaign, had to battle attacks on the candidate’s religion.

A recent advertisement from the Ramaswamy campaign featured Acton’s estranged mother, who called the governor-elect a liar. Acton’s stepfather was indicted after sexually abusing Acton when she was 12, and she and her brother were removed from her mother’s custody, according to NBC.

James Talarico

Democrat James Talarico beat Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican, to become Texas’ newest senator Tuesday night. This is the first time in three decades the Democratic Party has gained control over the Texas Senate.

The New York Times reported that Elon Musk spent about $200 million on advertising targeting, in order to keep the seat red. Despite these efforts, Talarico secured 55.1% of the votes to Paxton’s 43%, according to the AP.

“Old politics is dying, and a new politics is being born through each of us… through every Texan who believed in our state and believed in this movement,” Talarico said in his victory speech. “Now the real work begins.”

Chris Pappas

Democrat Chris Pappas won the New Hampshire Senate race over incumbent Republican John E. Sununu, with 56.2% of the votes to Sununu’s 42%, according to the AP. Pappas has served four terms in the House of Representatives, representing the 1st Congressional District.

Pappas will be the first openly gay man in the Senate.

His campaign focused on addressing the war in Iran and everyday affordability, seeking to distinguish himself from Sununu, who was endorsed by Trump and is worth nearly $36 million according to financial disclosures.

“Tonight we celebrate, and as we celebrate let’s think about a brighter future we can all build together,” Pappas said in a victory speech as reported by New Hampshire Public Radio.

Penny Flanagan

Democrat Flanagan, a former Minnesota lieutenant governor, ran against Michelle Tafolya, a former sports broadcaster, in a race for Minnesota’s Senate seat. She broke new ground becoming the first Native American woman elected to the U.S. Senate.

Tafolya took 43.6% of the votes to Flanagan’s 53.7%, according to NBC. Flanagan also broke new ground last night,

“The significance of this moment is not lost on me, and I’m really hopeful for what we can do,” Flanagan said in her victory speech.

Adam Hamilton

Democrat Adam Hamilton, the founding pastor of the U.S.’s largest Methodist congregation, defeated incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall 50.9% to 46.1%. It’s the first Democratic win in Kansas since 1932 .

Kansas, home to a population that’s 70% Christian and 30% Evangelical Protestant, has long voted for Republicans on the basis of faith-based issues. This is Hamilton's first position in elected office.

“This is amazing. We really did make history," Hamilton told his supporters. “We're not flyover country. We're the heart of the country.”

title: Staff predictions | Can Penn State stay undefeated all-time against Washington?
author: The Daily Collegian football staff
description:
Penn State and Washington meet Saturday for just the fifth time across the two programs’ storied histories, with this matchup also marking the second meeting as conference foes.

The Nittany Lions have been to Seattle once before in 1921, taking home a 21-7 win. That game was the seventh-ever game played in what is now known as Husky Stadium, although it wasn’t called that then.

Luckily Penn State is flying this time, not training for three days like it did back then, with Matt Campbell having his team leave Thursday in hopes of a better adjustment to the time switch, especially with the game set for 12:30 p.m. PT.

Will the Nittany Lions successfully handle the cross-country travel? Here’s what we think.

Andrew Deal: Penn State 24, Washington 13

Penn State and Washington are more similar than it may seem from an initial look. The Nittany Lions are 4-4, while the Huskies are 5-3 and about a minute away from being 4-4 after a last-minute victory over Nebraska last week.

Prior to its game against Purdue, Penn State has struggled against the run, but Washington isn’t a team that has shown capabilities of running with consistency, ranking No. 135 out of 138 teams in the FBS. Therefore, the Nittany Lions should force Washington to run the ball, while still containing the dangerous legs of Demond Williams Jr.

Penn State’s offense can’t be sustainable with how it functioned against Purdue. It may get a boost if either Chase Sowell or Koby Howard play, which can help the passing game, but if the game plan is the same, it won’t have success.

I expect the Nittany Lions to be even more complementary this week, with the expectation of at least Sowell being back to give a true threat at receiver. The run game will build off its performance from a week ago, continuing to keep things simple in the blocking schemes.

On defense, the speed of the linebackers should help contain the dual-threat aspect of Williams, while the corners get a chance at redemption for themselves after a lackluster performance against USC against another team that features a heavy passing game.

The momentum from a week prior will carry over fully, and Penn State will continue turning its season around with a win in controlling fashion to move just one game away from becoming bowl eligible.

Andrew Mercer: Penn State 21, Washington 14

The Nittany Lions finally got over the hump with their first Big Ten victory, and they beat Purdue through creativity and aggression. Penn State’s going to need more of that Saturday if it's going to win on the West Coast.

Campbell said Sowell is “probable” heading into the game, so he’ll likely resume his role as the primary target in the passing game while running backs Cam Wallace and Carson Hansen have a second go at being the “elite one-two punch” Campbell saw against the Boilermakers.

However, I have Penn State’s run game falling back to old habits. Wallace and Hansen found success last Saturday, but that was against one of the worst run defenses in the Big Ten, so I’m not quite convinced they'll be as effective against the Huskies. Only time will tell.

Despite that, I think Sowell’s return will be Penn State’s golden ticket, and he’ll surely find the end zone. Also, with Rocco Becht’s confidence in the tight end room improving, I have two of Penn State’s three touchdowns coming through the air.

As for defense, Penn State’s secondary came up in a big way against Purdue with two interceptions. They’ve proved throughout most of the season they’re the best unit on the team.

I have the safeties and cornerbacks combining for a defensive clinic while Tony Rojas once again puts in an All-America worthy performance as the Nittany Lions hold Washington to only two touchdowns.

Lexie Linderman: Penn State 24, Washington 17

Two bad rushing teams are going head to head this week, with Washington sitting dead last in the Big Ten in rush yards per game, while Penn State sits middle of the pack due to stellar performances on the ground against Buffalo and Purdue.

Both programs also have solid momentum heading into this one. The Nittany Lions just played their best Big Ten game of the year, and the Huskies are winners of two straight.

This game is going to come down to Washington’s pass offense against Penn State’s secondary. The Nittany Lions have the best pass defense in the Big Ten, but the Huskies’ offense runs through wide receivers Chris Lawson and Dezmen Roebuck.

I find it difficult to bet against Audavion Collins and Daryus Dixson, however, as those two will likely limit Roebuck and Lawson. If that happens, all Penn State has to do is contain Demond William Jr.’s legs and not get beat by the worst rush offense in the conference.

While Penn State’s rushing attack outshined the pass game, that will change this week with Sowell likely set for a return after missing last week’s matchup. He’s in for a tough matchup with safety Alex McLaughlin, though.

Becht is going to have to take care of the football, and if he does that, the Nittany Lions should have enough to win.

Noah Aberegg: Penn State 23, Washington 21

Penn State looked like a cohesive team against Purdue, and with the possibility of it having both top receivers back, I think that cohesiveness is here to stay.

The Nittany Lions solved the answer in the run game with a 135-yard performance from Wallace. He was paired with Hansen, who also had a season-best outing, and the two look to continue that ground attack against Washington.

If Penn State has one of its wide receivers back, most likely Sowell, that’ll provide a boost to the somewhat successful passing game. Becht appeared to have one of his best games of the season in terms of decision-making and accuracy, and that’ll only improve as he gets one of his explosive playmakers back.

The biggest reason for concern, however, is the threat of Williams, who is a dual-threat gunslinger that’s rushed for 211 yards in addition to his 1,495 yards through the air.

Penn State has struggled containing dual-threat quarterbacks in the past — especially the last time the Nittany Lions were on the West Coast, when UCLA’s Nico Iamaleava ran for 128 yards.

This is a different team than that, however, and I think the Nittany Lions can pull out the win with their offense working cohesively. They’ll need big stops from their defense and Tony Rojas to earn their second straight win.

title: Column | A blue wave swept the U.S., but there’s still work to do on shore
author: Teresa Phelan | Opinions Editor
description:
Well, well, well.

Less than 48 hours ago, I wrote a column about the midterm elections and the lack of faith in the ability to turn a Republican Congress into a group of politicians who represent the everyday American, without the votes to substantiate the change.

But here we are: The G.O.P. is no longer the dominant force in the U.S. House or Senate, which, for many, is a sigh of relief. A party full of corrupt, untrustworthy politicians will no longer lead policy that fails the same people they claim to help.

Since 1934, the president’s party has lost House seats in every midterm, save for 1998 and 2002. When American governments run hot, voters tend to spin the other way. But Democrats also took back the Senate and several governor seats, a range that makes this year’s result larger than history alone allowed us to predict.

James Talarico flipped Texas blue, the first time a Senator has done so since 1988. Talarico, a former school teacher, beat Ken Paxton, who his own party impeached in 2023.

Amy Acton became the 71st governor-elect of Ohio, defeating Vivek Ramaswamy, who aired a million dollars' worth of campaign ads featuring her mother, who lost custody of Acton after her stepfather was indicted for raping her when she was a child.

Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the Senate, Abdul El-Sayed is the first Muslim senator and Peggy Flanagan will be the country's first Native American woman U.S. senator.

In an effort to remain in power, Republicans gerrymandered district lines in North Carolina and Florida, and still lost. The attempts to trap people into thinking they have no choice in their elected officials fell short and will set the standard moving forward. Political scientists have a name for a map that backfires as such: a dummymander.

People are tired of hatred. They’re tired of money and status having more power than action. This is a country built on diversity, so it’s about time we elected officials who view it as a strength, not a weakness. Diversity is not a political talking point, our communities are made up of diverse backgrounds, experiences and identities.

America is built on the backbone of those before us. Politicians can continuously disregard the accomplishments of immigrants and other marginalized communities, but do not forget the privilege we are granted because of their sacrifices.

I’ve already started hearing, “But Donald Trump is still the president.” Of course he is, but he’s no longer surrounded by yes-men.

However, Republicans can (probably) read a vote count, too. Expect more of them to put distance between themselves and the White House over the next two years as they begin eyeing the 2028 presidential election.

It’s not time to get comfortable. The expectations are high, and they should be. We don’t need another group of politicians making promises they have no intention of keeping. Running a campaign on the basis of keeping the government out of bodily autonomy, returning affordability and shutting down international conflict needs to quickly become a reality.

Autonomy runs through courts (and, of course, confirmations); affordability through spending and tax bills; and foreign policy through war powers. Congress, now with a Democrat majority, has more leverage over the latter two, but the least over the first, as the president nominates judges.

Democrats nationwide have an obligation to deliver on their promises. Every single politician campaigns on being for the average, working class American. Few of them actually are. I hope to see new control of Congress as the mere first step in a long-term approach to making substantial change on behalf of their constituents.

The government is not a private club for billionaires, who think a six-figure donation earns them a seat at the table. It belongs to the mom who works two jobs and still finds time to show up on Election Day, the first-time voters, those who had the awkward conversations and those who refused to believe their vote didn’t matter.

It belongs to the women, men, Native Americans, Muslims who are just as American as you and me. You cannot tell Americans that freedom is the foundation of this country and then selectively decide whose freedom warrants protection. You cannot demand respect while refusing to extend that same kindness to others. Their hypocrisy rings loudly, but our empathy and love for one another is louder.

The Democratic Party cannot become the thing they’ve always criticized; there’s no more ignoring working-class Americans, no more being fed lies from the top down and no more ostriching those who disagree. Remaining complicit in systems of power that create discrepancies in wealth, status and access directly contradicts the progress we’re making and the future within our grasp.

These results should remind you that you’re not a pawn in their game. You can celebrate, but don’t lose sight of the values and beliefs that drove you to the polls in the first place. Don’t let them knock you off the board.

MORE COLUMNS

title: Penn State men’s hockey welcomes Notre Dame for first Big Ten home series
author: Dominic Megats I The Daily Collegian
description:
The Big Ten is an unforgiving, highly competitive conference when it comes to hockey, and the first conference series for the Nittany Lions threw them into that fire.

In a grueling weekend of conference play where both games went past regulation, Penn State left Minnesota with three points.

Still looking to put a tally in the win column of its conference standings, the blue and white return to Pegula Ice Arena, where they are set to face a struggling Notre Dame team.

Small improvements

Guy Gadowsky mentioned his team took “a step in a couple areas” before facing off with the Golden Gophers. Returning to Happy Valley, his team supported that claim after finding their rhythm throughout both games.

One of the most important things Penn State did well was return to its style of play. In many instances over the weekend, the Nittany Lions played a fast, aggressive game in which they suffocated the puck carrier and transitioned quickly from defense to offense.

“It’s a process,” Gadowsky said at his weekly press conference following the series. “You can’t just have one week of practice and meetings and expect that, ‘Hey, it’s all done.’ We still have a lot of work to do. Coaches are happy that we did definitely make strides in two of the three areas, but we still have a lot of work to do, specifically on one.”

Additionally, Josh Fleming was dominant in net for the blue and white. While Penn State showed moments of improvement, its defense showed the same weakness seen in its opening games.

However, Fleming stood on his head between the pipes. The sophomore started both games against the Golden Gophers, finishing the weekend with 60 total saves. Many of the key stops came in the two overtime periods and the Game 1 shootout.

“Friday night he was just so good,” Gadowsky said. “Obviously, he stopped many dangerous shots in the game, dangerous shots in overtime and, obviously, in the shootout. I think he absolutely deserved to play again.”

The Montreal, Quebec, native improved his save percentage to .912, earning a middle-of-the-pack spot in the Big Ten.

Several glimpses of success from the Nittany Lions over the weekend, plus the promising starts from their newcomers, will continue to be tested at home against the Fighting Irish.

Scouting Notre Dame

Notre Dame is off to a start similar to Penn State. The Fighting Irish began their season with a sweep over Niagara. However, they then faced three straight ranked opponents and haven’t won a game since the opening series.

Seniors Evan Werner and Danny Nelson lead the team in points with six through seven games. Werner was the lone goalscorer in Game 1 against Wisconsin in Notre Dame’s recent series and leads his team with four goals.

The Flower Mound, Texas, native is off to a familiar start, finishing last season by leading the Fighting Irish in goals with 17.

The Fighting Irish will be without forward David Klee and defensemen Jaedon Kerr and Leo Gruba. After reviewing an incident late in Game 2 against Wisconsin, the conference handed Klee a one-game suspension, causing him to miss the opening game. Kerr and Gruba will serve two games, missing the entire series.

Goaltending is where things get tricky for Notre Dame: They let in 16 total goals in their series against the Badgers. Freshman netminder Patrick Quinlan was at the brunt of the high-powered attack after letting in 15 goals over the weekend.

Currently, the Fighting Irish rank last in goals allowed and goals scored per game in the Big Ten. However, Penn State is right behind them in both categories.

Goals are sure to be scored in plenty when these two teams meet, creating an opportunity for the Nittany Lions to cover some ground in the conference.

title: Starting OL, key WR probable ahead of Penn State vs. Washington
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State released its first availability report Wednesday night ahead of Saturday's matchup at Washington.

Wide receivers Chase Sowell and Koby Howard are still listed on the report after being out against Purdue. Sowell is now probable, while Howard is questionable as of Wednesday.

Matt Campbell said Tuesday that Sowell is "in a really good spot." Howard, meanwhile, has been limited at practice according to Campbell.

"When he's ready, we're going to try to make sure he's on the field, but we're going to make sure he's ready to go," Campbell said.

Defensive tackle Armstrong Nnodim and left tackle Malachi Goodman are both listed as probable.

Nnodim was on last week's availability report as a game-time decision, but ultimately played. Goodman left the game against Purdue earlier and was replaced by Garrett Sexton for a few plays, but he ultiimately returned.

Kicker Cristiano Rosa, defensive tackle Alijah Carnell, cornerback Tyler Armstead, linebacker Alex Tatsch and defensive end Max Granville are all listed as out.

The Nittany Lions face the Huskies at 3:30 p.m. ET on Saturday.

title: Penn State men's soccer falls 2-0 to No. 11 Maryland in season finale
author: Henry Bustin | For The Collegian
description:
Penn State traveled to College Park, Maryland, for its regular-season finale, taking on the No. 11 Terrapins. The Nittany Lions entered this matchup still in search of their first Big Ten win under first-year head coach Rob Dow.

The blue and white will have to wait another year to give Dow his first conference win, as it fell to Maryland 2-0.

1st Half

The final game for the Nittany Lions kicked off with the Terrapins in possession of the ball, intent on scoring.

Sophomore Justin Ross started his second straight game in net for the blue and white, and he blocked several attempts within the first five minutes of the game.

Ross’ steady goalkeeping was challenged when an early goal was scored by Maryland’s Albi Ndrenika that slipped off of Ross in the sixth minute.

With Maryland focusing on passing defensively, the Nittany Lions took advantage of this and took possession of the ball throughout the ninth and 10th minutes.

Penn State applied more pressure, with the team working together and making strategic passes on the Terrapins’ side. The blue and white’s Moritz Weber and Peter Doran both made shot attempts on Maryland at the bottom center and top center of the net, respectively. Goalkeeper Laurin Mack managed to save them both, however.

With Maryland up 3-1 in the corner kick battle, it was able to take greater possession of the ball and play more intensely on the Nittany Lions’ side. The Terrapins’ efforts were challenged by Etienne Reck, who protected the goal box and kept pressure on Maryland.

The two teams continued to battle, with the ball moving between sides constantly. In the 27th minute, Nittany Lions’ senior defender Morgan Marshall shot on the Terrapins at the bottom center, but it was saved by Mack.

Penn State and Maryland traded shots in the 32nd minute, with both goalkeepers denying the attempts.

A long shot pass made to Maryland’s prompted the blue and white to try and find an opening, and soon after, a 2-on-2 allowed Penn State to apply heavy pressure, although Maryland managed to take possession with a little over a minute remaining.

Maryland led the ball over to Penn State’s side and made a last-minute goal attempt, although it didn’t go in and instead bounced off the net, finishing off the first half.

Ross shone for Penn State with four saves in the half, and the defense managed to stop many offensive plays by Maryland; however, with the Terrapins up 1-0, the Nittany Lions had to change their game plan in order to remove the deficit.

2nd Half

The half began with Maryland taking quick control of the ball and directing it towards the Nittany Lions’ side. The Terrapins applied pressure on Penn State with an early shot attempt in the 46th minute from Albi Nendrenika, which was skillfully saved by Ross.

Penn State then gained momentum, with shot attempts from both Amadou Kone and Peter Doran in the 52nd and 53rd minutes, which were blocked by Maryland.

In the 57th minute, the Terrapins’ Dominic Ayella found the back of the net, with assists coming from Zack Harris and Lilian Fichelle, giving Maryland a 2-0 lead.

Maryland continued its aggressiveness, but this led to a foul on Maxwell Sekyi, which granted a free kick to Reck, although it didn’t make contact with the net.

Maryland’s offense continued with its aggression, awarding two free kicks to Penn State in the span of a few minutes, although neither was able to score.

In possession of the ball, the Nittany Lions pressed up when a player tripped, resulting in a red card on Maryland’s Ljubomir Popovic for denying a chance at goal, creating an interesting change in the layout.

With Popovic off the field, Penn State continued to buffer as it played passively, with the offense taking advantage only in quick spurts before Maryland retook possession. The Terrapins displayed this when they nearly scored a goal on the Nittany Lions right after the red card removal of Popovic. Ross saved this attempt in the 73rd minute to keep the fight going for the blue and white.

With only 10 Terrapins on the field, the Nittany Lions were at a numerical advantage. In the 80th minute, the blue and white’s offense traded passes, trying to throw off Laurn Mack to find an opening. They nearly did, but Maryland managed to launch it out of their side.

Penn State returned soon after, and freshman defender Nehan Hasan made a shot attempt, but Mack blocked it away.

In the final minutes of the game, Penn State played more aggressively, maintaining pressure on Maryland’s side with consistent passes and offensive force against the Terrapins. They managed possession time against Maryland, but the ball was soon launched back towards Penn State’s side, where Maryland continued playing in the 89th minute.

The Nittany Lions couldn’t come up with anything in the final minute, ultimately being shut out in their season finale.

title: No. 12 Penn State field hockey falls to No. 10 Iowa in Big Ten Tournament Quarterfinals
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
Hannah Prince’s Big Ten postseason debut was all but a fairy tale.

Third-seeded Penn State made its debut with its first-year coach in the conference tournament, falling 2-1 in dominant fashion to sixth-seeded Iowa in Columbus, Ohio, in the quarterfinals.

The blue and white started in possession, but couldn’t make much of the opening action, as the game started with a feeling-out period between both sides. The Hawkeyes soon found space down the left-hand side around two minutes in and threaded a ball in the gap, with a cutting dash inside the Nittany Lions’ circle that caused goalie Aby Deverka to make a relatively easy stop.

Iowa continued over the next few minutes with slow, calculated passes inside, as it tried to hog possession.

Penn State got a chance on a restart from the side when Morgan Snyder caught the Hawkeyes uncharacteristically sleeping and flicked it downfield to a flying Joji Purdy for an easy score and the Nittany Lions’ lead.

As a downpour fell toward the end of the first quarter, the two sides began entrenched with attempts to break down each other’s backline, yet nothing substantial resulted.

Early into the second frame, the Hawkeyes got a penalty corner, but the blue and white held firm. The back line soon after broke, with Iowa pressuring relentlessly for the equalizer; Lara Pyle got possession back inside the circle, but her attempt at a clearance went right back to the Hawkeyes and allowed a score.

Through 10 minutes of play to end the half, neither side could take an upper hand, as Deverka logged four saves at the break to keep the Nittany Lions in the game.

The break did little to curb momentum, as Iowa resumed with pace after the intermission. The blue and white’s key attackers Ella Gaitan and Sienna Dunn remained shut down by the Hawkeyes’ defense throughout the quarter.

The final frame of regulation began with even more caution. Iowa, which had played from its back line all game, continued to pass back and build up play at a slow pace. Through the first four minutes, the blue and white were lucky to not concede.

At the 10-minute mark, the Nittany Lions once again lost possession in their own final third, but the Hawkeyes’ centering pass couldn’t find a stick to separate the game.

As the commentators put it, ‘the inevitable soon struck,’ and the Nittany Lions’ defense soon allowed an ugly goal to reward Iowa’s efforts. The Hawkeyes threaded another pass deep into Penn State territory and, with two defenders and Deverka in front of the ball, Iowa passed it out and Dionne van Aalsum smacked at it with a bouncing shot that trickled in.

With around 10 minutes to play, Iowa dropped back into a compact look and the rain came down once again, fitting for the dramatics. Even as Prince took off Deverka for an extra attacker, the Hawkeyes backline held firm for the win.

In the blue and white’s defeat, Deverka logged seven saves as Penn State’s offense went completely offline, logging only one shot on target and two total.

title: Pat Kraft’s ‘Own the Outcome’ shirts instill ownership for Penn State players
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Rocco Becht and tight end Benjamin Brahmer walked into their press conferences on Tuesday with shirts that read “Own The Outcome.”

Brahmer said that the shirts were a gift from Vice President for Intercollegiate Athletics Pat Kraft, who left them in all of the players’ lockers with a note.

“Just owning the outcome and understanding that we got to control what we can control and continue working as hard as we can in practice and whatever happens to us on Saturdays,” Brahmer said on Tuesday.

Over the last several weeks, the Nittany Lions have had to live up to that motto after starting the conference slate with four straight losses. After a comeback victory from Wisconsin on Sept. 26, Penn State was demolished at Northwestern.

It was then that the players had to own the outcome.

“Just own the outcome,” safety Jamison Patton said Wednesday. “Whatever it is, own it. Right, wrong, or whatever, move on from it, learn from it and grow from it.”

That’s exactly what the Nittany Lions did for two weeks as they showed continual growth against USC and Michigan. Penn State’s run defense improved against the Trojans, while wide receiver Chase Sowell emerged as a top threat against the Wolverines.

Last week against Purdue, all aspects of the game came together and earned the Nittany Lions’ first Big Ten win of the season.

After the rough stretch spoiled the start of the Matt Campbell era, the victory was evident of the work that has been done behind the scenes to turnaround the program. And it was the work of the players who remained committed to the team’s success amidst the turmoil.

“This group never wavered,” Campbell said Saturday. “They've never flinched. They haven't b— or complained. They just go to work and tried like heck to correct the areas and grow themselves forward.”

As the players have stayed true to themselves, so has Kraft. Despite the losing streak, his support for the team hasn’t wavered.

Kraft has continued to take his place on the sidelines for every game and has worked to motivate the team through the tough times — hence the shirts.

“We love the shirts,” cornerback Audavion Collins said. “We want to say a huge thank you to Pat Kraft.”

But this hasn’t been the first time Kraft’s positioned himself in a place of support for the team. Campbell spoke on Oct. 14 about Kraft’s availability for the program.

“I think there's been so much time, effort, and energy internally in ourselves alike,” Campbell said. “Pat has been certainly willing to be available, wanting to be available, and wanting to help every step of the way.”

In addition to his willingness to work with Campbell, he’s made himself a resource for all of the players, according to Patton.

With a newly revamped roster in Happy Valley, Kraft established connections with the Penn State players and instilled his belief in them before the season. He’s carried that connection throughout the season with his gift this week.

“Dr. Kraft came in pretty early as the team was assembled and came and talked to us and just showed his respect for us, and we respect him, and really appreciate his support,” Patton said. “And the shirts were a cool asset to that, just to show his gratification for us and us towards him.”

title: Penn State is ready for its annual cross-country trip, providing some players a chance to see family
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is set for its furthest travel of the season, making its way to Seattle, Washington, to face the Huskies at noon on Saturday. It’s the first and potentially only time the Nittany Lions appear on the West Coast this season, as USC came to Happy Valley and Penn State isn't playing UCLA and Oregon.

Matt Campbell said the team will fly out of Harrisburg on Thursday instead of Friday, a tactical decision meant to give the Nittany Lions time to adjust to the time change. He noted the extra day will allow the team to shake off the jet lag and get on a proper sleep schedule, and he did the same when Iowa State traveled out west.

“I felt like if we got in Friday, boy, you're going to be really pushing it,” Campbell said Tuesday. “We've done this trip a couple times even though we were in the central time zone. If it was a day game, we tried to go especially on Thursday, to get ourselves there, get settled in, and try to, from a sleep standpoint, get on the best rhythm that we possibly can.”

Campbell explained the travel plans were put together in the offseason. He knew as soon as he joined Penn State that West Coast travel was on the board, and he’s been able to draw on past experiences to curate the travel plan.

“Penn State has had this trip the last couple of years,” Campbell said. “You try to take all the information, then just make the best travel plans possible,” Campbell said. “But I don't think it's a debilitating situation.”

Defensive tackle Keanu Williams — a Clovis, California, native and transfer from UCLA — has been using his experience with cross-country travel to the East Coast to his advantage, as he already knows what works for him going into such a weekend.

Williams said he “had it worse” last year with the Bruins, as their schedule featured four long road trips to Northwestern, Michigan State, Indiana and Ohio State, each with a home game sandwiched between them.

Regardless, Williams said the football game stays the same, so the venue doesn’t really matter.

“Every other week, I'm going across the country,” Williams said of UCLA’s travel last season. “I feel like I'm more on the East Coast side of things now, so the travel is a little bit lighter for me. It's not that bad, but it's cool. It's football today. I still got to play football, so it's no big deal.”

The sixth-year senior shared how his preparation for long-distance travel differs compared to that of a more local game. Williams said he strives to get eight hours of sleep throughout the week, and he’s looking to get nine hours of sleep going into Thursday with rest in the middle of the day as well.

He’s especially excited to be back on the West Coast because it’ll be easier for his family to attend the game. Williams said being on the East Coast has made it harder for his family because they aren’t a drive or short flight away, but his mother made sure to mark the Washington game as one she needed to watch in-person.

“That was the one game my mom was like, ‘Yeah, I'm coming, so make sure you got some tickets on you,’” Williams said. “So, I got about 10 tickets. Not as much as some guys on the team, but I got 10 of them, which is still a lot so it’s good. So I’m happy to go back to the West Coast for a little bit and enjoy my time in the couple days there.”

Williams isn’t the only Nittany Lion closer to home. Cornerback Daryus Dixson and defensive tackle Siale Taupaki are also from California, defensive tackle Dallas Vakalahi is from Utah, defensive tackle Alijah Carnell is from Nevada and offensive lineman Vaea Ikakoula is from Hawaii.

“It's awesome because they take a gamble coming out here, right?” safety Jamison Patton said. “So just going back closer to their hometown and getting the love from their people back home is going to be big for them. It gives you a little bit of an edge to bring it back here for them. I'm excited for them.”

title: Penn State wrestling's Mitchell Mesenbrink, Shayne Van Ness named Big Ten Wrestlers to Watch
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian

Two Nittany Lions have earned preseason honors.

Mitchell Mesenbrink and Shayne Van Ness were named to the 2026-27 Big Ten Wrestlers to Watch List, the conference announced Wednesday.

title: Penn State field hockey’s Aby Deverka earns NFHCA Defensive Player of the Week
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Tack on another award for Penn State field hockey. Aby Deverka earned National Defensive Player of the Week honors for the second time this season, the NFHCA announced Wednesday.

The announcement comes after the third-year goalkeeper shut out the twice-reigning national champions on Friday. In the win over Northwestern, Deverka made seven saves to break the Wildcats’ 35-game Big Ten winning streak.

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell gives updates on injured WRs
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
Ahead of Penn State’s longest trip of the 2026 season against Washington, Matt Campbell met with the media for his second weekly media availability.

Campbell talked about both sides of the punting game, gave praise to cornerback Audavion Collins and had additional updates on his injured wide receivers.

Here’s what Campbell had to say.

Punt return, blocking

Washington has allowed the second most punt return opportunities in the country at 19, potentially giving wide receiver Zay Robinson chances to showcase his returning capabilities.

The receiver has broken some big returns with a long of 38 yards, while averaging 10.3 yards per return on 19 attempts.

“Zay is a guy that he’s got elite vision and elite lateral quickness,” Campbell said Wednesday. “He was a great point guard in high school, Won three straight state championships, averaged about 22 points a game in basketball, and I think he's got that point guard vision when he gets the football.”

Robinson has shown to be a reliable punt returner to set up Penn State with better field position. For a player who’s in his first full year as a returner, he’s been a consistent threat for the Nittany Lions.

“He's a great ball catcher, which is huge for him as a punt returner,” Campbell said. “For a young guy to be able to do what he's doing, his first time being truly the punt returner, it's been really impressive, and a lot of credit obviously goes to the other 10 guys out there because I think (special teams coach Justin Lustig) does a great job with those guys.”

On the other side of the ball, Penn State had a mishap in punt blocking coverage. One of Purdue’s two touchdowns was off a blocked punt that was returned for a touchdown. However, Campbell remains confident in the unit to be able to bounce back from that play in future weeks.

“You flinch and you make the wrong mistake fundamentally in the moment,” Campbell said. “And we have great faith in those guys. And the reality of it is you're going to get challenged again when you show something like that, and I think it'll be critical for us to learn from it. I always said the punt is the most important play in football, and executing that is critically important.”

Praise for Collins

Collins has been one of Penn State’s top players on defense, consistently limiting the opposing team’s top receiver.

On Saturday, the cornerback was a part of a defense that limited a high-powered Purdue passing attack to 142 yards in the air, while the Boilermakers’ top receiver, Asaad Waseem, had just 64 yards receiving.

“I think when you have a player like that, and I know I've been bullish on (Collins), I feel like he is the standard bearer of what this program should look like, how he comes out every day, what he's doing,” Campbell said.

Collins didn’t just make an impact on the defensive side of the ball against Purdue. Campbell and Taylor Mouser worked him into the offensive game plan, as he had a rush for 11 yards, showcasing his speed.

“How many ways can we get that guy to affect a win for a football team?” Campbell said. “It was awesome to be able to get him in. He didn't get the ball once; he did get the ball once on offense, but I think he presents a lot of challenges. And how many different ways can we use his skill set to help us win football games right now. That's the biggest thing for me, and what that guy's about is everything you want a star player to be about.”

Updates on Koby Howard, Chase Sowell

Campbell went a little further on his updates with both wide receivers Koby Howard and Chase Sowell. On Tuesday, Campbell said Howard was still “questionable” while Sowell was more “probable” for Saturday’s contest.

Campbell is being safe with both of his top receiving threats, waiting for them to be at full health before they get on the field. With Sowell, Campbell said “he’s a lot closer to being full strength.”

“I want him to be on the field confident and ready to rock and roll,” Campbell said. “And I think we've all seen when he's out there and fully ready to roll, and geez, even in the Michigan game, he probably wasn't fully healthy, man, a guy that can play through hard, and I think his confidence right now, how he's playing, it's a great energy for our football team.”

Campbell mentioned Sowell’s impact on the sidelines against Purdue, as he’s emerged as one of the leaders on the team, saying “his leadership was fantastic.”

Howard, on the other hand, is a player Campbell has had to control since he went down with an injury. This week, Howard’s been “very limited in terms of what he’s done” at practice. With the sophomore’s work ethic, he’s constantly been someone who’s wanted to still get work in despite recovering from an injury.

“If there's one guy you got to reel in, it's him,” Campbell said. “But I think it's what makes him really special. He's a guy that's straining to do everything in his power to help the team.”

title: Penn State women's basketball notebook | Tanisha Wright talks guard play, lessons learned
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State suffered an upset loss to Cleveland State in its season opener on Monday, 62-61. The defeat was Tanisha Wright’s first at the helm of her alma mater.

The blue and white hit the road for three straight games starting with Cincinnati this weekend, with a key chance to start the era under Wright on the right foot.

The Lady Lion legend met with the media over Zoom Wednesday morning to discuss the lessons learned, her guard play and the upcoming road trip.

Growing pains

Leading for just 11:30 en route to a defeat at the hands of a Horizon League team under a first-year head coach wasn’t in any 814 resident’s plans coming into the season. However, Wright is drawing lessons from the performance that the team will bring into the rest of the season.

“We got to approach every day like it's our last,” Wright said. “I know it's very cliché, but taking advantage of the opportunities presented for before us and not taking things lightly. I don't think we came out with this sense of urgency, and that's on me because I have to prepare them to have that sense of urgency from the very moment they step on the court.”

The lack of focus showed up in the shooting percentages, especially in Penn State’s 10-point first quarter. The Lady Lions went 4-for-19 from the field and made just one of eight threes in the opening frame.

Wright’s squad shot 31.8% from the field in the game and 22.2% from three-point range in the game.

“I think our shot selection wasn't the best at certain times. I think the right people at the right time need to be taking certain shots,” Wright said. “I thought we could have done a better job of generating that.”

One positive that Wright took away from the setback was the lack of turnovers. The Lady Lions gave the ball away 18 times in the exhibition victory over Pitt-Johnstown compared to 11 on Monday.

“We talk a lot about taking care of the ball, making sure that we get a shot on goal every single possession when we can,” Wright said. “It is a focus of theirs every single game to take care of the ball. So it's something that we consistently harp on; it's something that we consistently work on every day in practice as well.”

Backcourt performances

Only two true forwards, Petra Božan and Cristen Carter, appeared in the season opener. The other six players to check in for more than a minute were guards, and Wright was impressed with many of the performances.

Ava Black had a tough shooting night to going 4-for-14 from the field, but contributed in numerous other ways throughout her team-high 38 minutes.

“We see Ava being able to to really do all things on the court for us: rebound, shoot it pass it,” Wright said. “You saw her scoring in transition, being able to make the right reads at the right time. So I thought, again, Ava had an overall really good game, and I was happy for the kid because I think it's something that she's been wanting to show she's capable of doing.”

On the defensive end of the floor, Skylar Durley contributed five steals, including two high-leverage takeaways in the final minute. Wright explained that she recruited the former Mountain West Freshman of the Year to lock down opposing teams’ best players with her competitive fire.

Among other things, Wright said she was “really happy with the way Skylar is progressing and the attitude that she has towards defending at a high level.”

Finally, the WNBA veteran was asked about her four-star freshman, Kamrah Banks. The Indianapolis native played 11 minutes in her collegiate debut.

“Kam is still a young point guard, still learning,” Wright said. “I think what she does every day in practice is she's eager and she's a sponge and she wants to learn, and as long as she continues to do that, Kam's opportunities will still grow, and so I'm really looking forward to Kam continuing to be the person that she is and the player that she's she's molding herself into.”

Looking ahead

The Lady Lions will look to mold themselves into a winning basketball team with a three-game road trip. Penn State heads to Cincinnati to battle the Bearcats on Saturday, then sticks in Ohio for a Monday matchup with Dayton before traveling to Arizona State the following Sunday.

“We have to understand how hard we have to play and how we can't take anything for granted from the very tip, focusing in on the game plan, focusing in on our level of compete from the very beginning,” Wright said.

It will be Wright’s first road trip as a college head coach, and she is approaching it with a next play mentality.

“I have a great group, and the one thing they've done a great job with is bouncing back, having a bounce-back mentality,” Wright said. “And so, I look forward to them being able to show that they have the ability to move on to the next play and bounce back.”

title: Off the Record | Confused Clara
author: Miss Behave I The Daily Collegian
description:
Editor’s Note: Off the record is a weekly column written by a fourth-year Collegian staffer writing under an alias. It aims to promote a space for honest conversations about love, sex and relationships. Those interested in sharing their experiences or submitting a topic are invited to do so through this anonymous form.

Dear reader,

Clara wrote in seeking advice surrounding her partner and his myriad of female friends.

I think one of the most important parts of a relationship, platonic or romantic, is trust. From my experience as a young woman in college with young-woman-in-college friends, people are so quick to convince themselves of something that’s simply false.

Only you truly know your biggest fears and insecurities, so of course you have the ability to convince yourself he’s talking to other women, or he’s more than just friends with his sworn-platonic best friend.

It’s important to communicate these feelings to your partner, as they should be receptive in understanding your point of view. They should never have you questioning your own sanity. Don’t let him make you feel crazy, or convince you of something you know isn’t true.

Nearly every day, we take the leap of faith known as trust. You may tell your friend something you don’t want anyone else to know because you know she’ll keep the secret. She wouldn’t stab you in the back or go against your wishes (I hope), so you tell her. When it comes to romantic relationships, that level of trust doesn’t come immediately. It takes time to build, just like it took time with your friends, but you have to start somewhere.

Both parties should be openly communicative about any and all emotions that ruminate during the course of the relationship. It will help strengthen your bond and help you feel closer to your partner, ultimately building the trust between you two.

If you can’t trust him, you shouldn’t date him. Feelings only build and grow stronger, and if you continue to self sabotage, you can’t put your true, authentic self in a position to be loved by him.

If you’re convinced he and his girl friend are more than platonic, maybe you should think about why. Is it because of your own anxiety, or did he give you a real reason to question the situation?

If it’s your own anxiety, talk to him. Being open about your feelings will prevent them from building up to the point of overflow, and him knowing how you feel can only help you understand one another. If he gave you a real reason to be worried, it’s time to have a conversation. If he’s doing something that’s making you uncomfortable, he should know. His receptiveness will be telling.

The good, the bad and the ugly are all going to make their way to the forefront at some point, and you’re not going to be able to outrun them.

I would like to point out that open communication goes both ways. No progress is made if you sit there accusing him based on your own fears.

Your feelings are entirely valid. It’s understandable to feel unsure about other women in his life, but try and remind yourself of the facts, so they can drive you instead of your anxiety taking the wheel. Life becomes a lot more peaceful that way.

It takes practice to counter your anxiety, but I think this is a necessary life skill. Perhaps write down your fears and explore where they’re coming from. Is there a deeper-rooted issue prompting you to think this way? Are you not getting what you need out of the relationship?

I encourage you to be honest with your partner and yourself. Honor your core self above the fears that control you.

Until next time,

Miss Behave

title: Preview | No. 21 Penn State women’s soccer rematches No. 16 Purdue in first round of Big Ten Tournament
author: Zach Schroder | The Daily Collegian
description:
No. 21 Penn State is set to take on No. 16 Purdue for the second time this year in the opening round of the Big Ten Tournament. The Nittany Lions and Boilermakers will meet at 8 p.m. Thursday in St. Louis at Energizer Park, an MLS venue.

Since its match with the blue and white on Oct. 3, Purdue has gone 5-1 to end the year, beating two ranked teams and losing to one. While the Nittany Lions went 3-1, with a win, loss and draw against ranked opponents in that span. Both teams were unranked at the time of their first meeting but will now meet in conference tournament play as top-25 teams.

Penn State seems eager to see the Boilermakers again, according to coach Erica Dambach.

“Honestly, I think if you asked this team who they wanted to play again, they would have said Purdue,” Dambach said. “I think they walked off the field in the last game with a tie, very disappointed, let down in themselves, and are chomping at the bit to get back out there.”

Here's what you need to know about the rematch.

Previous matchup

A month ago, the Boilermakers came to Happy Valley and drew with the blue and white 2-2. Each team scored one goal in each half with neither able to score a winning goal past the 65th minute.

Purdue’ s match MVP was Jaiden Anderson, who was just named the Big Ten Forward of the Year. The junior forward from Huntington Beach, California, had a goal, assist and two shots on goal in 86 minutes against Penn State.

Paige Kalal was the most crucial for the Nittany Lions. The senior forward who transferred from Minnesota had one of the blue and white’s goals and assisted the other.

Dambach said Kalal will be getting more leadership, and also said a main focal point for them is figuring out who the best 11 are to start the game.

“I think a huge part of this Penn State 2026 team is the depth that we’ve been able to roll out there and how can we get at them when we hit the 25-minute mark in the first half,” she said.

Purdue

Anderson led Purdue in scoring against Penn State and has been a key contributor all season. The forward has 42 points with 18 goals and six assists. Anderson also leads the conference in goals and shots on goal, and ranks second in game-winning goals and points.

Senior midfielder Irene Campo and fellow senior midfielder Megan Santa Cruz are tied for second in points for Purdue, each with nine goals and six assists. A strong upper-class unit leads the Boilermaker offense.

“The biggest thing is being the aggressor. Going forward, we know we can score goals, we know we're dangerous. You got a lot of people firing on all cylinders,” Dambach said.

She also highlighted redshirt senior goalkeeper Mackenzie Gress, who Dambach said has displayed fantastic leadership.

Penn State and Purdue’s rematch should be an entertaining offensive game from two of the best teams in both the conference and the nation.

title: How to keep the peace when navigating complex roommate situations
author: Ally Sons | The Daily Collegian
description:
Becoming comfortable with confrontation and conversation is a normal part of growing up and a necessary part of finding your voice in college. It may seem uncomfortable to stand up for yourself and set clear boundaries, but nothing is more important, especially when living with someone.

In a world of canon-event-freshman-year roommates, shoebox-sized dorms and trying to find an apartment with people on a similar budget, making a new best friend out of your roommate can feel impossible to some. Being a good roommate is about so much more than just being friends, from staying tidy and being considerate of other people's spaces and time to simply hanging out with your suitemates.

Arguably, though, the most important part of living with someone is setting and respecting clear boundaries so your relationship can stay positive. This kind of conversation can feel difficult and awkward, but that doesn’t change how crucial it is to a good living situation.

If you want to know how to tackle these roommate issues, without unnecessary stress, here are some tips.

Set boundaries, quickly

Whether it’s at the beginning of the lease or right when you notice issues arising, being clear and thorough about what you need is important.

Going into the year with clear-set expectations and boundaries helps avoid problems down the road. Whether that's establishing what your individual and joint responsibilities are in the apartment or dorm or making it clear what you need from a space in terms of sleep schedules, guest visits and chores.

The sooner the conversation is had, the sooner and easier the issues are resolved.

Treat them the way you want to be treated

Kindness is key. Everyone grows up learning to treat other people the way you want to be treated, but in real life, high-intensity situations, it can feel difficult to stay true to that. It's important to remember, though, that this is a lot of people's first time sharing a space with someone else — they deserve a little bit of grace.

Remember that you care about this person and you're cohabitating with them for the rest of the year. Your end goal is a positive living arrangement. Everyone is going through different things and having different experiences while in college, so make sure to have compassion and love when addressing them.

"I" statements

"I" statements are an easy way to have difficult conversations without coming across as accusatory or like you’re blaming your roommates for situational issues.

Instead of directing your concerns at your roommates' behaviors, it can be better to say things like, “I would really like it if we could figure out a better plan to keep our kitchen clean. Would you be okay with starting a chore list that we can both prioritize?”

Be specific, work toward compromise

Before you enter into these conversations, make sure you go in with a specific goal. For example, if your issue is cleanliness, start with establishing specific tasks you want to see improved upon, like dividing dishes more evenly or keeping nightstands or the living room floor clean.

The clearer you are in your goals, the easier it will be to find a solution that works for everyone. This is a conversation aiming for cooperation and compromise, not a criticism of their character.

Bring things up when everyone’s calm

These conversations should be thought about carefully and planned for a time that works for both parties. Don’t pick a time right in between classes or when you have a lot of external stress and might speak out of anger.

Some good times could be Sunday mornings or in the evening after dinner. You could also give your roommate a heads up beforehand, telling them that you want to have a conversation clarifying apartment stuff later, that way they can be part of picking a time and don’t feel ambushed.

Avoid being passive-aggressive, talking to mutual friends about conflict

The more people you involve in these conversations, the more likely it is to seem like you are talking badly about your roommate. The longer you let your issues and concerns fester, and the more you talk about it with other people, the more resentment is going to grow.

These kinds of conflicts should stay strictly between you and your roommates, or, if you need to talk to someone beforehand, make sure it’s people outside your circle, like hometown friends or family.

It's also important to make sure that you handle these situations while staying respectful and being direct, and not taking little jabs or undercutting what your roommate says. These conversations don’t need to be aggressive at all. They should stay productive and positive, with an end goal of a happy, comfortable shared space.

Go to a neutral third party for resolution

If all else fails, and you feel you can’t find a solution, you can always go talk to a trusted individual who isn’t biased about the situation. Resident advisors can be great choices for those who still live in the dorms. Another option is a friend who you both agree is impartial. These types of figures can help moderate and resolve the situation.

title: Sports Editors Weekly | Can No. 12 Penn State field hockey win the Big Ten Tournament?
author: Myles Hannak & Gianna Dowling | Sports Editors
description:
Sports Editors Weekly is a dueling column written by Collegian Sports Editors Gianna Dowling and Myles Hannak. It aims to provide timely debate on Penn State sports performance and news each week.

Coach Hannah Prince is set to make her Big Ten Tournament debut on Wednesday against Iowa, and it couldn’t come at a better time. Penn State is 9-1 in its last 10 games and has a huge momentum boost after defeating then-No. 1 Northwestern on Friday.

This marks the first appearance in the Big Ten Tournament for the blue and white since 2023, and the last time they took home the trophy was in 2022.

Can Prince get Penn State back to the Big Ten mountaintop, or will the Nittany Lions’ momentum halt in the postseason?

Gianna Dowling: Coming for the crown

If the Nittany Lions have proven anything in the past month, it's that they know how to make a run and can do so against some of the nation's best.

The highlight of Penn State’s season was its eight-game win streak through October. Getting through the Big Ten Tournament may sound like a bigger task, but the Nittany Lions need to win just two games to reach the championship.

The blue and white have a chip on its shoulder in the first round, facing Iowa, who snapped Penn State’s win streak. The Nittany Lions enter this matchup with revenge on their mind and have a lot of momentum after a stellar season finale.

Prince’s squad has the possibility of another rematch looming in the semifinals against No. 1 Maryland — the team's only other Big Ten loss. Penn State was overwhelmed by the Terrapins 4-1 in their meeting on Sept. 17, but that was a different Nittany Lions squad, and this team has beaten a top seed before, so who’s to say it can’t happen again.

Another reason I have confidence the blue and white can take home the conference crown is that defense wins championships, and junior goalkeeper Aby Deverka is a brick wall inside the net for Penn State. After posting seven saves against Northwestern on Friday, Deverka leads the Big Ten with eight shutouts.

Additionally, the veteran offensive duo of Ella Gaitan and Sienna Dunn are primed to step up big on the field. Gaitan and Dunn haven’t been the only offensive threats, as underclassmen such as Lilly Holmes and Lara Pyle have shined in big moments for Penn State as of late.

The biggest bump the Nittany Lions will have is if they meet Northwestern in the championship game. But that doesn’t mean Prince and her squad don’t have what it takes to bring home some hardware.

Myles Hannak: Not enough firepower

Penn State is good, but not great.

Ella Gaitan and Sienna Dunn are one of the nation’s best attacking duos, while Aby Deverka stands in front doing her best impression of a brick wall week in and week out. Outside of that trio, the blue and white possess talent in its ranks that can defeat anyone, as evidenced by some of the results they put up this season.

That massive streak Penn State ripped off toward the end of the season makes me feel like that statement could come back to bite me, especially when most of those victories came against fellow Big Ten squads. But I don’t believe that can be replicated in the postseason.

The Nittany Lions lost three games to top-five-ranked opponents, and lost to then-No. 6 Iowa, as Penn State’s only top-ten win came against then-No. 1 Northwestern.

With a rematch looming against the Hawkeyes, confidence should be high that the blue and white can pull off a one-off result, but there shouldn’t be certainty that it can rip off consecutive victories against top-quality opponents — nothing has shown it has that level of stability yet.

title: Penn State wrestling contains top wrestlers, array of depth at 174, 184-pound weight classes
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
A key contribution to Penn State’s recent success has been its domination of the 174-pound and 184-pound divisions.

Both weight classes are set with proven winners and depth pieces with immense potential, positioning themselves for another deep postseason run.

Here’s how the two weight classes shape up in 2026-27.

174

If Mitchell Mesebrink ends up making the jump to 174-pounds, he’ll become the easy favorite to repeat as a National Champion within the division.

The reigning Dan Hodge Trophy winner and two-time national champion is the strongest pillar of Penn State’s wrestling dynasty. Mesenbrink posted another undefeated season with an extremely impressive 96.3% bonus rate, meaning he won all but one match by major decision, tech fall, or fall.

Over his three years at Penn State, Mesenbrink has amassed an 80-1 overall career record, with his lone defeat occurring during the 2024 NCAA finals against Iowa State’s David Carr.

While it isn’t nearly to the same degree as Mesenbrink, redshirt freshman William Henckel was flawless during his freshman season as well. Henckel went 9-0 in official matches and dominated the Southern Scuffle, defeating Caden Bellis to earn the 174-pound tournament title.

Prior to officially joining Penn State, Henckel earned a U20 silver medal in 2025, proving to be one of the top young wrestlers in his weight class. He’ll provide Cael Sanderson with an exceptional weapon in the room.

True freshman Jayden James enters the fray as the No. 3 ranked pound-for-pound recruit in the 2026 class. James flipped his commitment from Virginia Tech to Penn State and plans to grayshirt this season, allowing him to keep his 5 years of eligibility while not competing.

James’ resume on the domestic and international stage adds context to his high rank. The Morristown, New Jersey, native went undefeated over his final two seasons at Delbarton High School. James won a 2025 U17 World Championship gold medal and two silver medals in the U20 and U23 World Championships.

While he plans to grayshirt, he’ll still have the opportunity to learn behind two of the best wrestlers in the division.

184

After finishing as a NCAA runner-up for the second time in his career, Rocco Welsh will enter the season as a title contender in the 184-pound weight class.

In his debut season in the blue and white, Welsh dominated with a record of 29-2 while notching a 59% bonus rate during the year. Welsh claimed his first Big Ten Championship after defeating Minnesota star Max McEnelly in a 2-1 tiebreaker victory.

Welsh continued his run by cruising through the opening rounds of the NCAA tournament, winning his first three matches against Caleb Uhlenhopp, Rylan Rogers and Silas Allred by a combined 39-9. His final matches were as tight as they come, outlasting Michigan’s Brock Mantanona in a 4-2 battle and falling short 4-3 in the final in a rematch against McEnelly.

While Welsh is the main attraction, Asher Cunningham is a key lineup piece and a dark-horse contributor for the Nittany Lions at both 174 and 184.

During his redshirt freshman season, Cunningham compiled a 7-1 record in open tournaments, with his only defeat coming against Welsh in a 13-5 decision. His marquee victories included a 9-8 win over All-American Caleb Campos, an 11-3 win over Aaron Ayzerov and an 8-0 shutout against Christian Hansen.

With two outstanding options at 184-pounds, Penn State is primed for a good chance at an individual championship win during the 2027 Big Ten and National Championships.
