title: Stock up, stock down | RB Cam Wallace breaks out, WRs sit back in Penn State’s first Big Ten win
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State finally won a Big Ten game under Matt Campbell, as the Nittany Lions beat Purdue, 31-17, at Beaver Stadium on Saturday.

Without wide receivers Koby Howard and Chase Sowell, Penn State looked to the run game and aggressive decision-making to beat the Boilermakers. However, there were still some concerns the Nittany Lions must address.

Here’s whose stock rose and whose stock fell in Penn State’s first Big Ten win of the season.

Stock up: Cam Wallace

Because Carson Hansen was announced as the starting running back, it came as a surprise to see Cam Wallace receive the first carry.

Wallace hadn’t touched the football since getting two carries in Week 4 against Wisconsin, but he looked like a completely different player and finished with a career-best 135 rushing yards against Purdue.

“He has continued to stay the course,” Campbell said postgame. “How he's practiced has earned the right to go in and not just play, but honestly take advantage of his opportunity. That's what I'm really excited about.”

Wallace’s explosive 48-yard rush late in the first quarter helped set up Penn State’s second touchdown, and he finished the game as the Nittany Lions’ top running back, tallying 135 rushing yards and a touchdown, averaging 6.1 yards per carry.

Hansen wasn’t too far behind, accumulating 96 rushing yards and a touchdown, averaging 5.6 yards per carry.

Wallace didn’t get into the end zone until 9:23 remaining in the fourth quarter, a 2-yard rush up the middle — a reward from the coaching staff for his career-best performance.

Stock down: Wide receivers without Koby Howard or Chase Sowell

It wasn’t a surprise to see the wide receivers take a backseat role when Koby Howard and Chase Sowell were listed out before the game. Howard was the core of the offense through the first three weeks of the season before his injury, and Sowell later adopted that role.

Without either, Rocco Becht found the tight ends more often and even worked the running backs into the passing game while still looking for big plays out of wide receiver Brett Eskildsen.

Eskildsen was the most-targeted wide receiver with four opportunities, but he only had one catch. Becht tried to find him in the end zone, but the ball was underthrown and cornerback Don Saunders ran right into him. No flag was thrown.

Meanwhile, true freshman Amarion Jackson’s two catches for 31 receiving yards were the most by a wide receiver Saturday. Zay Robinson had a catch for seven yards.

Tight end Benjamin Brahmer was the top receiver overall with four catches for 58 yards on seven targets, closely followed by Andrew Rappleyea’s 45 yards.

Stock up: Pass rush

Although the Nittany Lions didn’t record a sack until defensive end Yvan Kemajou’s late in the fourth quarter, the pass rush was much improved.

Penn State hurried quarterback Ryan Browne six times, leading to Browne going 10-for-29 with two interceptions. Defensive end Alexander McPherson — someone who’s earned more playing time as of late — had two quarterback hurries in the first quarter.

Defensive end Caleb Bacon also hurried the quarterback twice, while linebacker Tony Rojas and defensive lineman Keanu Williams had the others. Kemajou would’ve had one of his own, but he was called for roughing the passer despite Browne still holding the football when contact was made.

Even when Browne got the ball out on his lone touchdown pass of the game, McPherson applied heavy pressure and Bacon whiffed on a sack, and the throw was made in desperation while falling to the ground.

Stock down: James Peoples

Running back James Peoples has been a regular in the backfield, averaging 8.14 carries per game with a high of 14 against Wisconsin. He’s been trending down since his 67-yard performance against the Badgers, with 20 yards on seven carries against USC being his best performance since Week 4.

Peoples stock plummeted again, as he didn’t get a single carry against Purdue. Wallace took Peoples’ spot in the depth chart Saturday and forced the coaching staff to keep him on the field, leaving the Ohio State transfer out of the equation.

Campbell called Hansen and Wallace an “elite one-two punch” after the game, and said the pair looked closer to how he wants Penn State’s run game to be for the rest of the season.

However, Campbell also said the same thing about Hansen and Peoples after the USC game, but Peoples has seemingly been eclipsed by Wallace. If that’s the case, there’ll be no room for Peoples to make an impact should Wallace win the long-term position battle.

Stock up: Aggressive decision-making on offense

Campbell has been known for his passive decision-making earlier in the season, drawing boos from the home crowd any time he sent Nathan Tiyce on the field to punt.

That all changed against the Boilermakers, as he routinely kept the offense on the field on fourth down. It worked splendidly for the Nittany Lions, who went three-for-three on fourth-down conversions.

Tiyce was seen working on rugby-style throws in warmups, and got to show his Australian roots on a fake field goal play. He threw the ball underhanded to Brahmer on fourth-and-7 for 13 yards, getting down to Purdue’s 7-yard line and setting up Rapplyea's touchdown to take a 7-0 lead.

Hansen’s 1-yard rushing touchdown later in the contest was scored on fourth-and-goal, and it was the eventual game-winning score.

Gutsy decision-making like this was a major factor in Penn State’s victory, and who knows what would’ve happened if Campbell was this aggressive against Wisconsin or Northwestern.

title: Iowa State professor gives lecture on AI’s potential to both protect, harm energy infrastructure
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
Around 20 students and faculty took their seats in 108 Chambers Building Friday to listen to a lecture by award-winning Iowa State University Professor Manimaran Govindarasu on finding new ways to protect power grids and energy infrastructure as cyberattacks using artificial intelligence (AI) increase.

Despite technical difficulties delaying the lecture’s start time by several minutes, Govindarasu, an Iowa State University Anson Marston Distinguished Professor in Engineering and Murray J. and the Ruth M. Harpole Professor in Electrical and Computer Engineering, surged past the obstacle and gave an hourlong talk on AI’s impact on cybersecurity, from cybercrimes to espionage.

Govindarasu said cybersecurity professionals are using AI to find vulnerabilities even in the foundations of the internet, such as PHP, the language behind up to 70% of websites.

During the lecture, he said this proliferation of AI and growing cyberthreats create a need for more investigations into how AI can help prevent attacks on power grids, including those improved on or created by the technology.

Govindarasu also said the protection of energy infrastructure in the face of increasing AI-based cyberthreats could potentially be achieved by enacting stricter security measures; like a “zero-trust” architecture, which would install stricter authorization and access controls within a system, making successful cyberattacks harder.

Govindarasu, who has conducted years of research into improving the cybersecurity capabilities of power grids, often with funding from several academic organizations and federal agencies like the U.S. Department of Energy and Department of Defense, said in an interview that there needs to be a more "adversarial" way of thinking among cybersecurity professionals to fully leverage the benefits of AI to better protect from energy infrastructure threats.

“The whole national security and economic security is centered around the security and resiliency of the grid infrastructure. If AI-based adversarial models are going to be leveraged by adversaries, could be hackers or terrorist groups, they can target our critical infrastructure,” Govindasaru said. “The first thing for a defender to understand is what adversaries can do so that we can stay ahead of the game in terms of using those same solutions for developing the most advanced security solutions.”

Nilanjan Chaudhuri, a professor in the College of Engineering whose research and interest areas include AI and energy systems, said he shares similar views to Govindarasu on how AI is currently being used both constructively and destructively.

He said harnessing the potential cybersecurity applications of AI will require the cooperation of multiple disciplines and backgrounds, such as engineering and computer science.

“One of the challenges in today’s world, so far as the cybersecurity risks are concerned to our critical infrastructure, is power systems,” Chaudhuri said. “You look at the opportunities as to how you mitigate those challenges, it's not just electrical engineering. It's a cross-disciplinary sweet spot where you can apply your talents and you can grow and be part of the workforce in future.”

Steve Zukley said that despite being required to attend lectures to further study for his master’s degree in electrical engineering, he found the intersection of AI and cybersecurity in Govindarasu’s talk to be particularly interesting, since it was something he “really hadn't considered.”

Since much of the U.S. power grid, including its computer systems, is several decades old, he said, there's an increasing need to find ways to keep pace with modern threats.

“If the power grid goes down during a blizzard or during a heat wave, people will pass away,” Zukley said. “Quantum computing is still kind of on the horizon but everyone has access to AI, the good guys and the bad guys, so I think that's the main reason that this is such an important talk to have.”

title: Preview | Penn State women’s basketball opens Tanisha Wright era against Cleveland State
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Basketball season has arrived. At 5 p.m. on Monday, Devyn Quigley and Co. will lace up their sneakers, Joe Putnam’s voice will hit the airwaves, and the Tanisha Wright era will officially tip off against Cleveland State inside the Bryce Jordan Center.

“We're ready to get started,” Wright said at local media day. “It's been a long time coming. We started this journey with zero players, so to be able to field the roster of 11 and the caliber of people that they are, we're ready to get started, so excited.”

The Lady Lions got started in the form of an exhibition against the University of Pittsburgh at Johnstown on Oct. 27. Penn State blew out the Division II Mountain Cats, 84-47.

In the lopsided matchup, Petra Božan played like a seasoned Big Ten opponent against a Division II team. The Split, Croatia, native scored the first four points of the game and finished with 20 points. She made nine of her 12 shots and physically dominated inside.

Božan was often spelled by Cristen Carter, who racked up eight rebounds, including six offensive snags. The two forwards did spend time on the floor together, a possibility that Wright addressed at local media day.

“Everybody knows that we have 11 players, and so we're going to take advantage and take the opportunities that present themselves,” Wright said. “There might be opportunities that present that they need to play together, and so we're going to take advantage of our full bench and use it to the best of our ability.”

It remains to be seen how much time the 6-foot-4 pair will spend on the court together in the regular season, but Wright previewed the strategy in the exhibition.

Another preseason theme is the reliance on Quigley and Enjulina Gonzalez in the backcourt. The duo played 33 and 35 minutes, respectively, against Pitt-Johnstown.

Quigley scored 16 points, Gonzalez led the team in assists, and perhaps most importantly, Gonzalez didn’t turn the ball over. The team totaled 18 giveaways, including four by Božan and three apiece by young guards Ava Black and Kamrah Banks. Carter and Savannah White also added three each, and Quigley turned it over twice.

Wright’s squad will need to rein that in as they enter the regular season. Out of the Horizon League, Cleveland State represents a solid opportunity for a fast start.

The Vikings were picked seventh in the Horizon League preseason coaches poll and have no projected all-league player. Last year, Cleveland State went 26-10 and made a run to the WNIT quarterfinals. However, none of its returning players averaged more than 4.1 points.

Like Penn State, the Vikings are also under a first-year head coach, and it’s a familiar face. Bob Dunn spent last season on Carolyn Kieger’s staff in Happy Valley after stints as an assistant at Miami, Cleveland State, George Mason and Wager.

At Penn State, one of the Cleveland-area native’s specialties was coaching the post, where he guided Gracie Merkle to the best field goal percentage in the country. Now, Dunn is trying to leverage his high major experience into success at his hometown school.

When Dunn returns to the BJC on Monday, it should be a fresh slate in blue and white. The lone returning player, Vitória Santana, didn’t appear in the exhibition game, so barring a surprise, the season opener will focus on introducing the new-look Lady Lions.

title: Projecting Penn State men’s basketball’s starting lineup ahead of 2026-27 season
author: Will Horstman | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State received big news Friday ahead of its season opener on Monday night against Canisius. Forward Roko Prkačin was cleared to play by the NCAA, making him on track to be available after missing the team’s two exhibition games.

Prkačin was a part of Mike Rhoades’ remake of the Nittany Lions’ roster this offseason. Rhoades added 11 new players to the team, which means the starting five will look very different this upcoming season as compared to last.

Here’s a projection of what the starting five will look like for the Nittany Lions once the season opens in just a couple of days.

Point guard: Dasonte Bowen

Dasonte Bowen seems to be the clear favorite to start at point guard. He missed the first exhibition game against St. Bonaventure, but returned when Penn State faced Drexel last Monday, starting at point guard.

Bowen brings experience, having played two seasons at St. Bonaventure and two years at Iowa. He averaged 10.9 points, 3.0 rebounds and 4.8 assists per game with the Bonnies last season.

He has a fifth year of eligibility because an injury cut his 2024-25 season short. Bowen was a late add in the transfer portal by Penn State not because no one wanted him, but because he’s not sure many people were aware he had an extra year.

“That could be why it took a little bit longer than most,” Bowen said. “But what stood out to me about here was just the honesty that coach came with instantly. He instantly told me nothing would be promised, but there'd be a great opportunity, and I'd have to come here and work and go from there. That stood out to me just because I'm big on those types of values.”

Shooting guard: Brant Byers

Brant Byers grew up a Penn State fan. He attended some Nittany Lions basketball games as a kid, and now he gets to play for them after transferring in from Miami (Ohio).

Byers brings a level of shooting Penn State hasn’t seen in a while. Byers shot 3-pointers at a 39.2% clip last season, which makes him a good fit at shooting guard in the starting five. He’s also 6-foot-8, so he’ll have a size advantage here.

Byers is brought in after Rhoades gave him a chance to build a basketball program at Penn State. He’ll get to help make it happen as a projected starter.

“A big part of why I came here is obviously I'm from Pennsylvania, so Penn State basketball has always been kind of personal to me growing up,” Byers said. “I've always been a fan, and then coach Rhoades and the staff also just made a pitch that I couldn't turn down.”

Small forward: Josh Reed

Due to injuries and other personnel decisions, Josh Reed played more at power forward last season than the team expected. Now, Penn State has the ability to keep him at small forward more often, which is his best fit in this starting five.

Reed is currently eligible to play and recently received good news from the Ohio eligibility lawsuit, in which he is a plaintiff, as he looked to play another year of college basketball after the 5-in-5 rule changes. The Ohio Supreme Court reversed a decision that made Reed and the other plaintiffs ineligible, so he’s good to go to play for Penn State.

It’s important to note that his status might change in the future as the legal process continues to play out. But Reed will certainly be a main contributor again after averaging 11.5 points and 4.1 rebounds per game last season.

“I’m just focusing on basketball, keeping that the main thing and controlling what I can control,” Reed said. “There's a lot of things right now that are out of my hands.”

Power forward: Roko Prkačin

It really can’t be overstated how important it was for Penn State to get Prkačin eligible for the 2026-27 season. He’s classified as a fifth-year player who has just one season of eligibility, but he’ll be a key player this season.

Prkačin is a true power forward for the Nittany Lions, who haven’t really had a player like this recently. He averaged 10 points and 4.3 rebounds per game with Nanterre 92 last season in France’s top professional league in France.

Prkačin said it was a straightforward decision to play for Penn State, and he wasn’t really considering other college teams.

“I spoke to coach Rhodes, and I really love his idea and program about everything, and really enjoy the culture he's building here,” Prkačin said. “I saw myself in that situation.”

Center: Ivan Jurić

Ivan Jurić is back for Year 2 as Penn State’s center. He really flashed his potential in his freshman year, so he could be primed for another step forward in his development this season. He’s ready to apply what he learned going through a Big Ten schedule last season.

“It's the little things that win games,” Jurić said. “Every team can beat every other team. I would say, like getting the 50-50 balls, just diving on the floor. It's those little things that literally separate the difference.”

Jurić averaged 10.2 points and 5.3 rebounds per game last season. He’s still the youngest player on a team that got much older this offseason, but he’s going to be one of the leaders on the court.

Projected top rotational players

Penn State doesn’t have as much depth as Rhoades would like, but it still has some key pieces who can come off the bench. Notably, guard Roberts Blums offers high-scoring potential off the bench.

Guard Thomas Allard has impressed during the offseason after making the jump from Division II. He could push for a starting spot, as Rhoades likes his mistake-free play, but it’s hard to see where with the roster fully available.

Forward François Wibaut will also play sizable minutes off the bench with his defense. Expect him to be relied on in late-game defensive situations.

Forward Tim Oboh will back up Jurić at center and guard Jay Rodgers will spell Bowen at point guard. It’s a 10-man rotation for Rhoades and the Nittany Lions, who look to improve from a 12-20 record last year.

title: Week 9 report card | Penn State offense bounces back, defense holds steady in win over Purdue
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s first Big Ten win in the Matt Campbell era is finally here after the Nittany Lions defeated Purdue 31-17 on Saturday.

They had success on both sides of the ball with a dominant running attack from Cam Wallace and a pair of interceptions from safeties Jamison Patton and Jeremiah Cooper.

Here’s how I’d grade Penn State in its win over the Boilermakers.

Overall: B+

Coaching staff: A

Campbell made a handful of aggressive decisions on fourth down, including electing for a fake field goal where punter Nathan Tiyce threw the ball rugby-style to tight end Benjamin Brahmer for a first down.

Offense: A-

While the Nittany Lions moved the ball via the running game and through the air, the lack of wide receiver contribution was somewhat alarming.

Penn State was without star receivers Chase Sowell and Koby Howard, so Brett Eskildsen and Amarion Jackson were the starters. The two, along with Zay Robinson, had just four catches for 55 yards.

Pass game: B+

Becht played some of his best Big Ten football against the Boilermakers, throwing with 67% accuracy for 175 yards and a touchdown.

He was able to get tight ends Andrew Rappleyea and Benjamin Brahmer involved, finishing the day with a combined eight catches for 106 yards.

Run game: A

While Purdue has the worst passing defense in the Big Ten, Penn State relied on the ground game without Sowell and Howard.

Wallace ran for 135 yards, averaging 6.1 yards per carry with a touchdown. Carson Hansen also had his best performance of the season with 96 yards on 17 attempts while also finding the end zone.

Offensive line: A-

For the first time in Big Ten play, Penn State's offensive line generated big gaps for the run game to develop. However, they were worse in pass coverage, giving up two sacks.

Defense: A-

Penn State’s defense performed well enough to come out with a win over the Boilermakers. However, it gave up two big passing plays in the first quarter that led to Purdue's only offensive touchdown of the day.

Pass rush: B

The fact that someone other than Rojas was able to generate a sack warrants celebration for the Nittany Lions. Defensive end Yvan Kemajou recorded his second sack of the season, while the rest of the defense recorded six quarterback hits.

Secondary: A-

It’s no secret that Penn State boasts one of the best secondaries in the Big Ten, if not in all of college football, led by cornerbacks Audavion Collins and Daryus Dixson.

Quarterback Ryan Browne, who averaged the fourth-most yards per game in the conference coming into Saturday, was held to just 142 yards against the Nittany Lions, but had passes of 38 yards and 32 yards in the same drive, leading to a touchdown.

Linebackers: B-

There was nothing special about Penn State’s linebacker play against Purdue, as Kooper Ebel had the best performance with three tackles and a pass breakup.

Special teams: F

Penn State's special teams had its worst performance of the season on Saturday.

Kicker Ryan Barker missed two of his three field goal attempts, while one of Nathan Tiyce’s two punt attempts was blocked and returned for a touchdown.

title: ‘Our fans make the difference’ | Despite sparse crowd, fans at Beaver Stadium make presence felt
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
The Beaver Stadium crowd was bleak on Saturday. Penn State’s run out of the tunnel was one of the quietest in recent years. There were loads of empty seats in the upper bowl, and the student section was never even close to filling up.

But late in the game, it didn’t feel like that, even with the student section emptying out as the night waned on Halloween. The crowd made its voice heard on a few flags, or lack thereof, and brought momentum back to the Nittany Lions when they needed it most.

“We have the most loyal fanbase in all of college football,” offensive lineman Cooper Cousins said postgame. “I know there's a lot of people out there that might like to degrade our fanbase and say a lot of nasty stuff about our university and our fanbase, but you look at our fanbase every Saturday, and it's people not only from around the state that are taking off work, are leaving their home, getting a hotel, and parking in an RV two days before the game.”

Cousins added, “I say it all the time, our fans are 12th man, and our fans make the difference. The more the merrier, and they showed up tonight and they packed Beaver, and we're nothing without them, so I appreciate them.”

It was expected that Saturday’s matchup against Purdue, which resulted in a 31-17 win for Penn State, wasn’t going to come close to reaching Beaver Stadium’s capacity. Tickets were available for as low as $3 before kickoff. A chicken basket inside costs $17.25

But Penn State was holding firm, with the athletic department’s verified tickets not dropping below $50. The announced attendance on Saturday was 102,041, which seemed like a stretch.

There were a lot of different factors contributing to a lack of fans in the stadium. For starters, both the Nittany Lions and the Boilermakers entered the contest at 3-4. Penn State had yet to win a Big Ten game, with a lot of the fanbase severely unhappy with the football program and Vice President for Intercollegiate Athletics Pat Kraft.

It was also Halloween, and a 4:15 p.m. kick is a bit late for some students who had their eyes set on a night out.

Regardless, those who came stuck around. And Campbell was impressed with the showing, taking the time to thank the fans in an opening statement postgame.

“To our fans that were here today, I thought we had the energy in that stadium,” Campbell said. “What they gave our football team was awesome, and I really just can't thank them enough. So I wanted to start off and certainly say that they were incredible.”

Linebacker Kooper Ebel said he didn’t even notice the crowd wasn’t as full Saturday considering how loud it got at some moments. Beaver Stadium was specifically rocking in the third quarter after defensive end Yvan Kemajou was called for roughing the passer, even though he made contact with Purdue quarterback Ryan Browne when the ball was still in his hand.

The crowd was booing nonstop in the minutes after and absolutely erupted after safety Jamison Patton picked off Browne just two plays later.

“It sounded just as full as normal, especially when you're at home and you're playing defense,” Ebel said. “We felt their support all the way throughout the entire game. I know, especially late in the game.”

But the lack of fan attendance on Saturday is concerning if it becomes a consistent trend. The Wisconsin game in Week 4 also had lots of empty chairs, and fans aren’t going to want to spend hard-earned money on a Penn State game if the product on the field isn’t what they expect.

There are only two home games left for the Nittany Lions, with one on the Saturday before the university’s Thanksgiving Break, so it’s foregone conclusion the student section will be thin.

The rest of the stadium might fill up, though, if Campbell and company can build off this win against Purdue.

“We love the fans out there,” cornerback Daryus Dixson said. “Win or lose, they always cheering for us. So it's always grateful to have fans out there.”

title: ‘He was the shining star’ | Penn State RB Cam Wallace has a career night after long journey back
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
When running back Cam Wallace plowed his way into the end zone in the fourth quarter, it capped off the best performance of his career, rushing for 135 yards and a touchdown. But it was a long journey to get there with many bumps along the way.

Wallace broke both of his ankles on a rush against Kent State in 2024 that ended his season. After working back from the injury in 2025, he entered his name into the transfer portal following the firing of James Franklin before withdrawing it and returning to the Nittany Lions.

“I've been through a lot in my career, so everything just falling in place for the work that I put in, I'm just happy for myself, for this team,” Wallace said postgame.

After suffering the injury, it took him almost a year to get back to full health and be back on the field. During the process, he worked through everything with his roommate, tight end Andrew Rappleyea, who also suffered a season-ending injury in 2024.

“To see him just trust the process, obviously come back here, make the right decision, and obviously the running back room has been a bunch of changes, different guys getting snaps, and then him just sticking, staying ready and getting his opportunity,” Rappelyea said. “I told him before the game, I was like, ‘Bro, you've been waiting for this. Like go out there and do your thing today, bro.’”

Wallace stayed motivated through his time off the field. He continued to remember his biggest inspiration, and never wavered when the situations weren’t in his favor.

“A lot of people don't make it out where I'm from,” Wallace said. “And just look back at those people back at home, man, they don't give up, and they're still going through their struggles back at home. So while I'm here at Penn State, I'm blessed with this opportunity. So why would I give up? And I can be an outlet for them down the road.”

Wallace entered this season as the fourth running back on the depth chart. Prior to the game against Purdue, his last carry on offense was a 2-yard rush in the first quarter against Wisconsin on Sept. 26.

After standing on the sidelines for over a month, his work in practice eventually forced Matt Campbell’s hand into playing him, and he took advantage of the opportunity.

“I think last Tuesday and Thursday in the bye week, inside runs, some scrimmage opportunities, and this guy was the shining star,” Campbell said. “I said it Wednesday in our team meeting, I said it Thursday, and then you went out to practice again on Thursday, and again he was the shining star. And to not be the guy playing, and then to come out and demand to play and make us play him.”

In Wallace’s four years at Penn State, he’s consistently been buried in the running back room. In the past three years, he’s sat behind running backs Nick Singleton and Kaytron Allen, both of whom are now in the NFL.

This season, he waited his turn, continuing to show flashes in practice, and when the moment arose after the bye week, he capitalized, giving Penn State its best rushing performance in Big Ten play.

“They come back in their fourth year and have a game like today, and are busting their tail in practice, busting their tail in the off season, grinding for the scout team, and now he gets his opportunity to shine, and he capitalizes and makes the most of it, and all the credit to Cam, the hard work that he's put in through his time here,” offensive lineman Cooper Cousins said.

Wallace said he “knew before tonight” that he was going to get the chance to prove himself on the field, and the way he prepared gave him the confidence to emerge as the top running back against the Boilermakers.

After the game, the locker room was in celebration of not only the win, but the performance Wallace had in the Nittany Lions’ first Big Ten victory of the season. Running back Carson Hansen said he couldn’t wipe the smile off his face for the night Wallace had, while Rocco Becht said he was proud of him after everything he’s gone through.

It was a night for Wallace where all the work physically and mentally that he went through to get to this moment came to fruition, having a career game just two years after suffering two broken ankles.

“People have it worse than me,” Wallace said. “You could say I had it the worst out of everybody. But, man, people had it worse than me. And I just think back on the people that had it bad, they kept going. I got people back home that's looking up to me, so if I give up, I'm giving them the mindset of oh, they can give up when something hard comes."

"So as long as I keep pushing forward and doing what I need to do, I'm giving those young kids and those guys back home that's looking at me motivation to keep going through what they're going through.”

title: Penn State’s ‘ability to respond’ to penalties, missed calls contributes to first Big Ten victory
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
A smaller but mighty Beaver Stadium crowd devolved into a symphony of boos after the referees missed a pass interference call on a Rocco Becht deep ball to wide receiver Brett Eskildsen in the second quarter against Purdue.

The Penn State faithful got even louder when the same situation happened to tight end Benjamin Brahmer on the next play.

Those two missed calls led to what could only be described as the worst-case scenario on fourth down. Punter Nathan Tiyce was crushed by Bisi Owens, and the ball sputtered to the turf. Jalil Hall scooped it up and took it to the house to tie the game, 14-14.

“It's college football, things are going to happen,” running back Carson Hansen said postgame. “You got to go out and just make a play, and you got to be able to step up in those moments of adversity. You can't let the circumstances dictate your behavior.”

Despite numerous calls going against Penn State on Saturday night, the Nittany Lions never wavered, winning their first Big Ten game under Matt Campbell, 31-17.

Campbell was animated on the sidelines after the missed interference call on Eskildsen, even staring down the referee as Hall ran to the end zone. But if you asked the rest of the team, they’d say they gave it no second thought.

Campbell said the team did let situations like these affect their mindset in the past. However, he noticed major improvement two weeks ago in Ann Arbor, Michigan, as the Nittany Lions fought through adversity to keep the game close.

He said the difference against Purdue was Penn State’s “ability to respond.” Instead of allowing emotions to get in the way, the Nittany Lions marched right back down the field and Hansen scored on fourth-and-goal 15 plays later.

“It was team,” Campbell said. “Defensively, it was a great situation. After the block kick, you can easily see the momentum. It was a tie game, we go right down the field and score. Those are where we're growing. That's not in the stat line, that's not in the flashy stuff, but that's what I've watched in this team.”

The officiating got in the way on the defensive side of the ball, too. Penn State would’ve forced a punt in the third quarter if it weren’t for defensive end Yvan Kemajou’s roughing the passer call. Quarterback Ryan Browne still had the ball in his hand when Kemajou hit him, and the crowd made sure to let the referees know they were upset.

A call like that could debilitate an undisciplined team, but that wasn’t the case for Penn State. Safety Jamison Patton was in the “right place at the right time” for an interception on the very next play, which contributed to a field goal that extended the Nittany Lions’ lead to two scores.

Patton called his timely pick a “momentum shift,” something cornerback Daryus Dixson further elaborated on.

“Momentum is everything,” Dixson said. “It’s about just having high hopes for yourself and for the team that we're gonna break out of whatever calls that don't go our way. Even when we got the stop, and then we got the flag on it, nobody got down on ourselves. We were just thinking, ‘let's go, next play.’”

Dixson said the team remained “level-headed” after the roughing the passer penalty, only focused on making good on the next opportunity. On offense, Becht’s philosophy was much the same — there wasn’t anything the players themselves could do about the officiating except continue to play hard.

“I think you’ve just got to continue to go play-by-play,” Becht said. “Don't worry about what the refs are doing, don't worry about what the defense is doing, just worry about us. Control what we can control, and just make the play.”

title: ‘It feels awesome’ | Penn State players celebrate 1st Big Ten victory after continued growth
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Offensive lineman Anthony Donkoh stood on the field with arms stretched wide and a smile from ear to ear while the victory bell rang in the background. For the first time in 42 days, Penn State had won.

The Nittany Lions defeated Purdue 31-17 to earn their first Big Ten victory under Matt Campbell. The win marked the end of a four-game losing streak and showcased the work that’s been going on behind the scenes to break that skid.

“It feels awesome,” linebacker Kooper Ebel said postgame. “We've been so close in so many games. We've had a handful of one-score games. To be able to finish a game the right way, play complementary football, and build some momentum going into the back half of the season after bye week is awesome.”

Even though Penn State has been close in recent games, it hasn’t been enough to win. After being blown out at Northwestern, the Nittany Lions had back-to-back one-score games against USC and Michigan as miscues overtook the bits of success on the field.

During that period of struggles, Campbell said everyone stayed true to the process. Even though the losses continued to stack up, the team’s growth was evident as the deficits cut from eight points to three points and eventually a win.

“This group's never wavered. They've never flinched,” Campbell said. “They haven't b— or complained. They just go to work and tried like heck to correct the areas and grow themselves forward.”

That work ethic was the result of the players knowing the potential they had. Throughout nonconference play, the team showcased what they were capable of, but had fallen short against Big Ten opponents.

“When you have so much talent like we have and it's just not being shown, it's just like damn bro, we’re 0-4 in the Big 10,” tight end Andrew Rappleyea said. “It feels good to just get a dub with the guys.”

While Penn State’s notable postseason chances are obsolete, Campbell has emphasized fighting for victories the rest of the season for the seniors who have faced adversity this season and in years past.

But for some of the players, the continued fight has been important to see different players step up and make the most of their moments. Against Purdue, freshman wide receiver Amarion Jackson had his first career start, while running back Cam Wallace led the team on the ground.

“Seeing some of the guys getting those opportunities go, (Amarion Jackson) getting his first start at receiver in, it was cool,” Rappleyea said. “It was a good day for the guys.”

Going into this week’s game against Purdue, many players knew it was finally time to turn the tides. Penn State was coming off a bye week and had been making incremental progress over the last few weeks.

“I said to a bunch of the guys there was no sane world we could have afforded to lose this weekend,” Rappleyea said. “We knew that, and it felt good for guys to back up against the wall and go do their thing.”

While the win was a morale boost after a long period of struggle, it also provided a momentum boost for the rest of the year.

The Nittany Lions have four games left of the season, needing two more wins to become bowl eligible. Saturday’s victory was a step in that direction for Year 1 under Campbell.

“Obviously, you know it sucks for the prior results, but we continued to stay the course, continued to grow, and everybody just continued to stay bought in,” Rocco Becht said. “Nobody complained. Nobody wanted to walk away. Everyone wanted to just come to work every single day, and that's what our result was tonight.”

title: 3 takeaways from Penn State’s first Big Ten win under Matt Campbell against Purdue
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Two 3-4 teams in Penn State and Purdue took the field at Beaver Stadium on Halloween for a chance to reach .500 on the season.

For the first time this season, the Nittany Lions came out on top in a Big Ten matchup, defeating the Boilermakers 31-17.

Here’s three takeaways from the first conference victory under Matt Campbell.

Run game has potential

After running back Carson Hansen was announced as the starter before the game, running back Cam Wallace recorded the first run of the contest from the fullback position.

That was foreshadowing of what was to come for the Nittany Lions, as Wallace went on to have the bulk of carries against Purdue. He finished the day with 22 carries for 135 yards and a touchdown.

“Cam had an incredible two weeks,” Campbell said postgame. “He has continued to stay the course, and how he's practiced has earned the right to go in and not just play, but honestly take advantage of his opportunity. And that's what I'm really excited about.”

But it wasn’t just the amount of carries he had that generated offense — Wallace came through with multiple big plays, including a 48-yard rush in the first quarter and a 12-yard pickup in the second quarter for a first down where he broke a pair of tackles.

While Wallace was the leading back, Hansen had arguably his best performance of the season with 94 yards on 17 attempts and a score. He had his biggest run of the year with a 42-yard rush off the left side on Penn State’s opening drive.

“I thought both those guys, Carson and Cam, were an elite one-two punch tonight,” Campbell said.

Becht’s legs also played a factor against the Boilermakers, as he rushed 11 times for 27 yards. He also found the end zone.

Despite James Peoples and Quinton Martin Jr. recording more carries this season, neither saw the field. This was the first game split between Wallace and Hansen, and it appeared to pay off.

The Nittany Lions were able to carry momentum on the ground with the two, finishing the day with 250 rushing yards.

Aggressive decision-making wins games

Rocco Becht couldn’t find Benjamin Brahmer on back-to-back plays near the end zone on the first drive, so punter Nathan Tiyce rugby-pitched the ball to him on a fake punt to convert on fourth down.

One play later, Becht passed the ball to tight end Andrew Rappleyea, who dove in the end zone, putting the Nittany Lions on the board early.

“Coach Lustig does a great job with our special teams,” Campbell said. “That’s great execution, Nathan Tice. Thank goodness we got an Aussie, that underhand pitch looked pretty sweet, and then did a great job finishing on it.”

That was just one of the three times Campbell elected to go for it on fourth down, and the Nittany Lions converted all three, with two leading to touchdowns.

In the second quarter, Becht kept the ball on fourth-and-1 and earned just enough distance with his legs to convert, although the drive later ended with a Purdue touchdown from a blocked punt.

Penn State’s third conversion came at the Boilermakers’ 1-yard line, with Hansen scoring a touchdown in his fourth straight game.

After there was a lot of noise regarding Campbell’s lack of aggression in fourth-down situations earlier in the season, his aggressiveness was on display against the Boilermakers, ultimately leading to a pair of touchdowns.

No wide receiver steps up without Howard, Sowell

Without leading receivers Howard and Sowell, Brett Eskildsen and true freshman Amarion Jackson were named starters, marking Jackson’s first career start.

However, the two had very underwhelming games, combining for just 48 yards on three catches. Wide receiver Zay Robinson saw the field, but also only had one reception for seven yards.

Instead, it was the tight ends and Wallace who earned the bulk of Becht’s passes.

“I kind of think that's what offensive football is,” Campbell said. “You have a good player go down, the next guy's got to step up. I thought the tight ends stepped up in a great way, and obviously the running game had that too.”

Brahmer and Rappleyea each had four receptions, combining for nearly half of Becht’s completions. The two tight ends had 103 receiving yards, including a contested 33-yard pickup on third down from Brahmer.

Wallace was the only other player who had multiple catches against Purdue. However, his were mostly dump offs from Becht when he faced pressure.

There was a chance both Sowell and Howard would see the field, as they were listed questionable on Wednesday and Thursday. Their absences hindered Penn State’s passing game, but the run game stepped up to earn the victory.

title: No. 7 Penn State women's hockey dominates RIT, earns 7th straight win
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
After a close 1-0 win over RIT on Friday, No. 7 Penn State women’s hockey took the ice again, looking for its third straight series win.

It was all treats and no tricks for the Nittany Lions, as the squad left with an overwhelming 6-0 victory over the Tigers.

First period

The matchup started off with Penn State winning the opening faceoff and possessing the puck with four shots taken in the first two minutes. Just under three minutes into the opening frame, the blue and white’s Mikah Keller scored an even-strength goal assisted by Kayla McCarthy and McKenna Walsh to make the score 1-0 quickly.

After the goal, the period remained end-to-end between both squads until RIT’s Brac Kelley got called for a high-stick penalty, resulting in the blue and white getting a power play. Just under a minute into the power play, Penn State extended its lead when Abby Stonehouse was assisted by Sofia Ismael and Sophie Morrow.

Three minutes later, RIT got a power play of its own after an interference penalty on Walsh. The Tigers then got five shots off on the power play, but the Nittany Lions did a good job of thwarting the threat and denied RIT any chances of getting on the scoreboard. The penalty barrage continued three minutes later after RIT's Mackenzie Clark got called for holding. Nothing came of the Nittany Lions penalty, though, and the period ended shortly after with the score being 2-0 Penn State.

Second period

The second period started off with heavy Penn State possession as the blue and white got nine shots off in five minutes with RIT getting only getting one. The momentum continued until Penn State's Alanna Devlin was called for a penalty 10:02 into the game. Penn State's kill stopped the threat yet again, ending the Tigers' power play swiftly. After four more minutes of Penn State possession, Rits Kailey Favro got called for a cross-checking penalty, but Penn State didn’t make anything of it.

RIT came out aggressively in the final minutes of the period, putting pressure on Penn State's defense with a flurry of shots. Maddy Campbell ended up standing tall in net, making multiple saves to keep the Nittany Lions up 2-0 despite an RIT power play late in the period.

The Nittany Lions, however, tagged on a goal of their own late in the period after Danica Maynard found the net on an assist from Megan Hosman.

Third period

The Nittany Lions continued to control the pace of the game throughout the final period, with Campbell continuing to make saves to keep Penn State up. The blue and white’s defense also stepped up as Shelby Shane and Ashley Kokavec recorded important blocks to limit the Tigers' scoring opportunities.

Penn State extended its lead when Outwater scored an even-strength goal assisted by Morrow and Hosman.

The scoring didn’t stop there for the Nittany Lions, as Stonehouse found the back of the net twice more, completing the first career hat trick for the junior forward.

Both Stonehouse’s goals in the third period were once again assisted by Morrow and Keller, showcasing the all-around dominant performance for the blue and white.

All around, it was a strong showing for Penn State, extending its winning streak to seven games.

Up Next

Penn State returns to the Keystone State, traveling to face Mercyhurst in Erie. Game 1 puck drop is set for Friday at 6 p.m.

title: Penn State women’s volleyball continues dominance on Senior Night, White Out against Purdue
author: Daniel Almash | For the Collegian
description:
A hard-earned victory Saturday afternoon for the Penn State team. They came into this matchup against 11th-seeded Purdue after winning their last four games, and that winning streak continued in this one.

The Nittany Lions took this matchup in four sets and looked dominant all afternoon. The first set went to the Nittany Lions 25-17 to start the match; the Boilermakers took the second set 25-18; Penn State won a much-needed third set by a score of 25-21, and to finish off the afternoon, senior right side hitter Kennedy Martin rocketed her 24th kill on the day to give the Nittany Lions their 16th win on the year and 9th in Big Ten conference play.

Important performances that helped the Nittany Lions to victory included Kennedy Martin, who notched 24 kills, a .321 hitting percentage, and nine digs. She additionally recorded six attack errors on 56 attempts and six blocks.

Additionally, Senior setter Alexis Stucky added to this victory by recording 40 assists, five kills, and eight digs. She also added one service ace and hit .400 on 10 attempts. Other significant performances included Junior outside hitter Emmi Sellman, who recorded 12 kills, a .229 hitting percentage, and 4 blocks, and Freshman middle blocker Kendall Northern, who tallied seven blocks.

The Nittany Lions entered this game with a 62-12 all-time advantage in this series, with 31 of those victories coming in Rec Hall.

Penn State hit .340 in the fourth set, recording 20 kills and just four attack errors on 47 attempts. While Purdue hit .371 in the fourth set, with 17 kills and four errors on 35 attempts. Despite Purdue’s higher hitting percentage in the last set, Penn State still rallied behind seniors Martin and Stucky for a fifth victory in a row.

Up next

Penn State returns to face Minnesota on Friday at 7 p.m.

title: Penn State's top 2 receivers out against Purdue
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
Penn State will be without its top two leading receivers on Saturday.

Both Chase Sowell and Koby Howard are out against Purdue. Howard was doubtful coming into Saturday, while Sowell was listed as questionable.

Howard has been out for the last four games with an undisclosed injury, but had a chance to make a return this week. Matt Campbell said the staff wouldn't let him play, however, unless he was at 100%.

Sowell, meanwhile, has been banged up with lower-body injuries in both of Penn State's last two games. It's unclear whether the injury holding him out is related.

Defensive end Yvan Kemajou and defensive tackle Armstrong Nnodim are game-time decisions. Kemajou has started every game for the Nittany Lions this season.

Depth tight end Brian Kortovich is also a game-time decision.

Defensive end Alex McPherson and safety Jeremiah Cooper were both probable on Friday's report and are not listed on Saturday's, meaning both are good to go.

Other players out include defensive tackles Alijah Carnell and Liam Andrews, while defensive end Max Granville and linebacker Alex Tatsch remain out with season-ending injuries.

Penn State's captains for Week 9 have been announced.

title: John Summit's CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour puts Happy Valley in a trance
author: Brennan Kramp I The Daily Collegian
description:
Breakthrough house and EDM artist, John Summit, played at the Bryce Jordan Center Friday night for the sixth show of his CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour.

On April 15, the 25-year-old released his second album, “CTRL ESCAPE,” to massive acclaim, with his two month arena tour starting October 1. Penn State was the second college to host Summit on his tour so far — the first being his alma mater, the University of Illinois.

In Happy Valley, Summit performed with an energy like he was reliving his party days back at school, except with the fiery excitement that he was the guy on stage instead of the guy looking up at one.

Summit’s fans embodied that spirit as well. One Penn State student, Azeem Moussa, 20, of Orange County, California, said Summit’s music gets everyone amped.

“If you aren’t hyped up after listening to his music, I don’t know what to say to you,” Moussa, a third-year studying forensic science, said.

Summit’s newest album, compared to his 2024 debut, “Comfort In Chaos,” shows Summit getting heavier as an artist.

A far more reflective album, lyrically, it talks a lot about the brutal numbness of his early days as an auditor and CPA at Ernst and Young, before he bet on himself and took the less treaded path: his dream.

Songs like “STATUS: AWAY,” “SHADOWS” and “LIGHTS GO OUT” all show different layers to that previous life that can be looked back on honestly and appreciatively, now that he has found his passion.

Carter Rodowicz, 22, of Lehigh Valley, Pennsylvania, talked about how important Summit’s music is in that respect.

“His background, coming from being an accountant to doing something that he actually wanted to pursue…I think it’s a really great message for everyone,” Rodowicz, a fourth-year studying agribusiness management, said. “It’s sort of an inspiration.”

To start the show, opening act DJs Mesto and Alok put the crowd in a feel-good mood with some dark and edgy club beats that sent little ripples of raised hands through the general admission pit. Masses of concertgoers continued to trickle into their seats, yelling over the dubstep bass notes from the stage as they tried to figure out where their other friends were.

The concert attire couldn’t have been more fitting. The general consensus was narrowed to two options: loose-fitted business attire, as an homage to the new album, or a Halloween costume — the majority of which were George Washingtons, fairy princesses and a few Waldos which were all too easy to spot.

After a 10-minute intermission at the conclusion of Alok’s set, the lights went completely black. Then, the crowd erupted into a furious cacophony of cheers.

A massive cage emerged from behind the turntable as it played Summit’s artsy intro-video of him back in the office, crunching numbers and sending emails before finally releasing himself from his cubicle.

After hitting Ctrl Esc on the computer, the screen went blank, and a booming bass drop sent shockwaves through the arena. Summit casually walked toward his turntable.

With an entrancing array of strobe lights, beams, pyro-technics, thundering basses and rattling snares, Summit unloaded every ounce of energy he had onto the crowd.

The set was a flurry of current hits, B-Side gems and rousing remixes that all gave a different vibe, and, with it, a different motion to the fans.

Summit went from bouncing, to sweating, to jumping on top of the turntable deck and then to sweating even more. His smile persisted, and his power continued to increase with each transition, while intermittently picking up his mic and asking the question Penn State was too happy to answer.

“Penn State, I love you man,” Summit said. “Are you out there or what?”

The show concluded with a thrilling finish, as Summit laid down one last roaring tune that drove the crowd into one collective headbang.

Coming from another Big Ten school, Summit knows what it takes to rally a crowd like Penn State. Because of this, he operated with ease. There was no hesitation, just a confidence in playing music true to yourself.

Arthur Silva, 17, of Pittsburgh, spoke about how Summit’s current music is a perfect combination of all the things he’s mastered thus far.

“[His music] really embodies the genre,” Silva said. “If you were to think of house music, he would represent it.”

MORE LIFESTYLE CONTENT

title: Penn State men’s hockey earns shootout win over No. 18 Minnesota in first Big Ten game of the season
author: Dominic Megats I The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State took “a step in a couple areas” after its series sweep over Canisius, according to Guy Gadowsky at his weekly presser.

With struggles still lurking, the Nittany Lions turned their attention to their first Big Ten series of the season at No. 18 Minnesota.

The blue and white’s comeback bid took them into overtime; however, the added time wasn’t enough for either team, leading to a shootout. Penn State ultimately took the extra point in the shootout.

First period

The blue and white moved quickly and aggressively to open the contest. This style of play showed up in constant body checks and quick-to-form plays. It seemed as if Penn State was able to control the game early after finding their style of play again.

However, the Golden Gophers quickly adapted and answered the attack. After a swift offensive zone entry from Minnesota, Javon Moore intercepted a soft shot from Christian Humphreys and was able to get the puck past Josh Fleming.

The Golden Gophers' onslaught continued after the early goal. Minnesota forwards were able to speed past the Nittany Lions and create space in its offensive zone. Fleming was able to keep the deficit to one, attempting to spark an opportunity the other way.

After the majority of an opening period in which the Golden Gophers led 15-7 in shots, Penn State would only hurt itself more as time bled off the clock.

Marco Mignosa was sent to the penalty box after he was caught tripping. The late call put an aggressive Minnesota offense on the power play to begin the second period.

Second period

Starting the middle frame against the man advantage, the Nittany Lions were able to kill the penalty. The blue and white were third in the Big Ten in penalty-kill percentage heading into its first game against Minnesota.

The Golden Gophers didn’t pay any mind to the failed power play as they kept the pressure on. It seemed as if the ice had tilted completely in their favor since the 10-minute mark of the opening period.

At the midway point of the second period, the only thing going Penn State’s way was its penalty kill unit. In total, the blue and white killed all four of Minnesota’s power plays.

The Nittany Lions were able to reach double digits in shots at the 8:22 mark in the second period.

LJ Mooney nearly doubled the Golden Gophers’ lead after a Mac Gadowsky turnover in the neutral zone. The sophomore found himself on a breakaway that was ultimately shut down by a nifty glove save from Fleming.

Penn State got its first power play late in the middle frame. The Nittany Lions generated scoring chances as they stayed in their offensive zone for the majority of the man advantage. However, the Golden Gophers were able to kill the penalty, ending the second period still ahead 1-0.

Third period

The blue and white started the third period killing its third penalty of the game. The Nittany Lions looked to build off another kill and spark their offense late.

With its back now against the wall, Penn State was able to develop some sort of offense. Rebounds off of the Golden Gophers netminder, Luca Di Pasquo, opened continuous opportunities for the Nittany Lions.

With chances coming in abundance for the blue and white, Justin Poirier used the chance to show off his quick release. After receiving a pass from Justin Larose, the freshman ripped a wrist shot from the left faceoff circle that beat Di Pasquo’s glove.

Penn State found the offensive presence it had to open the game. Before the final media timeout of the third period, the Nittany Lions were outshooting the Golden Gophers 8-2, a completely different script than the first two frames.

The horn sounded to end regulation after a physical final two minutes of the third period. The blue and white’s first conference game needed more than 60 minutes.

Overtime

With the ice wide open in a three-on-three battle, scoring chances from both teams held the Minnesota crowd’s breath.

With most of the overtime period, Fleming continued to be the story of the game for Penn State as he made a handful of game-saving stops.

Neither team was able to find the back of the net in the extra five minutes. The contest headed into a shootout.

Shootout

The Nittany Lions took the shootout victory as Fleming made four saves. Both Reese Laubach and Dane Dowiak found the net.

Up next

Both teams return to 3M Arena at Mariucci on Saturday at 7 p.m.

title: No. 23 Penn State women’s soccer blows out Indiana in final match of regular season
author: Zach Schroder | The Daily Collegian
description:
No. 23 Penn State faced off against the Indiana Hoosiers in the final match of the regular season. The Hoosiers came into the game having been held to zero goals in their last three games and ranked dead last in the Big Ten Standings.

Ultimately, the Nittany Lions dominated Indiana 4-0 to win the final game of their regular season.

“I think these guys wanted to go into this postseason with a lot of momentum”, said coach Erica Dambach after the match. “They knew that they were gonna put their foot on the gas in order for that to happen.”

1st Half

Indiana kicked first, but Penn State quickly gained offensive possession and earned a fast corner kick in the first minute of action. The first shot of the game for the Nittany Lions came up the left side from freshman forward Ellie Kocher, but it was blocked.

The blue and white held the ball on the Hoosiers' defensive side for almost 10 minutes before Indiana made their first offensive push. After a long pass, Indiana fourth-year midfielder Kennedy Neighbors shot far right of the goal.

A long arcing pass led to a fast-break opportunity for Penn State. After some passing toward the right corner of the box, freshman midfielder Paige Pasinski passed to senior forward Paige Kalal, who crossed to freshman midfielder Emma Johnson, who put it in the top left of the net for her first collegiate goal. The Nittany Lions led 1-0 in the 12th minute.

After some back-and-forth possessions, the blue and white took hold and pushed upfield. Kocher scored the second goal of the game and her career off a crosser from Kalal, who got the ball from junior forward Aubrey Kulpa. Penn State led 2-0 in the 22nd minute of play.

Substitutions came in, and the Hoosiers made their second scoring attempt of the night when sixth-year midfielder Jenna Chatterton shot wide left of the post. A miscue from Indiana led to Penn State’s third goal of the night when a pass back to Hoosiers fifth-year keeper Dani Jacobson went wide of her and rolled into the bottom right. Penn State led 3-0 in the 30th minute.

The Nittany Lions mostly retained possession through the rest of the first half.

2nd Half

Notable to start the second half was a keeper change for Penn State. After not really being challenged in the first half, redshirt senior Mackenzie Gress came out, and redshirt sophomore Kealey Titmuss came in for her first collegiate appearance.

“She's just business [Titmuss], she’s been so good at training, and she deserves these minutes and just really glad that she’s back from the World Cup,” Dambach said.

Indiana earned an early corner in the half, but it was headed away. That header turned into an all-out sprint from Kocher and the Hoosiers' defenders. Kocher got the shot off, but it flew high over the crossbar.

At the start of the half, it looked like Indiana was gaining some rhythm on offense, but it fizzled as the half progressed. Penn State kept the pressure on with Kulpa taking another shot. Penn State sophomore midfielder Kennedy Ring went down with an injury; she walked off under her own power but went straight to the locker room.

Neighbors tried to get something going for the Hoosiers, but her shot attempt was blocked and went wide right. Penn State still led 3-0 in the 70th minute of action. Neighbors tried at the net once more, but was denied by Titmuss for her second save of the night.

Penn State redshirt senior midfielder Molly Martin also went down with an injury and had to be carried off by medical staff; Pasinski subbed in for her. Jacobson made another good play in the box for the Hoosiers; she had two saves in the 73rd minute.

Despite the 3-0 lead late in the game, the Nittany Lions didn’t pass up any attempts to be aggressive offensively. Senior defender Kaelyn Wolfe fueled the fire more with a goal to the bottom right off her right foot; she was assisted by fellow senior defender Brooklyn Antonucci. Penn State led 4-0 in the 78th minute.

The Hoosiers tried to score in the final minutes, but the Nittany Lions defense wouldn’t concede as the clock hit zero.

Dambach talked about the mentality as her team heads into the Big Ten Tournament, “You can feel the positive energy of momentum; we’re starting to put more complete matches together … it’s all about our attacking mentality, creating chances, creating shots.”

Up Next

Penn State heads to the Big Ten Tournament, which kicks off on Wednesday in St. Louis.

title: No. 7 Penn State women's hockey holds on against RIT in close 1-0 win
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions took their first win of the series on the road against RIT by a score of 1-0 in a hard-fought matchup.

Penn State improved its streak to five consecutive wins in the third game of its six-game road trip.

First Period

Penn State netminder Morgan Stickney was active early, making a couple of easy saves within the first two minutes. RIT applied pressure early on both sides of the ice, but the pressure became reckless as a penalty was called on RIT’s Addie Alvarez for Penn State’s first power play.

The Tigers bottled up the power play well, as the Nittany Lions could only send one shot during the two minutes.

The blue and white had opportunities in front of the net early, but they couldn’t finish the plays. Both teams opened the match with fast-paced offenses, but Penn State led the shot count 7-2 after 10 minutes.

RIT earned a power play of its own following a penalty on Alanna Devlin. Similar to RIT, the Nittany Lions killed the power play while allowing only one shot during that sequence.

With six minutes left, Penn State's offense became more cohesive, connecting passes that led to quality shots. Although they didn’t convert to goals, the Nittany Lions still dominated possession.

RIT’s goaltender Oceanne Thiffault made great saves to keep the score level, as Penn State’s attack kept inching closer to the opening goal. Penn State’s advantage in shot count grew to 21-5 with two minutes left.

Penn State’s defense remained aggressive throughout the first period, forcing RIT to lose the puck in their defensive zone, which led to more shot opportunities.

The score remained without a goal scored after the first period.

Second Period

RIT’s Kailey Favro blocked two of Penn State’s shots to open the second period, which was something the Tigers had done throughout the game. They notched six blocked shots to that point.

RIT earned a second power play following a hooking penalty on Shelby Shane. The penalty kill stood strong, once again allowing one shot to head Stickney’s way, and returned to full strength.

Penn State’s domination of possession started to let up. The match became a back-and-forth affair, where both teams continuously rushed down the ice and created quick breakaways.

Nittany Lions’ junior forward Abby Stonehouse drew a holding penalty on Madison Buziak to obtain another power play chance. The trend continued, as the blue and white took one shot during the power play.

RIT’s Thiffault has performed exceptionally with four minutes left in the second period, as she’s made 16 saves to keep the Tigers in the game. After Grace Outwater was sent to the penalty box for cross-checking, Thiffault made two stops to negate a potential short-handed goal.

Once Penn State returned to full strength, both the Tigers and the Nittany Lions received a penalty, leading to 4-on-4 play. Stonehouse caught the rebound on the left side and shot across the crease to open the scoring.

Stonehouse’s goal gave Penn State a 1-0 lead heading into the final period.

Third Period

RIT’s Thiffault continued to impress, making an acrobatic save on a shot from Ashley Kokavec in front of the net.

The Tigers had an opportunity to tie the game with 15 minutes left, but Zoe Ziotas sent her shot wide on a one-on-one with Stickney.

Both teams traded shots through the first eight minutes of the third period. Penn State outshot RIT by a wide margin, holding a 56-25 advantage.

Penn State created solid looks on the offensive end, and RIT would gain possession and lose the puck in the offensive zone. This continued for the majority of the third period.

The Nittany Lion’s defense remained active, which was a large contributor to their ability to hold their lead. RIT rarely held sustained attacks and the blue and white hustled back on breakaways to stifle those opportunities.

Penn State finished the job, holding the shutout and earning the 1-0 win.

Up Next

Penn State faces RIT in Game 2 of the series at the Gene Polisseni Center at 2 p.m. Saturday.

title: No. 14 Penn State field hockey defeats No. 1 Northwestern in tightly contested regular season finale
author: Owen Lomotan I The Daily Collegian
description:
After No. 14 Penn State’s 1-0 road loss to No. 6 Iowa on Sunday, the Nittany Lions looked to bounce back and finish on a high note against the No. 1 Northwestern Wildcats to build momentum ahead of the 2026 postseason.

Heading into this contest, Penn State had officially clinched the No. 3 seed in the Big Ten standings.

The blue and white played a well-balanced game, ultimately coming away with a 2-0 win over the Wildcats at home.

The opening minutes of the matchup were high-paced and energetic, as both teams looked to gain the edge.

Junior goalkeeper Aby Deverka’s first save was a quick kick deflection just three minutes into the first quarter.

The Nittany Lions dominated possession of the ball as the first quarter moved along, but Northwestern was able to match Penn State’s tempo stride for stride.

Penn State’s first real chance to score came with five minutes remaining in the first, but the offense ultimately failed to put one in.

The Nittany Lions had two shots rejected by Northwestern goalkeeper Juliana Boon as the first quarter came to a close.

Graduate midfielder Sienna Dunn forced substantial contact, earning Penn state an early free hit to begin the second quarter as the physicality ramped up increasingly.

Sophomore forward Olivia Marthins fell in the shooting circle with just under nine minutes remaining in the second, but no foul was called, and no corner was awarded.

The Nittany Lions continued to play solid on-ball defense, which allowed them to create several consecutive fast-break chances; however, none resulted in points.

Freshman midfielder Marie McCracken’s shot with two minutes remaining in the first half fell just short, leaving the score knotted at zero-for-a-piece.

The first half concluded with neither team having scored.

Northwestern earned its first penalty corner with 13:51 remaining in the third quarter.

The Wildcats were unable to score due to several defensive deflections, yet they earned a second penalty corner just seconds later. The Nittany Lion defense held firm, and the score remained even.

The intensity of both teams increased as the ball switched hands constantly through the midway point of the third.

Freshman forward Chloe D’Hage’s leaning tip shot missed just wide at the four-minute mark of the third.

Penn State earned its first penalty chance with 3:23 remaining. Sophomore defensive back Cooper Cutchins was able to put the Nittany Lions on the board with 3:14 remaining.

The third quarter concluded with a narrow 1-0 lead for the blue and white over the Wildcats.

Northwestern nearly tied it with 12:38 remaining in regulation, but Penn State held the advantage.

The Nittany Lions continued to force contact and give themselves opportunities to attack, but the Wildcats bounced back with a penalty corner at the 7:57 mark.

The Penn State defense held firm, but junior forward Morgan Snyder was given a five-minute penalty, forcing the Nittany Lions to play on the back foot for an extended period.

With 3:12 remaining in regulation, officials called back Northwestern’s penalty corner after further review.

When Snyder returned to action, the Nittany Lions continued to press as the Wildcats pulled goalkeeper Boon to add an extra offensive player.

Penn State’s penalty chance with 2:11 remaining resulted in another goal for the Nittany Lions, this time from freshman midfielder Lilly Holmes at the 2:04 mark.

The Nittany Lions ran out the clock and secured the victory.

“I am so proud of not only getting to the point where we have a really strong seed, or our RPI is obviously really strong, but next week it’s anyone’s game. That’s what I want this group to know: anything can happen in [the] postseason, so having the belief, but also knowing that if we play our best, we can absolutely beat anyone in the country, and we showed that today,” coach Hannah Prince said postgame.

This was Penn State’s first-ever win against a No. 1 seed in program history.

Up next

The Nittany Lions will begin postseason conference play on Wednesday in Columbus, Ohio.

title: Penn State men's basketball forward Roko Prkačin ruled eligible by NCAA
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
The NCAA has ruled Roko Prkačin eligible for the 2026-27 season, according to a release from Penn State Athletics on Friday.

Prkačin did not dress for Penn State's exhibitions against St. Bonaventure and Drexel. After the clash with the Dragons, Mike Rhoades said that the program was "honoring the process" when it came to his eligibility.

A 6-foot-8 forward, Prkačin averaged 10 points and 4.3 rebounds per game last season with Nanterre 92, a top-flight basketball club in France that also produced star San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama.

The Zagreb, Croatia, native also picked up a FIBA U16 EuroBasket MVP award and two Croatian League championships before making the jump to play collegiately in the United States.

Prkačin will make his NCAA debut when Penn State begins its regular season against Canisius on Monday.

title: Preview | Guard-heavy underclassman group to contribute to Penn State women’s basketball
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
When a coach fully overhauls a roster in a single offseason, there’s bound to be a significant number of young players who often make up a chunk of the squad.

Tanisha Wright’s first group of Lady Lions is no different.

The 11-player roster features five underclassmen: three freshmen and two sophomores. It’s a guard-heavy cohort, as four of the five will play in the backcourt under Wright.

Guards

Skylar Durley is likely the most accomplished underclassman for the Lady Lions. At Nevada last season, she was named the Mountain West Freshman of the Year while playing a key role for the Wolf Pack.

Durley averaged 32.0 minutes per game under coach Amanda Levens last season, posting 11.8 points, 6.0 rebounds and 2.3 assists per game while Nevada finished 10-21. Despite her experience, she saw no action in Penn State’s exhibition win over Pitt-Johnstown on Tuesday.

“I'm really excited about her being at this level and showing that she can compete (in) the Big Ten, which, as we know, is the best conference in the country,” Wright said at local media day. “Her being able to compete on a big stage, I'm excited about that.”

Kamrah Banks joined the Lady Lions as a four-star recruit out of Crispus Attucks High School in Indianapolis. There, she set a school record with 63 points in a game, breaking a record previously held by NBA Hall of Famer Oscar Robertson.

Banks was also named a McDonald's All-American nominee and averaged 20.4 points, 4.9 rebounds, 2.7 assists and 2.4 steals as a senior. The year before, she’d averaged 26.4 points per game.

“From Day 1 to now, Kam has grown so much,” Wright said. ”Penn State used to be called Point Guard U. Some great point guards have come out of this university, and so for Kam’s growth, I'm really excited for her opportunity to continue to grow and become one of the next great point guards out of this place.”

She made two-of-three field goals Tuesday and finished with four points in her first taste of college basketball.

Another Midwestern freshman, Ashlee Brown, played at Valley High School in West Des Moines, Iowa, before playing her final season at Example Academy and committing to Wright. There, she helped her team reach the Elite Eight at the Grind Session Women’s World Championship earlier this year and was named a McDonald’s All-American nominee.

She also saw no action Tuesday.

Ava Black was the only underclassman to be placed in Wright’s starting lineup against the Mountain Cats. She shot 4-of-10 from the field and 1-of-4 from three-point range, finishing with nine points.

Black transferred from Vanderbilt, where she averaged just 2.8 points per game, but shot 52.2% from the field. She earned some postseason experience as a Commodore, as the squad was a No. 2 seed in the NCAA Tournament and advanced to the Sweet 16.

Before playing at Vanderbilt, she was a standout at Tabor Academy in Marion, Massachusetts, and claimed a NEPSAC title.

Forward

The lone forward, Irene Garcia, is a first-year out of Urnieta, Basque Country, Spain. Garcia is the shortest of Penn State’s three forwards and stands 6-foot-1.

Garcia made the jump to State College after playing for Segle XXI Academy in Spain, a program her roster page describes as “a renowned government-backed elite female basketball academy near Barcelona.” While playing at the academy, she was called up to Spain’s U14 National Team in 2022.

She led the Lady Lions’ bench with eight points against Pitt-Johnstown. They came on 4-of-6 made field goals, though Garcia did go 0-for-4 from the charity stripe.
