title: Spooky films, community events | Here’s what’s happening in the valley
author: Brennan Kramp I The Daily Collegian
description:
Monday, Oct. 26

THON Dream Forward Picnic

Continue to show out for THON, the nation's largest student run charity, at the Dream Forward Picnic. From 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. get your grub on at the HUB-Robeson Center lawn to celebrate the beginning of the fundraising campaign.

With lawn games, merch stands and a wide variety of food, the picnic is a key event in this annual tradition and never ceases to deliver as a great afternoon of Penn State spirit.

Tuesday, Oct. 27

The Blair Witch Project

If found-footage horror is your jam, head down to the State Theatre at 7:30 p.m. for a viewing of the horror film “The Blair Witch Project.”

Released in 1999, “The Blair Witch Project” created a frenzy out of audiences, with some moviegoers even calling the police in fear that student film-makers actually went missing.

Tickets can be purchased online or at the theater.

How To Build Flavor

Hosted by the Student Farm and Food Systems at Penn State, this workshop will help you add a little more panache to your cooking.

This free event is a great opportunity to learn how to make your food more enjoyable and take a step up from salty ramen packet seasoning.

Head over to Headhouse 1 on 160 Curtain Road from 5 to 6 p.m. for this lesson in flavor.

Wednesday, Oct. 28

Sinners

Maybe you’ve heard about it, maybe you’ve seen clips or maybe you’ve already seen it. Either way, take a seat at the State Theatre for a viewing of the modern horror film “Sinners” that took home four Oscar wins out of 16 nominations at the 2026 Academy Awards.

At 7:30 p.m., watch Michael B. Jordan and Hailee Steinfeld perform in one of the most raved about horror movies in the last few years.

It’s probably still giving Josh Allen nightmares.

West Ghost Swing Halloween Dance

Every Wednesday at The Press, the Swing Dance Club hosts intermediate and beginner-friendly dance lessons from 7 to 8 p.m. followed by a dance party from 8 to 9 p.m.

This week’s party is spooky themed and free to attend. A partner or prior experience isn’t required.

“Monster Mash” the night away, and spook your skeleton with some West Ghost Swing.

Thursday, Oct. 29

Dark Storm Step Team’s Scream Fest

On Thursday from 6:30 to 8:30 p.m. in Heritage Hall, the Dark Storm Step Team will be hosting their annual Scream Fest.

This night of scares and sequences will feature horror-themed dance numbers from various dance teams on campus. These dances will showcase fear and grace all wrapped into one thrilling night.

There will be free food and no admission charge.

Friday, Oct. 30

Corpse Bride

Round out the week with the childhood horror classic, “Corpse Bride.”

Showing at the Friedman Auditorium at 6:30 p.m., the legendary Tim Burton film featuring Johnny Depp and Emily Watson will take you back to memories of classroom Halloween parties and mobs of trick-or-treaters passing down the block while rushing towards the bowl that says, “take one.”

Rocktober Climbing Games

Stop by the IM Building and try your hand at some games and competitions in the Climbing Suite.

From 4 to 6 p.m., you can test your skills on the wall and hopefully claim victory at the top. There’s no need to register or RSVP, simply stop by and enjoy the air up there.

John Summit

This Friday, Penn State will host EDM superstar, John Summit, as part of his CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour in the Bryce Jordan Center at 7 p.m.

Happy Valley will be the fifth show in Summit’s tour and the first college stop on the tour. Penn State students are getting amped for his amps after the release of his second album, “CTRL ESCAPE.”

Doors open at 5:30 p.m. and the BJC will showcase the talents of Alok and Mesto as the opening acts. Summit’s music was made for the partygoer, and Penn State definitely has no shortage of those kinds of fans.

Saturday, Oct. 31

Back To Back Screams

Close out your Halloween with a shriek at the State Theatre for a 10 p.m. viewing of “Halloween,” followed by the timeless, “Evil Dead II,” at midnight.

These two movies have become the horror version of “A Charlie Brown Christmas,” as an October staple that would make the spooky season incomplete without watching them.

Penn State Women's Volleyball

Penn State’s Women’s Volleyball will take on Purdue in Rec Hall at 12:30 p.m., with doors opening at 11:30 a.m.

The Lady Lions are 13-5 on the season heading into their matchup with the closely contending 11-6 Purdue Boilermakers. This win could be big for Penn State as they continue to grind out a competitive season.

title: Big Ten roundup | Indiana survives, midwest schools pull off upsets in Week 8
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Six teams may have had bye weeks, but the Big Ten still featured some exciting results in another crazy week of college football.

No. 6 Indiana survived an upset scare from Michigan in Ann Arbor, and both Minnesota and Wisconsin pulled off ranked upsets to keep the middle of the Big Ten chaotic.

Here’s what happened in Week 8 in the conference.

Indiana survives in overtime

Indiana went into The Big House looking to rebound after losing for the first time in 22 games. Michigan sent out true freshman quarterback Tommy Carr, who made his first career start.

Neither offense had any success in the game, as the Hoosiers led 6-3 with under 10 minutes left in the fourth quarter. Carr led Michigan on a game-tying field goal drive as time expired to send the game to overtime with a 6-6 score.

In the overtime period, Indiana’s offense scored with ease, something it couldn’t do all game. Josh Hoover completed a 21-yard pass to tight end Brock Schott, a pass that marked 25% of Hoover’s yards on the game, as he totaled 81 passing yards on 8-of-18 passing.

Michigan had a chance to respond following Indiana’s touchdown, but after a rush on fourth down to move the sticks for the first time, the offense stalled out. Carr’s fourth-down pass was incomplete and Indiana survived a scare against the Wolverines.

The Hoosiers moved to 7-1 on the season and remain in a strong position to have a first-round bye in the College Football Playoff, moving up to No. 4 in the AP Poll.

Minnesota, Wisconsin pull off upsets

Minnesota and Wisconsin both hosted teams inside the top 16, as the Golden Gophers battled No. 15 Iowa and the Badgers took on No. 16 USC.

Minnesota and Iowa had an old fashioned Big Ten battle. The Golden Gophers had a 10-3 lead heading into the fourth quarter after a 1-yard rushing touchdown from Darius Taylor.

Iowa marched 98 yards down the field with a little over five minutes left in the game to knot it up on a 37-yard touchdown pass from quarterback Hank Brown to tight end Reece Vander Zee.

Both teams went three-and-out on their ensuing drives, and Minnesota had possession of the ball with 1:46 left. A 39-yard completion from quarterback Drake Lindsay to wide receiver Jalen Smith set the Golden Gophers up in field goal range, and kicker Luke Drzewiecki sealed the game with a 46-yard field goal to pull off the upset and beat Iowa, 13-10.

For Wisconsin, it was a much different story. The Badgers’ defense slowed down USC’s high-powered offense, limiting the Trojans to just one touchdown and recording five sacks, including 2.5 from Sebastian Cheeks.

It was Wisconsin football at its finest, as the Badgers rushed for 142 yards and two touchdowns, leading the way to a dominant win. Running back Abu Sama III had 17 rushes for 71 yards as the leading rusher, while quarterback Colton Joseph played efficient football.

Joseph only threw 14 passes, completing 12 of them for just 58 yards and a touchdown, but it was enough for the Badgers to pull out the 24-7 victory, leading to a field storm in Madison, Wisconsin.

The win pushed Wisconsin into the top 25, slotting in at No. 25 in the updated AP Poll.

UCLA, Northwestern continue to roll behind rushing attacks

UCLA and Northwestern are both overperforming from preseason expectations. The Bruins are into the top 10 for the first time since 2022, and the Wildcats are ranked for the first time since 2020.

Both teams dominated their opponent in Week 8. UCLA relied on the run game against Michigan State, as quarterback Ty Dieffenbach continued to get settled into the starting role.

Running back Anthony Woods led the way with 112 yards and a touchdown, but Wayne Knight and Jaivian Thomas both reached the end zone as well, allowing the Bruins to win with ease, 28-10, against Michigan.

For Northwestern, it faced one of the worst teams in the conference in Rutgers. At its new Ryan Field, the Wildcats dominated the Scarlet Knights, beating them 42-14. Quarterback Aidan Chiles was sensational on Saturday, accounting for five of Northwestern’s six touchdowns.

Running back Caleb Komolafe recorded 150 rushing yards and a touchdown as the leader of the Wildcats’ 283 rushing yards. Chiles totaled 83 rushing yards as well as the ground attack continued to be the most successful part of offensive coordinator Chip Kelly’s offense.

Northwestern is currently fourth in the Big Ten standings with a 3-1 record, and it has a chance to make statements in November with games against Ohio State and Iowa.

title: Penn State recently terminated its Flock Safety contract. UPUA members work to address ongoing concerns
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
On Oct. 14, university police and Penn State Chief Financial Officer Sara Thorndike confirmed on-campus Flock cameras will be taken down after reviewing the operational value and cost of continuing their usage.

But concerns still linger on campus, and two members of the University Park Undergraduate Association’s (UPUA) are working together to plan out how the organization intends to address the issue.

James Dugery, 22, of Skippack, Pennsylvania, said he first learned about the presence of over 20 Flock Safety automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras in April. John Wozniak, UPUA’s division of undergraduate studies representative, had become interested in Flock cameras in April.

Dugery, a fourth-year studying political science, presented the issue during the UPUA’s July 22 meeting to seek assistance from other members in investigating the universities Flock cameras, including those installed at commonwealth campuses Behrend, Altoona and Harrisburg.

The cameras were installed on campus in August 2025 as part of a one-year pilot, and have raised concerns from community members on privacy and transparency from University Police & Public Safety (UPPS) on how the cameras are being used and what measures prevent their misuse.

Dugery said it was during a September meeting with Wozniak and other UPPS representatives that they both learned of the pilot’s lapse earlier in the month. Despite the development, Wozniak, a second-year studying finance and political science, said the issue of Flock cameras at Penn State is far from over.

He said he’d like to see UPUA continue to pursue a resolution on automated license plate readers (ALPR) and collect more survey responses.

“Even though that survey was created before the decision was made, I still think it's extremely important for students to make their say on it because it still gives us in UPUA a good metric as to how the student body feels about this subject,” Wozniak said.

He also said it was important for the UPUA to remain involved on the UPPS advisory board to ensure that student opinions at University Park are made clear, including having the UPUA president sit in on the advisory board meetings.

Dugery said he would also like to see the UPUA continue to receive new survey responses and that he would like to see the organization continue to pursue a resolution on ALPRs to provide a reference for future assemblies.

“We want to be thorough with the work that we've done, if this issue were to ever come back, because an administration can change its mind,” Dugery said.

Dugery and Wozniak’s combined findings, which included testimonies from Penn State students on their views on the presence of Flock cameras at University Park, and a meeting between Dugery, Wozniak and three other UPPS representatives knowledgeable about the pilot program, were compiled into an informational report presented during their Sept. 30 meeting.

The report included a roadmap of UPUA’s next steps in addressing student concerns about Flock cameras on campus, including a survey published on its Instagram on Oct. 5. The survey responses were used in the creation of a resolution establishing the organization’s official stance on the use of automated licence plate readers.

Parker Wallis, 19, of Villanova, Pa., has made several social media posts regarding his and other’s views of Penn State’s use of Flock cameras as part of his podcast, “Parcast with Parker.” On Oct. 11, Wallis made an Instagram post about the survey posted by the UPUA about the cameras and encouraged people to fill it out.

Wallis, a second-year studying broadcast journalism, said the report didn’t give him a clear answer on if and how the UPUA was going to take more concrete steps against Penn State’s use of Flock cameras prior to the announcement of their removal.

However, he said he found it important for students to make their voices heard through the survey so that the UPUA knows what direction it should take in the future should the issue of ALPRs come back to campus.

“We are the representation of the student government and they represent us so whatever voice we put out there … if we can thoroughly communicate to them that this is a problem, they will be by our side and they will help us and they will advocate for a position regarding those concerns,” Wallis said. “They're not a policymaker for Penn State — that's what the Board of Trustees are for — but they play a role in advocating for us, and that's what we need to do.”

title: Penn State graduate creates digital tool to help organize, mobilize Democrats ahead of midterms
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
When he started working for Ray Bilger’s campaign to represent Pennsylvania’s 15th Congressional District in March, Nish Barot said he began to hear about how the campaign was struggling to effectively coordinate its supporters throughout the district, even with the use of event and volunteer management tools like Mobilize.

Nish, 24, of State College, Pennsylvania, interviewed Democratic campaigns and organizations across Pennsylvania, Maine and Kansas over the next several months to see if they were experiencing similar issues to the Bilger campaign going into the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Through his research, Barot found these problems, which hinder the success of new campaigns in rural areas, were not isolated to the 15th District.

“The problem in rural communities is everybody starts at zero, they get to one, some people lose elections and some people win elections but all of the resources then get scattered and then we lose access to a lot of those volunteers and support networks so when the next candidate comes in, they have to start from scratch,” Barot said.

Bilger, who’s running against incumbent Republican Glenn “G.T.” Thompson, said his campaign has been working with other committees in the District to improve its local outreach, but difficulties with reaching out to and meeting supporters still remain due to disparities in the region’s infrastructure.

“A lot of what we have to deal with here are two lane roads and backcountry ways, so what would normally take a person maybe an hour, hour-and-a-half to get to one of the farthest locations takes about three hours. And then when you get there, it's a challenge to try to organize something on the ground,” Bilger, 66, of Bellefonte, Pennsylvania, said. “It goes into the broadband and the cellular infrastructure as well, because a lot of these places, because of the economic problems they face and have faced for decades, a lot of the print media that they used to have is gone. It's a piecemeal and you have to really go out there and find how people get their news.”

Having graduated from Penn State in 2024 with a degree in human-centered design and development, Barot realized he could use his knowledge and background to help improve the coordination of campaigns — especially grassroots ones like Bilger’s. He began working on a volunteer and campaign coordination tool InvolveOS.

InvolveOS, which first came online in June and is currently being used by several Democratic campaigns and organizations across Pennsylvania, is intended to improve the coordination of grassroots political campaigns by allowing them to upload and map out the presence and locations of donors and volunteers within a county or congressional district.

Barot left the Bilger campaign in September to work full time on InvolveOS. He said the tool provides campaigns with the ability to communicate with supporters.

Users can be added to it once they’re vetted by the organization using it, Barot said, but new users are only able to see the map of their own county or district. They can’t interact with other areas unless given permission by users in those areas.

He also said InvolveOS offers a “path to victory” projection based on voting records from previous elections and areas’ potential to be flipped in the midterms, which helps advise campaigns on how to best direct their resources.

Rose Petrunyak, who works for the Bilger campaign as its volunteer coordinator, said she used to have to keep track of how many people filled out sign-in sheets at events and manually compile the information of individual supporters into Excel spreadsheets.

With the help of the tool, Petrunyak said she’s able to import existing volunteers from her spreadsheets to InvolveOS’s map of the 15th District and upload new ones from event sign-in sheets. She’s also able to make and broadcast requests for volunteers, called “asks,” to help find volunteers best able to assist with certain tasks.

“If I'm looking for somebody that wants to do a postcard writing campaign in Warren County, I can go in and find people who are interested in doing that exact thing in that exact county,” Petrunyak, 55, of State College, Pennsylvania, said. “Then it shoots all of that to your email interface, so then you communicate after that via email. It's been amazing.”

She added that since she’s able to record her asks on InvolveOS to help track the participation time of the volunteers, she plans to thank those who have contributed the most time to helping the campaign.

Sarah Ocampo, Bilger’s campaign public relations manager, said she often uses InvolveOS’s data to help in researching how to contact media throughout PA-15 and to assist in tailoring media scripts to certain regions of the district based on what issues have been expressed in the past.

Ocampo, 18, of State College, Pennsylvania, said InvolveOS offers new ways for campaigns to support themselves, especially rural areas that don’t usually receive backing from the wider Democratic Party outside of presidential elections. Rural areas, Ocampo added, have a presence of Republicans, so drumming up support is more difficult for Democratic candidates.

“When you don't have a lot of support from either the party or your district, it's really important to get as much help as possible,” Ocampo, a first-year studying public relations, said. “It's a lot of work to keep in track of everything to coordinate and log everything, but InvolveOS does do that for the staff members of the campaign.”

Barot said his hope is for InvolveOS to spread throughout Pennsylvania, and he predicts the increased usage of the tool will make it easier to launch grassroots political campaigns in the future by allowing past campaigns to transfer their supporter networks onto new candidates through InvolveOS. But the expansion of InvolveOS would require additional support to pay for the infrastructure needed to run the tool and to fund the development of new features, such as text banking campaigns, he said.

Barot also said he intends for its users to remain solely comprised of Democrats, especially progressive Democrats, and he has no plans to offer InvolveOS to Republican candidates and organizations.

“If we look at Pennsylvania or just rural region states, Republicans have been in power for years, but we still have areas with no broadband connectivity, no cell service, hospitals that are decaying — just infrastructure that is poor,” Barot said. “It's time for change.”

Bilger said he sees having access to more tools like InvolveOS will help to “level the playing field” by allowing smaller campaigns to better compete with larger ones despite having more limited resources and funds.

Because of this, he said such tools, if used “smartly,” stand to have a greater impact for the future of the United States than just helping Democrats like Bilger win their elections.

“The whole purpose of this campaign is to win, but winning for a purpose: to finally get in and try to change politics in our country so that we have public servants who actually understand what public service means,” Bilger said. “Our jobs are supposed to be to serve every single person, to try to make their lives better, to try to make this country better … and I think this is one of the tools that we can use to do that.”

title: No. 16 Penn State women's volleyball defeats No. 18 Indiana, earns consecutive ranked wins
author: Riley Warner | For the Collegian
description:
After a 3-1 win at Rec Hall against No. 10 Oregon, Penn State took to the road to face No. 18 Indiana for another ranked matchup.

The blue and white ultimately defeated the Hoosiers 3-1, improving to 15-5 on the season.

Indiana and setter Teodora Kilkovic had the first serve of the set, resulting in an opening kill by Penn State middle blocker Kendall Northern, assisted by Penn State’s starting setter, Alexis Stucky.

Following this first Nittany Lion kill, the Hoosiers quickly bounced back. The two teams alternated kills for the next few points of set one. This didn’t last long, as following an early tied score of 6-6, Penn State would proceed to dominate the remainder of the set.

Libero Ava Falduto would serve two aces for the Nittany Lions, and Stucky would have one of her own as well. Opposite hitter Kennedy Martin had six kills, leading the offensive barrage.

Indiana struggled to catch up as the blue and white excelled on both ends: the Nittany Lions committed only six errors on 15 kills, compared to the Hoosiers’ six errors on 10 kills. Penn State earned set point on an attack error by Indiana outside hitter Jaidyn Jager and won the opening frame 25-16 on a kill by outside hitter Whitney Lauestein.

Indiana started the second set strong with a kill by outside hitter Izzy Clark and earned a second point off a Northern attack error. The second set proceeded to be the opposite of the first. The blue and white were composed and more attack-driven in the first set; however, after those two scores, the team had to play catch-up for most of the set.

The Nittany Lions’ serves were subpar in the second set, as five of their nine errors came from serves. Despite having three aces in the previous set, Penn State’s setters couldn’t produce one this set, whilst the Hoosiers created two of their own.

Penn State displayed a stronger desire to come out from behind compared to Indiana in the set prior. While the blue and white did go on to lose this set as a result of both service and attack errors by Martin, the score difference of 25-22 was narrow.

The Nittany Lions made a third-set comeback, starting the set they would go on to win with four sequential points: two kills, an ace by Falduto and a Hosier attack error. The red and white made a legitimate attempt to take control of the score, profiting from an ace by Hannah Leftridge and kills by opposite hitter Avry Tatum.

These helped tie the score early in the set to 7-7 and 8-8. However, Indiana's effort proved to be for little, as Penn State went on to add 12 more kills and three aces, two of which came back-to-back from Martin.

Entering the fourth set, Penn State was leading Indiana 2-1. The Nittany Lions started the set strongly with a kill by Lauenstein and an ace by Falduto, but the remainder of the set would be a battle. Errors continued for both teams, and the Nittany Lions still struggled to deliver solid serves and avoid attacking errors.

Still, the blue and white continued their fight, producing two more aces both delivered by middle back Gabrielle Nichols, one of which yielded in a match set and granted Penn State the win.

Up next

The blue and white return to action Thursday for its Military Appreciation Night against Ohio State, which starts at 7 p.m.

title: ‘It’s really special’ | Annual THON 5K crosses the finish line
author: Sophie Fried | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State THON’s annual 5K took place at the Bryce Jordan Center on Sunday, marking the first event for the THON 2027 Dream Forward Campaign and beginning the race towards THON weekend on Feb. 19-21, 2027.

THON is the world's largest student-run philanthropy that aims to provide emotional and financial support to Four Diamonds families who have been impacted by childhood cancer.

Prior to the start of the race, runners and supporters joined together at the BJC to enjoy merchandise, food trucks, a children’s race and musical entertainment. The event was crowded with families, volunteers, staff and alumni.

At 11:30 a.m., racers started their journey across campus, passing notable places such as the Berkey Creamery and Pattee and Paterno Library. Throughout the race, volunteers handed out water to the runners and encouraged them to keep going.

Emma Sabulsky, 19, of Elkins Park, Pennsylvania, is a member of THON’s Rules and Regulations Committee, which works to ensure the safety of all those present in the BJC during THON weekend. Sabulsky said that supporting THON and its mission is what’s driving her to cross the finish line.

“As college students, we’re coming together and we're fighting for this,” Sabulsky, a second-year studying advertising/public relations, said. “I think that’s really what's pulling me through.”

According to Sabulsky, THON weekend is a one-of-a-kind experience for anyone who volunteers or attends. Although this is her second year supporting THON, it's her first time participating in the 5K, and she loved how the race brought people together for such an important cause.

“I don’t think there's anything like it,” Sabulsky said. “I haven't experienced anything like it, so I think it’s really special.”

Caleb Mowery, 21, of Cannonsburg, Pennsylvania, is a Technology Committee captain, and has participated in THON every year since he arrived at Penn State.

Throughout his time as a THON volunteer, Mowery, a fourth-year studying computer science, said that his favorite memory was from his sophomore year when he stayed for Final Four, the last hours of THON where families affected by pediatric cancer share their stories and the final fundraising total is announced.

“It’s such an emotional moment, and it really brings together what we do this for,” Mowery said.

According to Mowery, navigating THON your first year can be overwhelming because of the wide variety of committees and organizations students can participate in, but if you take the leap, it will all be worth it.

“The more involved you become, the more in love you're gonna fall with it,” he said. “That’s something that I can promise.”

Layne Anderson, 21, of Malvern, Pennsylvania, is also a member of the Rules and Regulations Committee and said when it comes to THON, it’s important to be open-minded and say yes to everything.

“It’s positively affected my life just by knowing that this is going to such a great cause,” Anderson, a third-year studying biobehavioral health, said. “Having all of Penn State focused on something that is so amazing.”

title: Penn State women's soccer draws No. 24 Michigan to close out road trip
author: Darius Harandi | For the Collegian
description:
Following a 2-1 win over No. 5 Michigan State, their first road win against a top-five opponent since 2021, the Nittany Lions stayed in the Mitten State, heading down the road to Ann Arbor to face the Spartans’ in-state rival, No. 24 Michigan.

Despite leading twice in Ann Arbor, Penn State couldn’t hold its leads as the Wolverines answered both times, forcing the Nittany Lions to settle for a 2-2 draw.

Unlike Penn State, the Wolverines have yet to secure their ticket to the Big Ten Tournament. With the season nearly over, Michigan, Wisconsin and Iowa are among the teams still fighting for the final two qualifying spots.

The last time the teams met, in 2024, Penn State won 6-0 at Jeffrey Field. However, wins in Ann Arbor have become rare in recent years, as the Nittany Lions haven’t won at U-M Soccer Stadium since Oct. 7, 2018.

First half

Penn State opened the first half outshooting Michigan 3-0 in the first 10 minutes.

The Wolverines started to find their footing in the 17th minute when Michigan forward Ella Jablinskey drew a 20-yard free kick after a foul by Penn State forward Ellie Kocher. Midfielder Adi Walick sent it wide.

The Nittany Lions struck first, taking a 1-0 lead in the 20th minute when defender Bella Ayscue sent a deep cross to defender Lilly Burger, who headed it over Michigan goalkeeper Malia Zillman.

Burger and Ayscue both arrived in Happy Valley as members of Penn State's 2024 signing class.

Penn State maintained the pressure to the 23rd minute when midfielder Paige Pasinski slipped in a pass behind the Wolverines’ defense to forward Aubrey Kulpa. Zillman saved the follow-up shot.

The intensity boiled over in the 40th minute when Michigan midfielder Lilley Bosley and Penn State midfielder Kennedy Ring exchanged two-handed shoves after a battle for possession.

Second half

The first big chance in the second half came in the 52nd minute, when Kulpa drew a free kick. The deep shot narrowly missed the top-left corner of the net.

Penn State continued its offensive pressure in the 55th minute when Ayscue lofted a deep pass from her own half to a running Kulpa. Michigan defender Ellie Fife stopped the breakaway with a lunging tackle in her own box and cleared the ball. Fife appeared to injure herself but stayed in the game.

Michigan responded immediately with a cross finding forward Elle Ervin. Penn State goalkeeper Mackenzie Gress barely saved the shot.

Michigan whipped the subsequent corner into the back post to defender Anabelle Egeland, who headed it. Her header was saved thanks to the quick reflexes of Gress. The play led to Michigan’s second straight corner, where Gress again saved the oncoming shot, catching the ball and regaining possession for Penn State.

Still down one goal, the Wolverines kept up the pressure to the 58th minute, when combination play left defender Campbell Jewell with acres of space in front of the goal. She curled her shot past Gress, but it hit the post

In the 65th minute, Penn State midfielder Dikte Bang found herself with a clear opportunity on goal when she was brought down before getting a chance to shoot. The referee pointed to the penalty spot. Michigan coach Dave DiIanni challenged the call, and after video review, the decision was overturned.

Michigan found a much-needed equalizer in the 68th minute thanks to Ervin, who smashed a half volley into the upper netting from an extremely tight angle, claiming her sixth goal of the season. After a video review challenge by Penn State coach Erica Dambach, the goal was allowed to stand, tying the match 1-1.

Penn State responded in the 80th minute when Kulpa dribbled past two Michigan defenders and placed her shot in the bottom left corner to put the Nittany Lions back ahead 2-1. The goal extended the junior’s season tally to eight.

Only four minutes after Penn State retook the lead, Ervin pounced on a loose ball after a scramble in the box and headed it into the back of the net in the 84th minute. The goal tied the match 2-2 and completed Ervin’s brace.

Up next

Penn State returns to Jeffrey Field at 7 p.m. Friday to host Indiana in its Kick or Treat match, the program’s regular-season finale.

title: 2027 LB Blake Betton flips commitment from Penn State to Wisconsin
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State has lost another piece of its 2027 class.

3-star linebacker Blake Betton has flipped from the Nittany Lions to Wisconsin, per Hayes Fawcett of On3.

Betton initially committed to Penn State on April 11 and took an official visit on June 5, the lone one he took during the visiting season.

The linebacker ranks as the No. 466 player in the class, No. 35 player at his position and No. 4 player in Minnesota, according to 247Sports composite.

Betton held offers from many Big Ten schools in the midwest, and chose to stay in the area at Wisconsin. Betton was first offered by the Badgers on Sept 15, 2025 under Luke Fickell, and will now join Wisconsin’s 2027 class that’s hovering around the top 25 in the nation.

He was in attendance for Wisconsin’s game against USC on Oct. 24.

Penn State’s class is down to 21 players in 2027 as the Nittany Lions sit at 3-4 this season.

title: No.19 Penn State field hockey falls to No. 6 Iowa in a 1-0 defensive battle, snaps win streak
author: Annie Gleba | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State played its last away game of the season before the Big Ten playoffs against No. 6 Iowa. The Nittany Lions eight-game win streak came to an end after the tight defensive battle where Iowa took the win in this ranked matchup 1-0.

At the start of the game, both teams were locked in a defensive battle, with the ball changing hands every couple of minutes. There were rare chances on either side at getting the ball near the net for a shot.

In the first big offensive move of the game, Iowa was awarded back-to-back corners; the first corner was called off by the second corner, which was then blocked by Aby Deverka. The goalie had to work hard this game to keep some of the top goal-scoring athletes in the Big Ten from reaching the back of the net.

Iowa worked hard to defend its turf in its last home game of the regular season, as well as its senior day. The Hawkeyes have 11 seniors on this squad, three of them being fifth-years. They had more control over the ball in the first quarter, with five shots, but no shots on goal at the end of the first.

The Nittany Lions were still yet to find an answer going into the second quarter with no shots or penalty corners.

On the season, Penn State has collected a total of 93 penalty corners, with Iowa having 63. Despite this, the blue and white didn’t earn a single penalty corner with only a few minutes remaining left in the first half of the game. On the other side, Iowa was awarded three.

At halftime, the game is where we started with a score of 0-0. It’s a low-scoring, defensive game, with Iowa being able to take eight shots and Penn State only able to get off one.

Even though the Hawkeyes brought more pressure and took more control of the ball, the Nittany Lions didn’t back down, though, making defensive stops where it counted and relying on their goalie to keep the net safe.

Taking the most shots for the Hawkeyes was Tea Fortpied; the sophomore got three shots off her stick in the first half. The Chaumont-Gistoux, Belgium native has an average of 0.214 shot percentage and only has 14 total shots on the season.

Starting the second half, Frederique Van Cleef took a shot at the goal, but it bounced off the post. The play resulted in a penalty corner for Iowa, where it was able to convert its first goal from Dionne van Aalsum.

Penn State has held up a strong defense after the goal, not wanting the game to get away from

them in this low-scoring battle. With the last break between quarters Iowa is up with 11 shots and four shots on goal; Penn State trails, able to get up only two shots, with one of those being on goal.

Blue and white goalie, Deverka, had three entering the quarter, helping out her offense as much as she could.

With about eight minutes left in the last quarter, the Hawkeyes had another back-to-back chance to score with penalty corners, this time unable to score on either.

Winding down in the last few minutes, the Nittany Lions opted for an extra defender on the field, taking Deverka out of the net.

Penn State earned a penalty corner with under a minute left to play in the game, but with a shot deflected wide, the score remained 1-0. In another chance with nine seconds remaining, the Nittany Lions got another penalty corner, but once again came up short, snapping the blue and white’s win streak.

Up Next

The blue and white will come home for its last game of the season against Northwestern, Friday at 3 p.m. on Big Ten Plus.

title: Penn State men's soccer earns 1st draw against nationally ranked opponent this season
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State has had a less-than-desirable season, still sitting in the bottom of the Big Ten and coming into the match against Wisconsin with only two wins under their belt.

The Nittany Lions had their last win against Yale 50 days ago on Sept 4. Followed by losses until their first draw and conference point against Michigan earlier this month.

While it came later than they might have wanted, the Nittany Lions finally seemed to break through with a 2-2 draw against Wisconsin, marking their first tie against a nationally ranked opponent since their match against Maryland last season.

Keeper Daniel Peluffo-Wiese had his work cut out early, saving six shots in the first half and three in the second to reach a career high. He was able to keep the Badgers off the board in the first, and the Nittany Lions afloat throughout the half.

“What a bounce back from the last game, where he gives up five. I think off a long throw there in the second half showed his class distribution, great leadership, fantastic, gave a lot of security in front of the back,” Dow said.

Penn State found its footing and were able to turn the match into more of a back-and-forth, with players like Etienne Reck and Grant McIntosh taking two shots on the net to keep up with the Badgers' speedy play.

Everyone’s fingers were crossed after Reck was fouled twice in the 33rd minute and awarded two free kicks, and the opportunity to lead against Wisconsin in the half.

While the shots were missed, junior Noah Förster scored the first goal of the game to put the Nittany Lions on the board. Assisted by Reck and Toby Grant, the ball bounced off the top of the crossbar down and back, where Förster was able to score in the top right.

With their confidence boosted, Penn State came into the second half swinging. Förster took another shot in the first minute that was just saved off the glove of Badger goalie Michel Judewellin.

The Badgers responded with aggression, as Amadou Kone was pushed down without a foul call, before being hit again.

Wisconsin took the puck up the ice, with an initial shot by Joon Han blocked by a slap from Peluffo-Wiese before Gianluca Del Priore had the chance to score in the top left of the net as Peluffo-Wiese was getting back up, tying the game.

The Badgers statistically had the upper hand through the rest of the match, with 21 total shots over the Nittany Lions 13, but Puffo-Wiese's saves and the agility of players like Grant, Reck, and McNish kept the blue and white alive.

Both teams continued to fight as the score remained tied until there were eight minutes left to go. Badger Emile Kisse landed the ball in the top right of the goal and made it seem like Penn State would yet again lose in the final minutes of a match, their downfall all season.

Sheridan McNish had other plans, as Grant, Förster, and he fought in the box to score the team’s second goal, tying it up again with four minutes left to go.

The Nittany Lions walked away with their first tie against a nationally ranked opponent in three years, and played one of their best games all season.

“I thought today was their best performance in terms of intangible talents of the game. The grit, the resiliency, the focus, determination,” Dow said. “It wasn’t a pretty match and for us to grow like that at the hardest time in the year to play, I can’t remember the last time other than when I was in college out of playoffs.”

As their season comes to an end, with no chance at a post-season run, Dow wanted his team to leave it all out on the field.

“I ask them to show up with the personal pride to finish as high as possible in the league and to leave their legacy here. There are tough days, but we’re gonna remember them to shape and set the foundation going forward,” Dow said.

title: Budget-friendly Trader Joe’s foods for fall
author: Talia Rittenhouse | The Daily Collegian
description:
Trader Joe’s has released new items for the pumpkin spice season, and each has its own perks — whether it's the flavor, texture or type of meal.

None of the foods I purchased exceeded $6, so these items are perfect for college students who want to make the most of the fall season under a strict budget. Most seasonal products will likely be sold out by the beginning of November, so now’s your chance to secure some fall treats.

That being said, here are my recommendations.

Pumpkin Brioche Twist - $4.99

This fluffy brioche comes in very thick slices, with sweet cinnamon and sugar swirled throughout the bread.

I do wish more of the pumpkin flavor came through, as there’s only a light hint of it. It essentially tasted like a classic cinnamon swirl bread, which I still enjoyed, but wouldn’t necessarily categorize as an autumn-exclusive item.

I tried this bread both untoasted and toasted with some butter. I preferred it toasted, as it gives it a crispy exterior and a light, airy interior.

After considering the flavor and quality, I think this is a great buy for college students who like to have a sweeter breakfast, even though I’m not totally sold on it putting you into the fall spirit.

Rating: 8/10

Butternut Squash Mac & Cheese - $3.79

The aroma of this dish smells like the kitchen on Thanksgiving. However, unlike the hours spent hovering over the stove to make a full Thanksgiving meal, this mac and cheese only takes 4-6 minutes in the microwave.

Midterm season unfortunately coincides with fall, so as much as we want to watch the leaves shift colors and get carried away by a cool breeze, we’re usually spending our time studying. But this meal is perfect for a quick dinner, leaving you more time to revel in coziness.

Within the dish, there’s blended butternut squash and cheese holding the rigatoni together, but you can’t really taste the butternut squash in it. The flavor of the butternut squash was presented by the sweetness factor in the macaroni and cheese.

The flavor is cheesy, on the sweeter side, with some spices to it. I would prefer this dish a little more if there was more cheese in it, as it was slightly dry.

Despite a few minor flaws, it was still delicious. This could be a way to have your favorite childhood comfort food with a little bit of a nutritional twist to it.

Rating: 7/10

Pumpkin Streusel Muffin -$5.99

This is a gluten-free treat, but if I hadn’t read the label, I wouldn’t have known. It was moist, fluffy, sweet and subtly spiced. Most importantly, it had the perfect amount of pumpkin flavor.

There could have been a bit more streusel on top to fulfill its name, but I honestly enjoyed it as is. Sometimes, having an overabundance of streusel topping makes a baked good so sweet that it overpowers the other flavors of it (and this is coming from someone with a sweet tooth).

This is a great purchase if you’re looking for a quick on-the-go breakfast or a snack to get you pushing through long days of classwork.

Rating: 10/10

Apple Pie à la mode Ice Cream - $3.99

If you enjoy eating apple pie à la mode on Thanksgiving, there's no need to wait for the holiday anymore — Trader Joe’s has you covered with this ice cream.

The base of the ice cream is vanilla, and there are pieces of pie crumbles mixed in. It also features a soft apple filling.

In each bite, you get a bit of each flavor. I was shocked by how much this tasted like an apple pie à la mode. Oftentimes, when getting an intricate ice cream flavor, each bite doesn’t always fulfill your expectations. This one, however, does.

I could go on and on about how perfect this flavor is. I wouldn’t change a thing about it, except the fact that I only just started buying it.

Rating: 12/10

Maple & Sea Salt Kettle Corn - $2.99

This kettle corn tastes almost like another version of Boom Chicka Pop. It’s just as addictive as it is crispy and has the perfect amount of salt and maple.

The maple is light and not too sweet, which I prefer, because if it were stronger, I think it would be too overpowering and not as ideal for a quick snack.

Having this popcorn as the side in your lunch or as a snack throughout the day would be great, as it provides that crunch factor, but also the sweetness through the maple, all tied together with sea salt.

Again, I wouldn’t change a thing about it. This is a great buy for students, as it’s only $2.99 for a large bag, so you get the most bang for your buck.

Rating: 10/10

title: Penn State men’s hockey goaltender Ryder Fetterolf shines in first-career win against Canisius
author: Chase Fisher | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State netminder Ryder Fetterolf began his Nittany Lions’ tenure 0-2, allowing an unexpected four goals per game and an .884 save percentage. Some unfamiliar territory for the reigning CHL Goaltender of the Year.

But the Pegula Ice Arena crowd finally saw the Fetterolf that was advertised heading into the season Saturday. The freshman dialed back to his OHL self against Canisius, saving 26 of 28 shots and halting many Grade-A chances from the Golden Griffins, headlined by a sprawling save in overtime which sprung defenseman Jackson Smith’s game-winner.

“(He played) very good,” coach Guy Gadowsky said Saturday night. “He found a way. I think the whole team, including him being the leader in this, deserves some credit for not panicking after we got down, and I thought he was really good when he needed to be, and you can see what a battler he is.”

Fetterolf's shaky start to his collegiate career was a bit of a shock.

Again, he was the CHL and OHL Goaltender of the Year last season, boasting an eye-catching 29-9-3 record, 2.07 goals-allowed average and .923 save percentage in Canada. Fetterolf, who was drafted in the fourth round of the 2026 NHL Draft by the Carolina Hurricanes, was arguably the team’s hottest acquisition in the offseason.

In the Nittany Lions’ 3-2 overtime win over Canisius on Saturday, he put together a dominant performance for his first-career college win.

Not to mention, he did so in unusual circumstances — Fetterolf saw just seven shots in the first period and three in the third before an onslaught of shots and Grade-A chances in the second frame and overtime.

“I think it's tough because he didn't see a lot at the start,” Gadowsky said of how difficult it is for a goaltender to stay focused after a lack of action. “… I know he had to kill a couple penalties, but because of the blocks, etc., he really didn't have a lot of rubber in the third, and then dropped the puck in overtime, just as you know a couple Grade-As against him. So I think you have to give him a lot of credit for maintaining his focus with work, not much work, heavy work (and then) not much work.”

The first-year netminder made several of his marquee saves after lulls in action.

Fetterolf halted several one-timers from open players in the slot, and even made an eye-catching stop on a breakaway from Ethan Wolthers, who went from his forehand to his backhand, back to his forehand before Fetterolf stretched his left pad out just in time for the save.

He said he was able to stay focused in those circumstances because he doesn’t overthink. He doesn’t want to chase that next save or get in his own head. He also noted his competitiveness as to why he’s able to stay locked in during lulls of action, which he gained while growing up with three other siblings.

“Being a spectator of the game without letting these thoughts creep in, saying, ‘I haven't faced a shot in five minutes. What's the next shot going to be?’” Fetterolf said. “Kind of just letting it come to me, and then kind of using my competitiveness to get to my next spot.”

title: Penn State men’s soccer draws No. 13 Wisconsin in a chilly, chippy game
author: Zach Schroder | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State faced No. 13 Wisconsin under the lights at Jeffrey Field on Saturday. The Nittany Lions went into the game still winless in the Big Ten and came off an embarrassing 5-0 loss to Rutgers in their last matchup.

Ultimately, Penn State would draw with the Wisconsin Badgers 2-2 in a high-flying game.

“I thought today was our best performance in terms of intangible talents of the game, the grit, the focus, determination," said Dow. “You know it wasn’t a pretty match … for us to grow like that at the hardest time of the year to play.”

First half

The Nittany Lions began the match with possession and quickly earned a corner kick after a tackle forced it out. Badger sophomore goalkeeper Judewellin Michel punched out the curving kick.

Penn State goalkeeper Daniel Peluffo-Wiese was tested early when Wisconsin junior forward Emile Kisse shot bottom right, but it was saved. Peluffo-Wiese was under heavy pressure in the first couple of minutes, saving two more shots through the 4th minute. The Badgers got four shots off just 6 minutes into the game.

“What a bounce back from the last game where he gives up five”, said coach Rob Dow about his keeper after the match, “great leadership, a lot of security”.

The blue and white eased into the match after the 10th minute; they played contested passing balls near midfield, with each team getting a quick trip or two to the opponent's half. Sophomore defender Joe Sheridan deflected a pass and immediately called for help. He walked off by himself; freshman defender Sheridan McNish subbed in for him.

A Penn State corner kick turned into a prime scoring opportunity for the Badgers after a fastbreak attempt, but the blue and white defense snuffed it out. Wisconsin Senior forward Markie Hrvojevic had another great opportunity but soared the ball way over the crossbar.

Peluffo-Wiese was under heavy pressure in the half and made a great one-handed save in the 29th minute. Kisse again delivered the shot, who was everywhere. Despite numerous opportunities, the Badgers could not convert a score through the 31st.

After a Penn State throw-in from Grant McIntosh, a crosser turned a header into a header, and junior defender Noah Forster put it in over the keeper for the first score of the game. Reck and redshirt sophomore defender Toby Grant assisted Forster. Penn State led 1-0 in the 36th minute.

Wisconsin's attack slowed in the final minutes of the first half compared to the pressure they opened with. The Badgers had six shots on goal at the half, but the Nittany Lions also had six saves. Penn State still led 1-0 heading into the second half.

Second half

The blue and white got out of the locker room with a hot start. After a foul led to a free kick, Penn State to a shot that Michel saved amazingly in the bottom right.

Peluffo-Wiese dove and blocked a shot but was then on the ground for a putback by senior midfielder Gianluca Del Priore that went into the back of the net. The Badgers tied it up in the 51st minute.

McIntosh earned the first card of the game with a yellow for dissent after the Badger goal was reviewed. Senior midfielder Noah Andreas earned the Nittany Lions another yellow for unsporting behavior while he chased a fast break from Wisconsin.

Both teams were chippy in the middle minutes of the second half, with four fouls and lots of wishes for others. Peluffo-Wiese had another good low save after a Wisconsin throw-in. In the other box, Michel ran out and grabbed the ball to deny a Nittany Lion shot attempt.

“I loved how we rose to that occasion and invited this type of contact; they were alphas in that type of physical play. The referee did a great job managing cards until late in the match, it was a good physical game”, said Dow.

Penn State got lucky twice after one shot rocketed off the right post and another flew over the net. McNish earned the blue and white their third yellow card for unsporting behavior in the 80th minute. The Nittany Lions defense was under heavy pressure heading into the final 10 minutes of play.

The pressure proved too much for Penn State as Kisse hit the go-ahead goal to the top right off his left foot. Wisconsin led 2-1 in the 81st minute. The Nittany Lions answered when McNish headed the ball to the top center; Forster and senior defender Morgan Marshall assisted. The equalizer made to 2-2 in the 85th minute.

Penn State kept up the offensive pressure in the final minutes. Reck had a shot blocked in the final 30 seconds, but they would not be able to convert.

Dow was confident with a late challenge in the final minute, but it came up empty. “The only thing I saw is I thought we should have won the game.”

Up next

Penn State will have its Senior Day and faceoff against Duquesne on Wednesday at 7pm at Jeffrey Field

title: Penn State men’s hockey stays in win column, sweeps Canisius
author: Maggie Hardy | The Daily Collegian
description:
In the first of the two-game series Friday night, Penn State stood arm-in-arm along the blue line and joined the Roar Zone in the Alma Mater for the first time this season, after breaking its 0-4 start by downing Canisius 5-1.

History repeated itself Saturday, and the Nittany Lions completed the series sweep with a 3-2 overtime win over the Golden Griffins.

“We didn’t have our best start, but I think this weekend, kind of figuring out our game…we knew all along that we’re going to be a competitive team,” freshman goaltender Ryder Fetterolf said. “Getting the first sweep feels great, and it’s kind of just giving us a small taste of what we got ahead.”

The blue and white seemed to carry its momentum over from the previous victory and came out strong in its rematch against Canisius.

Senior defenseman Casey Aman came inches from putting Penn State on the board after his shot trickled past goaltender Jack Lisson. Still, the puck was kicked away by a Canisius defender just before it crossed the goal line.

The physicality also picked back up right where it left off, and the Nittany Lions were given the game’s first power play after defenseman Carter Patterson was called for cross-checking about halfway through the period.

Despite a few good chances, the blue and white couldn’t get anything through.

Senior defenseman Mac Gadowsky was the one to finally break the ice for the Nittany Lions with just under four minutes left in the period.

After receiving a pass out by the blue line with no one around, Mac Gadowsky fired a long-range shot that found its way through traffic and into the back of the net.

With under two minutes to play, senior captain Dane Dowiak was called for tripping, sending the Nittany Lions into the first intermission with a one-goal lead, but about 30 seconds of the penalty to kill off.

The blue and white successfully returned to 5-on-5 play to begin the second period, but much of the remaining middle frame didn’t go its way.

The Golden Griffins had their best chance of the night when senior forward Ethan Wolthers went unseen behind two Penn State defenders and was left open on a breakaway. Fetterolf — who had been extremely solid for the Nittany Lions so far — made the save to keep the team ahead, however.

“I thought (Fetterolf) was really good when he needed to be, and you can see what a battler he is,” Guy Gadowsky said.

The blue and white continued to hold onto its lead, although struggling to regain its momentum from the first period. With under five minutes to play in the period, Canisius finally got on the board after sophomore forward David Elmy picked up a blocked shot and fired it past Fetterolf.

Another solid save by Fetterolf a few minutes later turned into some shoving after the whistle, and matching roughing penalties ensued on Canisius’s Joe Messina and Penn State’s Shea Van Olm.

It took less than 10 seconds for the Golden Griffins to capitalize on the 4-on-4 opportunity when senior forward Rhys Chiddenton’s shot found the back of the net and sent his team into the second intermission with their first lead of the night.

Penn State’s third period looked to be off to a rocky start when defenseman Nick Fascia was called for tripping just three minutes in. Still, the penalty was negated about 30 seconds later when Canisius’ Hunter Price went to the box, also for tripping.

Neither team capitalized on its man-up opportunities, but less than a minute after returning to equal strength, the blue and white evened the score once again. Sophomore Justin Poirier sent a one-timer from the left circle off the crossbar and into the net to tie the game with about 15 minutes still to play.

With a tie game and only a minute to play, former Nittany Lion turned Canisius defenseman Jason Gallucci was given a delay-of-game penalty.

Despite the late-game man-advantage, 60 minutes wasn’t enough to decide a winner, and Pegula Ice Arena headed to overtime.

It was a short-lived overtime, and defenseman Jackson Smith called game just 15 seconds in, after Fetterolf made a diving save that sent Smith and Poirier on a 2-on-1 the other way. Smith ripped a shot to the top corner of Canisius’ goal and sealed Penn State’s 3-2 victory.

“Great save by (Fetterolf), that was huge, and then a little rebound and he got another save,” Smith said. “I kind of stretched the zone a bit and took a chance. I got a nice pass from (Poirier) and took my shot.”

Up Next

Penn State is back on the road to open Big Ten play against Minnesota, with puck drop scheduled for 8 p.m. Friday at 3M Arena at Mariucci.

title: 3-star RB Jordan Hall commits to Penn State
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State has added another piece to its 2027 class.

The Nittany Lions earned a commitment from 3-star running back Jordan Hall, he announced Saturday.

The Cincinnati native was previously committed to Miami Ohio, but decommitted in August. He received offers from hometown Ohio State on Sept. 5 and Missouri on Sept. 16, but visited Happy Valley for the White Out game and wound up committing to the Nittany Lions two weeks later.

The Princeton High School star is the No. 32 player from Ohio and No. 60 running back in his class, according to 247Sports composite.

The Nittany Lions now have two running back commits, with Hall joining 3-star Chukwuma Odoh.

Matt Campbell visited Hall at his high school game on Friday night, making one final push to add him to his first full recruiting class at Penn State.

title: No. 6 Penn State women's hockey battles St. Lawrence into overtime, winning with a last-minute goal
author: Henry Bustin | For The Collegian
description:
Following a 3-1 victory against St. Lawrence University’s Saints on Friday evening, No. 6 Penn State women’s hockey led a close match against the Saints for the second day, going into overtime and clinching a last-minute goal to win 2-1.

First period

The period began with intense back-and-forth pressure between the Saints and the Nittany Lions, creating an exciting atmosphere in Appleton Arena.

St. Lawrence stopped an attempted goal from the blue and white. Soon after, freshman goalie Morgan Stickney skillfully deflected a goal and then blocked another attempt by St. Lawrence’s Riley Reeves.

As the teams continued to battle, Nittany Lions’ freshman Kylie Amelkovich attempted a high shot, which St. Lawrence blocked.

A power play began soon after, and on the breakout, Penn State led the puck up the ice, but its hustle was cut short as St. Lawrence launched it upward.

With under 10 minutes left in the quarter, St. Lawrence applied pressure during a 4-on-4 power play against the blue and white, with a quick shot that Stickney deflected yet again.

Soon afterward, a penalty was called on Penn State during a power play with 1:02 left, directly after Stickney deflected a goal.

As St. Lawrence’s Brooke Mulvihill tried to advance the puck toward Penn State’s net, the blue and white’s junior forward McKenna Walsh disrupted her attempt and sent it flying to St. Lawrence’s side so Penn State could keep applying pressure.

With even strength between the teams and six minutes remaining in the period, St. Lawrence launched several attempts on Penn State, which Stickney continued to deflect away.

With 2:51 remaining in the quarter, 10 shots had been attempted, six from the Nittany Lions and four from the Saints; none entered the net.

As 14.4 seconds remained in the quarter, St. Lawrence nearly scored a goal, but Stickney deflected it away.

Second period

The period kicked off with St. Lawrence applying pressure in the first minute, with Stickney blocking a goal attempt.

The Nittany Lions drove the puck up and launched it at the net, which the Saints’ goalie, Kassidy Lawrence, just managed to save.

As St. Lawrence tried to advance towards Penn State’s goal, blue and white sophomore defender Sophie Morrow stole the puck from the Saints and drove it away from Penn State’s crease, but it was soon returned to the Nittany Lions’ side.

With 15 minutes remaining, two shot attempts were made on Penn State, but Stickney skillfully blocked them both. Stickney had nine blocks with 10 minutes remaining in the period, displaying her superior goalie skills as well as those of Penn State’s defense.

The two teams continued with goal attempts, and Amelkovich nearly scored but wasn’t successful.

Soon after, with around 8:30 remaining in the period, a backhand assist to St. Lawrence first-year Sonia Mehta allowed her to score a first-career goal on the Nittany Lions, granting the Saints a 1-0 lead.

The teams continued to battle it out, with Stickney rejecting numerous attempts made by the Saints.

A buzzer-beater shot was launched by the Nittany Lions but did not go through. The period ended with the Saints still ahead 1-0, making the final frame vital for Penn State to make a comeback.

Third period

The period started with the Nittany Lions in possession of the puck. They were looking to remove the deficit that the Saints had been banking on from the previous two periods.

With 18:27 in the period, a penalty was called on Penn State for a hugging call, granting the Saints a Power Play.

St. Lawrence made a few shot attempts during the power play, which were blocked by Stickney.

With 14:08 remaining in the period, Nittany Lions’ freshman defender Megan Hosman launched a successful slap shot goal in the midst of a power play, tying the game 1-1, boosting the morale of the blue and white.

Soon after, with 12:40 remaining, a penalty was called on the Nittany Lions, resulting in a power play for the Saints. They applied heavy pressure in Penn State’s crease, but defensive players Hosman and Morrow, combined with the goalkeeping of Stickney, prevented any successful goals.

The Nittany Lions and the Saints continued the game with several power plays after penalties were called, most notably on Abby Stonehouse for roughing with around 11 minutes remaining. This allowed multiple opportunities for the Saints to make goal attempts, with several coming from Mulvihill, Hehl, and Haslam, but none were successful as Stickney continued to deflect.

The Nittany Lions retaliated with shots of their own but also were unable to score on the Saints.

The period ended tied 1-1, prompting the two teams to go into overtime.

Overtime

Overtime began with Penn State’s Mikah Keller winning the faceoff. Several shot attempts were made by Amelkovich, Danica Maynard and Grace Outwater, but none made contact with the net.

The two teams went back and forth with strategic plays like drop passes and slap shots, but it appeared they were at a near-stalemate until, with 31.1 seconds remaining in the period, Outwater scored, securing the Nittany Lions' series sweep over the Saints.

Up Next

Next Friday, the Nittany Lions take on the RIT Tigers at the Gene Polisseni Center, with puck drop slated for 6 p.m.

title: Penn State men’s hockey gets first win of the season behind captain’s multi-goal effort
author: Maggie Hardy | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State captain Dane Dowiak sat at the podium Tuesday night after the team’s 5-2 loss to Robert Morris and took ownership of its 0-4 start to the season.

“I know I got to be better. I got to lead this team right. I haven’t done that yet,” Dowiak said after the loss. “So we’re going to do a little bit of self-reflection, take a look in the mirror and turn this thing around.”

Dowiak was true to his word and led the Nittany Lions to their first win of the season, downing Canisius 5-1 behind his own two-goal performance.

“(Dowiak) played a really excellent team game,” coach Guy Gadowsky said. “Often when guys do that, they get rewarded.”

The senior forward’s first tally provided an early spark to the blue and white’s momentum. Less than three minutes into play, freshman forward Justin Larose sent a slot pass to Dowiak from behind the net, and his shot beat goaltender Jack Lisson.

Penn State has struggled with maintaining leads this season, so when sophomore defenseman Jackson Smith was called for interference shortly after the goal, it needed a crucial penalty kill.

After letting up only one shot, the Nittany Lions successfully returned to 5-on-5 play.

Nothing came of the rest of the period, but the blue and white entered the first intermission with a one-goal lead and holding an 11-5 edge in shots.

Penn State was back on its heels when, under two minutes into the middle frame, Canisius freshman Ben Brunelle notched his first collegiate goal after picking the corner on Josh Fleming’s net and equalizing the score.

The Nittany Lions only spent the next two minutes tied at one-a-piece before freshman Andrew Kuzma also registered his first collegiate goal and pulled the Nittany Lions back ahead.

After Smith’s initial shot was blocked, freshman forward Kale Dach picked up the loose puck and found Kuzma down low before firing it into the back of the net.

The physicality between the two non-conference opponents started to ramp up as the second period played on, and two more penalties, this time on the Golden Griffins, were called.

Nothing came for the Nittany Lions on the first power play, but Dowiak capitalized during his team’s second man-advantage of the period. The captain was waiting down low, and once he received a pass from sophomore forward Lev Katzin, Dowiak threw the puck on net, which was redirected off a skate and in.

“(Dowiak) made several excellent changes, including on the power play,” Gadowsky said. “He back-checked extremely hard. He was covering up for people.”

The third period was much of the same, with the blue and white maintaining a majority of puck possession.

The score held until late in the final frame, when Kuzma tallied an empty-net goal to join Dowiak with a multi-goal game.

The Nittany Lions still had one more goal to send the Golden Griffins home with, however, after a shorthanded opportunity led to Smith firing the puck off the crossbar and in with just five seconds to play, and sealing the team’s first win of the season, 5-1.

“We all knew after the (Robert Morris) game that ‘it’s really time now,’” Smith said. “It’s pretty cool if we can come back from this tough start, but now we have a chance to have a pretty cool story.”

title: Homecourt helps propel No. 16 Penn State women's volleyball to win over No. 10 Oregon
author: Matthew Bakken | For The Collegian
description:
No. 16 Penn State returned home to a ruckus crowd at Rec Hall after a long West Coast trip. No. 10 Oregon had a long trip of its own, both geographically and during the game, as the Nittany Lions cruised to a 3-1 victory.

“I mean, we love playing at home. It's nice, and it was a great crowd tonight,” Penn State head coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley said postgame.

It certainly was, as Rec Hall had a booming echo throughout, with the blue and white giving the home crowd plenty to cheer about after a taxing road trip.

The Nittany Lions have had to deal with the Western powers of the Big Ten as of late, splitting a trip to Southern California last weekend.

“Mean, it's, I mean that's, you know everyone's got to do it in the league though. So you know it's it's a tough travel, but you know I think the teams that you know are focused and can you know stay the course, you know do a good job,” Schumacher-Cawley said about the contrasting travel toll for Penn State. “It was nice to see us split last weekend and you know win at home.”

Despite every Big Ten team having to deal with the effects of the long travel. It’s hard not to think that the travel had an effect on Oregon, as the Ducks came out sluggish in the first set. Conversely, Penn State with some help from the Rec Hall crowd had a noticeable edge to them.

An edge even in a 3-0 win at USC last weekend, the Nittany Lions lacked with the toll of traveling that far away. The advantage of being able to close out and finish Oregon in the fourth set might not have taken place had the game been in Eugene. As just a week ago UCLA used its home-court advantage to stun the blue and white late at night.

It’s hard not to think travel dictates how Penn State plays, as the Nittany Lions boast an impressive 10-2 mark at home compared to middling 3-2 away and 1-1 neutral court records. Those two home losses also came to two teams currently in the top-10 in Nebraska and Tennessee. Any concerns about the blue and white not being able to compete with the top teams could be squashed after defeating a top-10 Oregon tonight in a dominating fashion.

Despite the big one tonight, Schumacher-Cawley’s focus was on the future.

“You know this is the first year for the Big Ten Tournament, so putting ourselves in a great position for that,” Schumacher-Cawley said. “And you know it's nice to see us get better every match and continue to do that. We have eight more regular season matches.”

Luckily, the Nittany Lions don’t need to see the West anymore, even if it was won. Just the comforts of Happy Valley, three more home games and five short Midwestern road trips remain on the season as Penn State pushes not just for the Big Ten Tournament but the NCAA Tournament as well.

title: No. 16 Penn State women’s volleyball gets top-10 victory over No. 10 Oregon in Dig Pink match
author: Joey Bolger | For The Collegian
description:
No. 16 Penn State held its annual Dig Pink game at Rec Hall on Friday night, welcoming No. 10 Oregon in a Big Ten heavyweight clash.

Penn State won in four sets to get its first top-10 victory since Sept. 11 against then-No. 4 Stanford. Kennedy Martin led the Nittany Lions with 25 kills and got the last kill to seal the match for the Nittany Lions.

The Nittany Lions came out with two liberos in senior Jocelyn Nathan and junior Ava Falduto, an interesting move from coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley, as Nathan and Falduto have been on the court at the same time for most of this season.

“So we’re you know we’re just trying to use everyone and get the best out of them to find ways to score points and win,” Schumacher-Cawley said.

The blue and white came out firing early in the first set, taking a commanding 10-5 lead with Kendall Northern putting up three kills. Setter Alexis Stucky also shined during the first set, grabbing two kills and eight assists.

Penn State committed six service errors in the first set, allowing the Ducks to keep the slate competitive.

A thunderous swing from Martin sealed the first set for the Nittany Lions 25-17. Penn State’s offense was efficient, having a .545 hit percentage and having a perfect sideout percentage. Oregon couldn’t get anything going on offense, having a .071 hit percentage.

However, in the second set, the Ducks started to come alive, holding the lead for a majority of the set with Sjakkie Donkers and Alanah Clemente having seven kills.

Just as the momentum shifted in Oregon’s favor as the Ducks went up 19-16, Penn State responded with a 3-0 scoring run, forcing Oregon to take a timeout and regroup.

Both teams went back and forth at the end of the second set, but a kill from Donkers put the Ducks right back into the match, winning a scrappy second set 25-23 and tying the match at 1-1.

Penn State’s offense showed some flaws in the second set as its hitting percentage dipped from .545 to .333.

Backed by an electric home crowd, Penn State took an early 9-6 lead in the third set with Martin having three kills. Momentum continued to go in the Nittany Lions' direction, going up 13-8 and forcing Oregon to spend a timeout early on in the third set.

Coming out of the timeout, both teams put out an impressive rally which ended with a Penn State kill by Whitney Lauenstein, putting the home crowd on their feet.

Down 18-12, the Ducks went on a 3-0 scoring run, forcing the Nittany Lions to take a timeout. This decision paid off as Penn State grabbed the first two points coming out of the timeout.

Penn State held off the Ducks to close out a convincing third set, 25-19, thanks to a block assist by Gabrielle Nichols and Martin, which put the Nittany Lions up 2-1.

Martin played a huge role in the third set, having eight kills along with a block assist to end the set. Penn State’s offense bounced back after a defensive second set, improving its hitting percentage to .353.

The Martin show persisted in the fourth set, claiming five kills of Penn State’s eight points early on.

The Ducks’ energy never wavered as they went on a 3-0 scoring run to gain an 11-9 lead. Donkers led the offense with three kills early on to give Oregon life.

Resiliency was a main factor for Penn State all night, as every time Oregon looked to gain momentum or start to pull ahead, the blue and white found a way to fight back into the set.

“When we’re at our best, all communicating, all working as a unit, fearless,” Lauenstein said. “Going for everything, swinging away, not thinking about the next or not thinking about errors.”

Once again, both teams traded blows late in the fourth set with both sides refusing to leave Rec Hall without a major Big Ten win.

Penn State held the momentum late into the match, sealing the fourth set, 25-20.

“We’re just very unified when we’re at our best,” Nathan said.

Up Next

The Nittany Lions will make the trip to Bloomington on Sunday to take on the No. 18 Indiana Hoosiers on FS1 at 3 p.m.

title: Penn State men’s hockey snaps 4-game losing streak backed by 2-goal game from captain
author: Chase Fisher | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State captain Dane Dowiak spun around and fell flat on his back celebrating a goal in the first period. He made sure to stay upright after potting his second.

With questions to be answered and statements to be made, the Nittany Lions penciled in their first win of the season, defeating Canisius 5-1 behind a much-needed performance by their captain.

“Great night, and very important to us too,” coach Guy Gadowsky said. “We needed that. It was absolutely a great team win. Great crowd, which helped a lot.”

Here’s how Penn State finally got into the win column Friday night, ending a four-game losing streak and delivering a monumental sigh of relief to a Nittany Lions fanbase that really needed one.

First period

So much for the slow starts. Penn State scored first for just the second time this season — both at home — thanks to a nifty pass from left wing Justin Larose.

The freshman trailed linemate Justin Poirier two minutes into the game as he swerved around a duo of Canisius defenders, into the Golden Griffins zone and behind goaltender Jack Lisson.

After Poirier lost his footing, Larose scooped up the puck and put it on captain Dane Dowiak’s tape in the slot, who lifted the puck over a sprawling Lisson and into the back of the net to give Penn State a 1-0 lead. Talk about a response from the captain after he, like Gadowsky, called the team out on Tuesday night.

“He made several excellent changes for the team,” Gadowsky said. “... He back-checked extremely hard. He was covering up for people. He played a really excellent team game, and often when guys do that, they get rewarded.”

That was all the scoring for what was a physical first frame. The Nittany Lions hit a post, had a 3-on-1 rush and a few other opportunities, but never cashed in. Canisius, on the other hand, was stymied, as Penn State dominated puck control and outshot the Golden Griffins 11-5.

Second period

Canisius came out of the locker room firing.

After controlling the first minute of the period and applying heavy pressure on Penn State, center Ben Brunelle corralled the puck at the red line before skating into the Nittany Lions’ zone.

Brunelle, while staving off defenseman Ethan Weber, fired the puck from an unusual angle, picking the top-left corner of the net and tying the game at one 1:18 into the frame.

That didn’t last for long; Penn State answered almost immediately.

Defenseman Jackson Smith wristed a shot from the point that ricocheted off Lisson, leaked into the slot and landed on the stick of center Kale Dach.

Dach, who made a last-ditch effort to reach the sliding puck, one-handed it to left wing Andrew Kuzma for an easy one-timer to retake the lead. It was Kuzma’s, who had open-heart surgery in 2024 that caused him to medically redshirt, first collegiate goal.

“Andrew Kuzma scores the first goal after everything that guy has been through was really really cool to see,” Gadowsky said. “He deserved it and his family could not have handled his situation better, and so you cheer for guys like that so much. So I give him so much credit. So great to see.”

The Nittany Lions padded their lead 10 minutes later, with Dowiak tallying his second score on the man-advantage. The senior center leisurely controlled the puck by the bottom of the right-wing circle before firing it into a cluster of skaters, where the puck deflected off a player and into the Canisius goal, extending Penn State’s advantage to 3-1.

Third period

The third period showcased less theatrics.

Canisius had two power-play opportunities, but neither team generated many high-danger chances. Nittany Lions center Kaden Pitre dinged a post, which was about the best scoring opportunity for either program.

However, Kuzma drilled an empty-netter — his second score Friday — to ice the game. Smith scored with five seconds remaining in regulation to extend Penn State's lead to 5-1.

After a low-eventful third frame, the Nittany Lions prevailed, holding onto its lead and defeating the Golden Griffins in regulation. Penn State outshot Canisius 44-24, with netminder Josh Fleming dazzling in net, posting a .957 save percentage.

Injury report

Sophomore center Luke Misa slammed hard into the boards early in the first period Friday night, hobbling off the ice with the referees' help and going immediately to the locker room. He returned in the second period.

Up Next

Penn State concludes its stretch of six consecutive non-conference contests to open the season on Saturday, as the Nittany Lions are scheduled to finish their two-game set with Canisius. Puck drop is slated for 5 p.m. ET at Pegula Ice Arena.
